events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9��Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ��———————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description: The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.title: Exhibit | De y para el pueblo / By and for the People: Revolutionary Mexican Prints
events.description: The exhibit features highlights from The Bancroft Library's extensive collection of prints. events.title: Exhibit | Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: The Rowell Exhibition Cases, Doe Library, 2nd floor
events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Exhibit | Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.description: In August 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with youth and elders from the nation's Indigenous communities. That expedition, Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here (https://www.ourlifeishere.org), was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. An exhibition in Doe Library's Bernice Layne Brown Gallery gathers reproductions of works made during and after the voyage together with rare books, maps, and photographs drawn from UC Berkeley's own libraries—The Bancroft Library, the Earth Sciences & Map Library, the Environmental Design Library, Morrison Library, and the Main (Gardner) Stacks. Six cases move from the conditions that shaped the voyage, through the journey itself, to the living Marshallese knowledge and youth-led activism that carry it forward. Interpretive text is punctuated by QR codes linking to films, poems, and the organizations at the center of the project. This presentation is part of a series of exhibitions, installations, courses, and public programs across UC Berkeley during the 2026–27 academic year (https://cici.berkeley.edu/komij-mour-ijin-our-life-here-uc-berkeley), guided by the Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative. The exhibition was co-curated by independent curators Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll, in partnership with UC Berkeley librarians Becky Miller and Susan Powell. The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell.

events.title: Exhibition: "Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations"
events.location: Worth Ryder Art Gallery, Anthropology & Art Building, Rm 116
events.description: The Department of German and the Department of Art Practice are excited to announce the opening of Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations, curated by Antonio Somaini with Hannes Bajohr and Sonja Thiel, in dialogue with the France–Berkeley research initiative The Latent Spaces of Culture, and on display at the Worth Ryder Art Gallery. This exhibition examines some of the concealed dimensions of contemporary AI culture — the planetary infrastructures of extraction and computation, the often invisible human labor, the latent vector spaces within which culture is compressed and processed, and the models' hallucinations. Hidden Layers tackles these phenomena from two different perspectives: AI Infrastructures and AI Hallucinations. Featuring works by Nouf Aljowaysir; Gašper and Nina Beguš & Metahaven; Grégory Chatonsky; Kate Crawford & Vladan Joler; Asma Kazmi & Jill Miller; Andrea Khôra; Occitane Lacurie & Barnabé Sauvage; Greg Niemeyer; and Mario Santamaria & Alex Saum-Pascual. events.title: Photography Installation: Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands
events.description: At Giannini Hall, 36 photographs selected from the recently published Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands (Radius Books, © 2026) by Mark Klett and William L. Fox extend the two men's decades-long collaboration tracing the nuclear history of the American West and the broader Pacific sphere. Installed along the building's main hallway, the images move between the physical remains of nuclear testing—bunkers, craters, camera towers reclaimed by jungle—and the everyday textures of Marshallese life: canoe building, weaving, seawalls raised by hand. Paired with archival images from the testing era and drawn from Fox's field notes and essays, the photo essay holds both histories at once: the violence of nuclear history, and the resilience of a culture that continues to inhabit these islands. An artist and curator-led tour with Mark Klett and William L. Fox will take place on September 23 at 4 PM. —Mark Klett is a photographer interested in the intersection of places, history and time. His background includes working as a geologist before turning to photography. Klett has received fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Japan/US Friendship Commission. His work has been exhibited and published widely in the United States and internationally, and is held in over eighty museum collections worldwide. He is the author/co-author of twenty books. Klett is Regents' Professor Emeritus at Arizona State University where he taught for forty years. —Presented by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative in partnership with the Rausser College of Natural Resources.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation. —Image Credit: "The concrete bunker destroyed by the 15-megaton Bravo explosion"2023. events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.description: In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. events.title: Maayan Levy: Toward the development of metabotherapy
events.description: Diet can be a powerful, low-cost lever for treating disease. We previously showed that a ketogenic diet suppresses intestinal tumorigenesis in mouse models of colorectal cancer, mediated by the metabolite beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) acting through HCAR2 to induce the differentiation factor HOPX (Dmitrieva-Posocco et al., Nature, 2022). A follow-up trial in Lynch syndrome patients confirmed that BHB supplementation reduces colonic epithelial proliferation, and a clinical trial for colorectal cancer prevention is now underway (NCT05338307). We asked whether the same metabolite could address a different problem: CAR T cell therapy fails in roughly half of patients and rarely works in solid tumors. Screening diets in mouse lymphoma models, we found that a ketogenic diet- again acting through BHB- potentiates CAR T cell function, fueling the TCA cycle and reprogramming T cells away from exhaustion toward a more cytotoxic state. BHB supplementation alone dramatically improved tumor clearance and survival in lymphoma and solid tumor models, and enhanced T cell metabolic fitness in healthy human volunteers, motivating an ongoing Phase I trial combining BHB with CAR T cell therapy in lymphoma patients. Together, this work suggests that a single, inexpensive dietary metabolite can be repurposed across cancer prevention and immunotherapy to meaningfully improve patient outcomes.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: How to Publish Your Book
events.description: Getting started on your publishing journey can be both daunting and mystifying. Editor Ryan Kendall of Duke University Press provides tools to approach the process with confidence and clarity. Kendall addresses common questions that authors have when approaching the publishing process for the first time. What should you consider when choosing the best press for your work? How do you find the right editor for your project? When is the best time to reach out to an editor, and how should you do it? She offers tips and strategies for navigating the process successfully, including how to increase your chances of placing your manuscript with a press and how to ensure a smooth review. events.title: Lecture | Taking God Seriously in Modern Islamic Politics: Muhammad al-Ghazali (1917–1996), Science, and Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt
events.description: Abstract: In his new book, Mediating God: Muhammad al-Ghazali and the Politics of Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt, Arthur Zárate argues that although God stands at the center of contemporary Muslim moral and political visions, the deity's presence is often neglected in scholarship. This talk explores why that neglect persists and what comes into focus when theological claims are taken seriously in the study of modern Islamic politics. Focusing on the Egyptian theologian Muhammad al-Ghazali (1917–1996), it examines his engagements with modern scientific discourses to show how science became one avenue through which divine presence was encountered and affirmed. Debates over science, it argues, were simultaneously debates about God, and competing understandings of the natural world underwrote competing visions of political and social reform. Ultimately, the talk proposes "activist theology" as a more adequate framework than "Islamism" for understanding al-Ghazali's politics.Bio: Arthur Zárate is a historian of the modern Middle East whose research explores the intersections of politics, science, and theology in modern Islam. He is the author of Mediating God: Muhammad al-Ghazali and the Politics of Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt (Oxford University Press, 2025). His work has appeared in Comparative Studies in Society and History and the Journal of the American Academy of Religion, and is forthcoming in the International Journal of Middle East Studies. He is Assistant Professor of Global Humanities at San José State University, where he teaches in the Honors Humanities Program. He is currently writing a second book on Sufism, spiritual experimentation, and Muslim and Coptic saintly mediation in modern Egypt.

events.title: Life ascending: mechanisms of environmental adaptation in extreme high-elevation Andean mice
events.description: A fundamental goal in evolutionary biology is to understand how the realized niche of a given species has been shaped by local adaptation to extreme environmental conditions, such as those that prevail at range margins. Investigation of local adaptation of montane species at their upper elevational range limits may be especially informative in this effort. Andean leaf-eared mice, Phyllotis vaccarum, live on the summits of 6700 m volcanoes in the Puna de Atacama, far surpassing the known elevational range limits of all other terrestrial vertebrates. Such elevations were previously thought to be uninhabitable by mammals due to severe hypoxia and frigid temperatures. In addition to holding the record as the highest-dwelling mammal, P. vaccarum also has the broadest elevational range, as it is distributed from sea level along the desert coast of northern Chile up to the crest of the Andean Cordillera. Here I report results of physiological and genomic analyses that provided new insights into mechanisms of physiological adaptation to extreme elevations in P. vaccarum. Our genomic analysis also revealed unanticipated dimensions of environmental adaptation related to feeding ecology.

events.title: OEW Seminar - Ming-yen Ho (Internal, BPP JM Candidate)
events.description: Topic: "Picking Winners or Building Them? Central and Local Government Venture Capital in Chinese Semiconductors"Abstract: When does state equity investment in private firms spur productivity growth and innovation? I examine this question by comparing firms backed by local government, central government, and private venture capital funds across six 4-digit sectors in China's semiconductor industry. I find that central government funds invest in more productive firms in the nation, while local governments back local champions that are on average younger, smaller, and less productive. Firm managers' prior educational and employment ties to local VC fund managers predict local government investment. Event studies suggest however that local-backed firms experience larger post-investment gains of about 27\% in revenue productivity relative to private VC and central government invested firms. Local government fund managers are more likely to enter the board of their portfolio firms, adding directors with graduate degrees, foreign education, and technical expertise. Local VCs participate more in management relative to central government VCs because they hold a smaller portfolio and are geographically closer to their portfolio companies. Corporate governance is associated with 42\% of the observed local-central differences in productivity effects, while differences in invested money does not explain the gap. The findings suggest that decentralized government venture capital can promote growth in high-tech sectors by providing capital and managerial resources to less established firms.

events.title: Differential Geometry Seminar: Desingularizations of Conformally Kaehler, Einstein Orbifolds
events.description: Speaker: Claude LeBrun, Stony BrookIn this talk, I will discuss the following result, which was proved in joint work with Tristan Ozuch.Suppose we are given a sequence of smooth compact oriented Einstein 4-manifolds with fixed positive Einstein constant that Gromov-Hausdorff converges to a 4-dimensional Einstein orbifold. Suppose, moreover, that the limit metric is Hermitian with respect to some integrable complex structure on the limit orbifold, and that this orbifold has at least one singular point. Finally, suppose that every gravitational instanton that bubbles off from the sequence is anti-self-dual. Then, far out in the sequence, all the given Einstein manifolds are actually Kaehler-Einstein. As a consequence, the limit orbifold is also Kaehler-Einstein, and must in fact be one of the orbifold limits classified by Odaka, Spotti, and Sun.

events.title: Two Provinces, Two Paths: Canada and the Independence Debate in Alberta and Quebec
events.description: The question of whether to remain in Canada or seek independence will play a major role in upcoming provincial elections in Alberta and Quebec. Proponents of independence in each province offer different arguments rooted in unique regional histories. However, they also share a sense of alienation from "Canadian" culture and national identity. This panel will discuss the recent rise of sovereigntist and independentist politics in each province. What factors are causing this resurgence of sovereigntist sentiment? How are proponents of Canadian federalism responding to their grievances? And how are international developments, including heightened Canada-US tensions, shaping the trajectory of these movements?About the PanelistsMartha Hall Findlay is the Director and Palmer Chair in Public Policy, School of Public Policy, University of Calgary; a member of the Expert Group on Canada-U.S. Relations. A former two-term member of Parliament, she served on the Official Opposition shadow cabinet as well as on committees concerned with trade, finance, and public works. Before politics, she worked as an international corporate lawyer and senior executive for Suncor Energy and the Canada West Foundation. She is currently overseeing the official Alberta government report on the economic impact to the province of leaving Canada.Philippe Gervais is the Vice-President, Communications and Institutional Relations for McGill University. He has more than 30 years of experience in public relations, crisis management, government relations, and public opinion research. He has worked for both the Federal and Quebec provincial governments, and he has advised political campaigns at all levels of government across Canada.Kristina Michaud was elected to the Canadian House of Commons at age 26, becoming one of the youngest federal representatives ever elected. From 2019 to 2025, she served as a Bloc Québécois MP and as the party's critic for Public Safety and Climate Change. Originally from eastern Quebec, she now works as a political analyst and commentator for various television and radio programs and writes in La Presse.Martin Pelletier is a financial columnist, author, senior portfolio manager, and investment fund manager. He is a recognized market strategist, regularly contributing to Canada's Financial Post and appearing in Canadian and US media to provide insights on topics including equity and bond markets, monetary and fiscal policy, and oil, gas, and commodities.

events.title: Arash Afraz: How Does the Activity of Visually Responsive Neurons Generate Visual Perception?
events.description: We typically study the mechanistic underpinnings of vision by observing how "visually responsive" neurons in the brain respond to and encode visual stimuli. While highly informative, this approach is indirect and correlational and does not reveal the causal contribution of these neurons to visual perception. In this talk, I will introduce a new methodology, Perceptography, that quantitatively and graphically determines the causal role of cortical neurons in perception. I will then propose a new roadmap and theoretical framework for understanding visual perception.

events.title: Astronomy Colloquium - Kyle Kremer (UCSD)
events.description: Title: Globular Clusters: Astronomical Factories of Gravitational-wave and Electromagnetic TransientsAbstract: Globular clusters host robust populations of white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes, creating unique environments where dynamical interactions drive the formation of a wide range of astrophysical sources. In recent years, these systems have emerged as key sites for the assembly of merging black hole binaries, connecting directly to the gravitational-wave sources observed by the LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA network. In this talk, I will synthesize recent advances in our understanding of compact object populations in globular clusters and the dynamical processes that govern their evolution. I will highlight how these processes shape the formation of gravitational-wave sources and connect to a broader landscape of cluster-driven phenomena, including black hole–star binaries, radio pulsars, and fast radio bursts. As the new field of multi-messenger astronomy continues to expand, globular clusters are emerging as powerful laboratories for compact object astrophysics, providing a unified framework for interpreting both gravitational-wave and electromagnetic transients.Host: Dan Kasen

events.title: Ned Wingreen: Collective dynamics in B cell affinity maturation
events.description: In the humoral immune response, B cells that produce high-affinity antibodies are generated through a Darwinian evolutionary process called affinity maturation. Affinity maturation, which takes place in germinal centers (GC), is driven by cycles of selection (mediated by T cells), division, and hypermutation of B cells. Recently, it was found that the T cells themselves also exhibit dynamic behavior throughout the course of the GC reaction, undergoing affinity-dependent proliferation. A model suggests that this reciprocal stimulation enforces a robust "homeostatic" regulation of the relative number of B cells and T cells in the GC, leading to a constant ratio of GC lymphocytes. But the model also points to a problem: the high mutation rate of GC B cells can lead to "backsliding" of affinity. The proposed solution – a fitness-dependent mutation rate – has been experimentally verified, and has implications beyond B cell affinity maturation.Division(s): INFORMAL SEMINAR

events.title: Stone Center for Environmental Stewardship Lecture: Kevin Washburn (Chickasaw), "Tribal Co-Management, Landback, and Indigenous Cosmology"
events.description: Kevin K. Washburn is a Professor of Law at the University of California, Berkeley School of Law. He is part of the advisory group for the UC Berkeley Stone Center for Environmental Stewardship. Professor Washburn's research explores the way federal law and policy works, and sometimes fails, for tribal nations in the United States. In this talk, he will explore the complicated relationships between tribes, conservation advocates, and land conservation policies. He will discuss how, on the one hand, tribes sometimes resent conservation groups because their actions can infringe on tribal sovereignty. On the other hand, conservation groups are sometimes concerned that tribes won't exercise their sovereignty in ways consistent with the goals of the conservation movement. Washburn will describe the dramatic improvement in these relationships in recent years, and the reasons such trust is well-placed and should continue to grow. The special seminar will be held in 132 Mulford Hall and via Zoom. There will be a special reception following from 4:30pm - 5:30pm in the lawn outside Mulford Hall.

events.description: Speaker: Yongwook Paik (KAIST) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: Drawing on insights from the co-authored book The Korean Startup Ecosystem: Past, Present, and Future, this lecture offers an insider's perspective on Korea's evolving innovation landscape. It traces the nation's transition from a conglomerate-driven growth model to an innovation-led economy, highlighting the critical interplay between venture capital, government policy, conglomerates, and entrepreneurial culture. The talk demonstrates how Korea's global cultural powerhouses—including K-pop, K-dramas, and K-beauty—are strategic outcomes of this systematically built ecosystem. Through a comparative lens, the lecture examines the institutional features that distinguish the Korean and U.S. markets across key dimensions like financing, risk tolerance, and policy intervention. It concludes by outlining strategic implications for global founders, investors, and policymakers, followed by an interactive Q&A session. The English edition of The Korean Startup Ecosystem: Past, Present, and Future is available for download for free at the following link for those who are interested: https://bit.ly/4tNQSAJ (https://bit.ly/4tNQSAJ) Speaker Bio: Professor Paik is a tenured professor at the KAIST College of Business and an affiliated professor at the KAIST College of AI. His research explores the intersection of entrepreneurship, innovation, strategy, institutions, and public policy. He serves as an editorial review board member and referee for numerous top-tier academic journals in his field, and his research has appeared in premier publications such as the Strategic Management Journal, Organization Science, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal, and the Journal of Economics & Management Strategy. Before joining KAIST in 2018, Professor Paik served as an assistant professor at the University of Southern California's Marshall School of Business and Washington University in St. Louis's Olin Business School. He holds a Ph.D. in Economics from the University of California, Berkeley. Prior to his academic career, he was a patent attorney at the leading South Korean law firm Kim & Chang, advising both multinational corporations and entrepreneurial ventures. A seasoned advisor in the innovation ecosystem, Professor Paik cofounded the venture capital firm TBW Investment, which was later acquired via M&A. He is a Board Member of Hanyang Eng Co., a major KOSDAQ-listed semiconductor and high-tech facility engineering firm, and currently serves as a policy advisor to South Korea's National Economic Advisory Council.

events.title: Julia Nelsen | Translation as Rediscovery: Introducing Fausta Cialente
events.description: Fausta Cialente (1898-1994) was one of Italy's most significant twentieth-century authors. Though she won critical acclaim—albeit late in her career—Cialente remained overlooked for decades until the recent rerelease of her literary works in Italian. A Very Cold Winter (Transit Books, 2026) is the first of Cialente's novels to be rediscovered in translation by Julia Nelsen. In conversation with Professor Mairi McLaughlin, Nelsen will discuss her translation of A Very Cold Winter, situate Cialente within the broader landscape of modern Italian and international literature, and explore the role translators play in recovering unsung voices.Julia Nelsen translates between English and Italian. In addition to her work on Fausta Cialente, her essays and translations have appeared in journals including Circumference, Two Lines,Firmament, and the Chicago Review. Alongside translation, she currently serves as policy analyst for the UCLA Academic Senate, and previously taught writing and literature courses and managed international partnerships between Europe and the West Coast. She holds a PhD in Comparative Literature from UC Berkeley and a Masters in European languages from the University of Milan.Mairi McLaughlin is Professor and Chair in the Department of French and an Affiliated Member of the Departments of Linguistics and Italian Studies at UC Berkeley. She specializes in French/Romance Linguistics and in Translation Studies and has published extensively on language contact, the language of the media, and journalistic and literary translation. Her books have been published by Garnier, Legenda, and Oxford University Press, and she has published articles in journals such as French Studies, The Italianist, Langages, META, Perspectives, and Target.If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: This Death is Not One
events.description: In conversation with Salar Mameni, Associate Professor of Ethnic Studies at UC Berkeley The publication of The Right to Maim by Jasbir K. Puar in 2017 was critical to advancing studies on disability and to further articulating how the body figures in the nexus of capacity and debility across racializing and extractive neoliberal lines. It offered a complex and rigorous anti-capitalist account of disability that is useful to both scholarly work and political and social organizing. However, despite its paramount contribution to scholarship on Palestine, delivered by its scathing analysis of the Israeli biopolitical policy—its right to maim—in how the injured Palestinian body is produced and reproduced, its reception was difficult, and hard to stomach. It cohered a political logic in writing before it was visibly evident on the ground. In the moment and aftermath of the Great March of Return (2018-19), Puar's offerings became much harder to ignore, as the event crystallized a mass maiming campaign of Palestinian protesters inside the edges of the militarized borders of Gaza.This Death is Not One (Bilnaes 2026) is the first translation into Arabic of the chapter "Will Not Let Die": Debilitation and Inhuman Biopolitics in Palestine, alongside the postscript of The Right to Maim. Not simply a reissue of previously published work or a translation, This Death is Not One includes a new preface from Jasbir K. Puar revisiting the right to maim from within this moment of genocide in Gaza that interrogates the new vectors of living and dying under settler-colonialism, and how maiming, in fact, speaks of extermination; an introduction by Nasser Abourahme reflecting on the book's stakes in the present and its reception in the past, alongside searing analysis of genocide in excess of the law, and what this reveals and forecloses in how we understand the juridical body and militancy in the wake of Zionism; and original drawings by Xaytun Ennasr that inscribe a relation between land and body mapped through cosmological patterns tracing the relation between martyrs, who are referred to as moons, and the moon, a symbol for martyrdom in Palestine.

events.title: "Endangered Palestinian Memories" Critical Palestinian Geographies Graduate Seminar
events.description: This event is a brown bag discussion with Saad Amira (al-Quds Bard College) and Samar Awaad hosted by the Critical Palestinian Geographies Reading Group (CPG Reading Group). UC Berkeley graduate students across departments are welcome to attend. The seminar highlights the works of contemporary Palestinian scholars, exposing students to emerging spatial and geographic methods of story telling, with emphasis on political ecology, geographies of movement, and foodways during war. During the seminar, Amira and Awaad will lead a roundtable discussion on readings such as Awaad's "Culinary Traditions in the Jerusalem Countryside: Communities Displaced by the 1948 Nakba, and Those Who Remained," and Amira's "The Traitor Wears a Fez": Palestine and the Stories of a Mailman Before the Nakba" This is the first meeting of the CPG Reading Group for Fall semester. Contact Mariam Aref Mahmoud mariamaref@berkeley.edu and Estrella Pacheco estrellapacheco@berkeley.edu (mailto:estrellapacheco@berkeley.edu) to find out more about upcoming events. Samar Awaad is a chef, storyteller, culinary artist, and researcher, where she specializes in Palestinian food culture. She founded Qam7 Wa Zeit (http://www.qam7wzeit.com), a participatory initiative sharing her culinary research while advocating for food sovereignty and documenting the links between cuisine, memory, and the Nakba. Her research interests include food pathways, political ecology, settler colonialism, and gender in Palestine with a deep commitment to preserving Palestinian culture and heritage. She currently serves as Treasurer on the Board of the Khalil Sakakini Cultural Center in Ramallah. She is a member of global and local storytelling and research initiatives, including the Endangered Palestinian Memories Initiative. She holds a contemporary culinary diploma, an MPH from Emory University, and a B.Sc. from the University of San Francisco. Find her on Social Media: Instagram: @Samar.Awaad (http://instagram.com/Samar.Awaad), and @Qam7_wa_zeit (http://instagram.com/Qam7_wa_zeit). Facebook: Qam7 wa Zeit (https://www.facebook.com/qam7wazeit). Website: www.qam7wzeit.com (http://www.qam7wzeit.com) Saad Amira is an academic and curator who leads the Urban Studies and Spatial Practices Bachelor degree program at Al Quds Bard College in Palestine. His work lies at the intersection of oral history, critical geography, settler colonialism, and political ecology. Amira is the founder and director of the "Endangered Palestinian Memories" initiative (www.palmemories.com (http://www.palmemories.com)), through which he has documented 150 oral testimonies, archived and digitized dozens of family albums and personal archives, and utilized interactive storytelling to present this colorful work. Sherine Ebadi is a PhD candidate in the Department of Geography at UC Berkeley. Her research looks at immigration governance through the lens of legal geography to explore how visa programs are regulated relation to conflicts and war. Ebadi's work focuses on the lived experiences of migration and displacement of Afghan and Iraqi translators for the US military, and the social and psychological aftermaths of serving with the US military in exchange for the promise of US citizenship. Find out more (https://geography.berkeley.edu/sherine-ebadi).

events.title: Architecting Human Power in the Age of AI (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) In a workplace increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, many professional development sessions focus on what tools to learn next. This session takes a different approach. It focuses on what AI cannot replace: the distinctly human ability to decide what matters, what you stand for, and how you choose to show up. This is not an AI skills workshop. It is an invitation to become more intentional about your human advantage. As AI expands what is possible, our opportunity is not to compete with technology, but to become clearer about what makes us uniquely valuable and then use AI to amplify it. By knowing what deserves your attention, what guides your decisions, and how you want to show up, you can engage AI with greater clarity and intention rather than simply using it to do more, faster. Led by Executive Coach and former Fortune 500 Marketing Leader Sarah Peterson, this interactive 90-minute session combines provocative ideas, personal reflection, and practical application. Drawing on her own journey from high-achieving executive through burnout and realignment, Sarah introduces her Leadership DNA Pyramid, a framework inspired by the strategy used to build iconic brands and adapted to help individuals navigate change, complexity, and an increasingly AI-enabled workplace. Participants will work with three dimensions of the broader Leadership DNA framework that become increasingly important as AI accelerates how we work: Priority, Value, and Presence. They will make three intentional choices: one priority to focus their energy, one value to guide their decisions, and one quality of presence to embody in how they work and lead. They will then move from insight to implementation by identifying the behaviors and actions that will bring those choices to life over the next 90 days. Together, these choices create a personal compass for working and leading with greater clarity and intention in an AI-enabled world.Learning Outcomes: –Recognize their distinctly human contribution as a source of advantage in an AI-enabled workplace. –Define one priority that deserves their focus and energy over the next 90 days. –Identify one value to intentionally guide their choices and decisions. –Choose one quality ofpresence they want to embody in how they lead, collaborate, and contribute. –Turn Priority, Value, and Presence into Practice by defining concrete behaviors and actions they can begin applying immediately.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as this virtual workshop date draws near.

events.title: A Conversation with Senator Lisa Murkowski
events.location: Hertz Hall, 101 Cross-Sproul Path, Berkeley, CA 94704
events.description: Join the Goldman School of Public Policy for an in-person conversation with U.S. Senator Lisa Murkowski, one of the Senate's most independent voices and a leading voice on political leadership and bipartisan governance in an era of deep political polarization. Over more than two decades in the U.S. Senate, Murkowski has helped shape some of the nation's most consequential policy debates while earning a reputation for independence, institutional stewardship, and a willingness to challenge presidents and party leaders alike. Drawing on her memoir, Far From Home: An Alaskan Senator Faces the Extreme Climate of Washington, D.C., she will reflect on the defining moments of her career, the evolution of American politics, and what it means to govern with conviction in a divided democracy. The discussion will explore Murkowski's journey from Alaska to the U.S. Senate, her historic 2010 write-in reelection campaign, and the transformation of American politics from the Tea Party era to today. As institutions face growing public scrutiny and political divisions continue to deepen, she will offer a candid perspective on the challenges confronting American democracy, the future of bipartisan governance, and the role of political leadership and public service in sustaining democratic institutions.This event is part of the Goldman School of Public Policy's Democracy Book Club series, which features authors whose work enriches our understanding of democracy by examining the institutions, policies, and civic traditions that shape democratic life. —Lisa Murkowski is a third-generation Alaskan proudly serving as the state's senior senator. Since joining the U.S. Senate in 2002, she has earned a reputation for her collaborative approach and her ability to work across the aisle to reach commonsense solutions. She and her husband live in Anchorage, Alaska, where they raised their two sons.David C. Wilson is the dean of the Goldman School of Public Policy and a Professor of Public Policy at the University of California, Berkeley. A leading scholar of political psychology and public opinion, his research explores race, democracy, and political behavior. Before joining Berkeley, he held senior academic leadership roles at the University of Delaware and worked with the Gallup Polling Organization. Wilson is also a U.S. Army veteran who served 19 years in the Army Reserves, including tours during Operations Desert Storm and Iraqi Freedom.

events.title: Dr. Os Keyes, "The Life and Death of the Life and Death Committee"
events.description: The story of the Seattle Artificial Kidney Center's "Life and Death Committee", or "God Squad" - a lay panel tasked with deciding who received treatment, and correspondingly, lived and died - is a classic one within both the history of medicine and the history of bioethics. But much of what we know about it, how we conceptualize it, and correspondingly, the lessons we draw from it, is, Dr. Keyes argues, false. Drawing on newly-discovered archival resources, this talk revisits the shifting function and viability of the Life and Death Committee over time, demonstrating that its purpose was broader than often-conceived, and that its' eventual fate calls into question many of the conclusions historians have drawn about it. RSVP: https://forms.gle/HsSUUoqqdW8uwicq5 (https://forms.gle/HsSUUoqqdW8uwicq5)Os Keyes is a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Massachusetts Lowell. Their scholarship in the history of medicine focuses on the structure of decision-making in spaces from kidney dialysis to gender-affirming care, and has been published in venues including the Bulletin of the History of Medicine.

events.title: Karen Van Dyck | The Greek Alphabet in America
events.description: The history of Greek assimilation in America can be traced in the slow erasure of Greek as a symbol of difference and indecipherability, the most recognizably unrecognizable alphabet – "It's all Greek to me!" By the 1930s and 1940s, looking and sounding different led to the substitution not only of different faces and races, but of typefaces. If, during the mid-century, nations were intent on keeping things as separate as possible and popular fiction and film made sure Greeks and Greek in America were erased and the Latin alphabet won out, in the 1970s and 1980s, a more cosmopolitan moment, Greek's indecipherability became the grounds for literary experimentation and, particularly for women writers, a "politics of transliteration." The idea that Ancient Greek and English were superior to Modern Greek was replaced by a multilingual understanding that more than one language and alphabet could creatively coexist.Karen Van Dyck, Kimon A. Doukas Professor of Modern Greek Literature in the Classics Department at Columbia University, works on questions of translation, migration, gender and classical reception. She is the founding director of Hellenic Studies and an active member of the Institute of Comparative Literature and Society and the Istanbul and Athens Global Centers. Her translations includeThe Greek Poets: Homer to the Present (Norton, 2010), Austerity Measures: The New Greek Poetry(2016, Penguin) and Margarita Liberaki's Three Summers (NYRB, 2019)If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Nina Buchmann in Psychology & Econ Lunch Seminar
events.description: Presenting: "Rejection Regard"Abstract: We define and test a novel demand-side explanation for low female employment, which we call rejection regard: employers' concern for the welfare of rejected applicants. Where jobs are scarce, and men are expected to provide for their households, an employer may treat rejecting a man as more costly than rejecting an equally or better qualified woman. We test for rejection regard in a field experiment with employers in Egypt who are choosing applicants from our applicant pool in return for wage subsidies. We experimentally vary employers' perceptions of rejected applicants' welfare by randomizing applicants into an outside-option treatment: a job offer from the research team if they are rejected by the employer subjects. We test whether (i) employers are less likely to hire applicants who have been offered the outside option and (ii) the outside option reduces the gender gap in hiring.

events.description: The stationmaster in Zvare, a remote valley town in Georgia, is bracing himself for change. Soon the high-speed trains of the New Silk Road will race through the old train station built in 1890, during the period of Tsar Nicholas II. The Chinese-led construction project is blasting through the mountains to construct the world's third-longest tunnel, and this brings the opposition of the local residents, who do not want their land to be spoiled. events.title: Student Probability/PDE Seminar: The KPZ Fixed Point and the Directed Landscape III
events.description: Speaker: Fraydoun Rezakhanlou, UC BerkeleyThe KPZ equation was proposed in 1986 by Kardar, Parisi and Zhang as a model for stochastic growth interfaces. It is conjectured that many stochastic height functions will converge to KPZ fixed point under 1:2:3 scaling. Simultaneous construction of KPZ fixed points for different initial data yields the directed landscape. In these talks I will give an overview of the existing results for the KPZ fixed points and their associated directed landscape.

events.title: The Smart Curb: How Cities Can Control Their Most Valuable Asset
events.description: Gene Oh, CEO of Tranzito, will present The Smart Curb: How Cities Can Control Their Most Valuable Asset at the ITS Berkeley Transportation Seminar on Sept. 25, 2026. Join us for cookie hour at 2:30 in the ITS Library, hosted by TRANSOC.Abstract: The curb is the most contested real estate in all city urban cores, and it's allocated to whoever arrives first. Ride-hail, on-demand delivery, and shared micromobility have layered ever growing demand onto a finite supply legislated by multiple agencies with overlapping jurisdiction and objectives. The resulting costs are not paid by the operators generating them, but by bus riders stuck behind double-parked pickups and corridor communities absorbing the emissions - a transfer from the haves to the have nots. Pricing and enforcement alone cannot close the gap, and autonomy will only widen it: AVs need curb space that is predictable and reservable. Until this is solved, AVs cannot scale. The solution is to grow supply. Gene Oh will present a "stacking" approach - a single linear foot serving several use cases across the day, once exclusive curb contracts give way to dynamic, networked regulation - and argue that it takes a property manager of the curb, arbitrating access on behalf of public agencies.Bio: Gene Oh is the founder and CEO of Tranzito, with over 20 years in new mobility. He leads the company's strategy to help cities actively manage the curb, the most contested space on the street, positioning Tranzito as the property manager of the public right-of-way. Gene's view is that as ride-hailing, shared micromobility, delivery, and autonomy drive up demand for curbspace, agencies need to manage private operators rather than compete with them, keeping public transit as the backbone of the system. Under his leadership, Tranzito grew from secure bike parking into citywide smart infrastructure, including the $500M+ LA STAP program (3,000+ smart bus shelters and 200 urban panels) and the 97-hub LADOT Integrated Mobility Hubs program, where he serves as Executive Director. Gene treats this infrastructure as a connected network of smart-city nodes, tied together by Tranzito's open CurbOS platform, and designed the public-private partnership models that let agencies partner with private operators at the LADOT and Caltrain SF mobility hubs. His next focus is smart loading zones and dynamic curb management, which combine sensing, digital signage, policy, enforcement, and field operations into a single managed program launching through the IMH network. Gene specializes in strategic design, stakeholder management, and business development, and keeps Tranzito self-funded to stay focused on public benefit.

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Phillip Milner, Associate Professor, Cornell UniversityTaming the Halogens using Metal-Organic Frameworks Fluorinated molecules represent a double-edged sword: they are present in 30% of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals, but are also persistent organic pollutants of growing concern due to their long environmental lifetimes and high global warming potentials. Herein, we will discuss how porous materials such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) present a unique opportunity to capture and utilize fluorinated (and other halogenated) building blocks to design new catalysts and reagents for applications in the synthesis of complex molecules. We will first focus on catalytic strategies that leverage MOFs bearing metal-halogen bonds as recyclable catalysts for challenging reactions such as halogen exchange, C-H functionalization, and contra-thermodynamic alkene isomerization. Then, we will discuss how MOFs can be used to directly capture fluorinated gases to allow for their safe handling as solid reagents, enabling a diverse range of thermal, photochemical, and electrochemical reactions. Last, we will show how ozone-depleting and greenhouse gases can be captured from realistic mixtures and employed directly as building blocks for fluorochemical synthesis.The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.title: Music Studies Colloquium: Hilde Roos (University of Stellenbosch)
events.description: Staging Settler Society: Opera Production in NamibiaHilde Roos (University of Stellenbosch) This presentation examines opera production in Namibia from 1960 onwards. Its primary focus is on opera production before Namibia's independence in 1990, although some attention will also be given to developments after independence. Drawing on the framework of settler colonialism and archival materials, the presentation reconstructs a largely undocumented cultural history. Building on the work of Patrick Wolfe and Lorenzo Veracini, it conceptualises settler colonialism as an ongoing structure and analyses opera not simply as an imported European art form, but as part of the cultural infrastructure that sustained settler society in Namibia during the period of South African occupation. Produced under the auspices of the Arts Association (AA) of Windhoek and later the South West African Performing Arts Council (SWAPAC), more than 25 opera productions were staged in Windhoek during South African occupation. These productions featured artists from Namibia and Europe, as well as visiting companies from South Africa. The presentation will furthermore investigate how opera functioned in relation to racial segregation, land occupation, and institutional life, asking how performance practices contributed to the formation of settler identity and the normalisation of apartheid within Namibian society. During South African occupation, the settler community in Windhoek consisted primarily of Afrikaans- and German-speaking populations. Attention will be given both to the prominence of European repertoire and to the archival silences surrounding indigenous Namibian participation. By situating operatic activity within broader systems of governance and cultural power, while remaining attentive to the lingering memory of the genocide of the Herero and Nama peoples (1904–1908), this paper engages with the role of so-called high culture in colonial contexts and contributes to emerging intersections between opera studies and settler colonial theory. A reception will follow.

events.title: Establishing Chronology in Tibetan art: a Study of Taklung Paintings
events.description: This lecture addresses chronology in early Tibetan art. Dr. Casey highlights over a decade of research on a group of approximately 100 paintings from Taklung and Riwoche monasteries in Tibet. The main purpose of the study has been to establish a reliable foundation for assigning dates to Taklung paintings. The Taklung painting corpus particularly lends itself to the task of building a chronology. Almost three-quarters of the paintings bear inscriptions with chronological implications. Using visual lineages (the succession of teachers represented in the top, side, and, occasionally, the bottom registers of paintings), inscriptions, narrative scenes (in which principal structures in the Taklung Monastery compound may be linked to specific dates), and style analysis, the speaker identifies fundamental parameters that help to create firm chronological designations for these c. twelfth to mid-sixteenth century paintings. Tibetan textual historians and historians of Tibetan religion will appreciate the evidentiary underpinnings of the chronology put forth. And anyone interested in understanding the history of Tibetan Buddhist culture will appreciate the wealth of information contained in these remarkable, often very well preserved works of art.Jane Casey is an art historian specializing in Himalayan art. Educated in the History of Science (A.B.) and in Fine Arts (A.M. and Ph.D.) at Harvard University, since 1991 she has worked as an independent art historian, curating exhibitions at The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York and at Casa Asia, Barcelona. She is a Guest Professor at the Zhejiang University Center for Buddhist Art in Hangzhou, and a Research Fellow in Tibetan Art at the Palace Museum in Beijing. She resides in Marlborough, New Zealand.

events.title: Rethinking the Republican Interregnum in South Vietnam (1964-1967)
events.location: Lewis Latimer Room, The Faculty Club
events.description: Speaker: Y Thien Nguyen (Assistant Professor of Asian Pacific Studies, California State University, Dominguez Hills) This talk reframes the widely disparaged interregnum period in South Vietnam (1963-1967) as a critical juncture in which civil society and non-state actors actively shaped the political realm, contributing to the rise and fall of governments and eventually to the emergence of the Second Republic of Vietnam (1967-1975). In addition to exploring the routinization of oppositional politics, it charts the development of a dominant discourse of "true democracy and freedom" which conditioned the actions and political language of state and non-state actors as well as popular apprehensions of political legitimacy.This talk is funded byThe Republic of Vietnam Endowment for Vietnamese Studies,made possible by the generous donation fromMr. and Mrs. Nguyễn Đức Cường.Speaker bio: Y Thien Nguyen specializes in the study of modern Vietnam and Vietnamese refugee experiences. His work examines the ideological, political, and institutional connectivity between the Republic of Vietnam and Vietnamese America. He received his PhD in Sociology from Northwestern University and previously served as a Teaching Fellow in South East Asian History at the University of Leeds, UK and a Research Associate for the US-Vietnam Research Center at the University of Oregon. He is currently completing his book manuscript entitled Diasporic Legacies: The Making and Remaking of Vietnamese Anticommunism. He has published multiple academic works on the Republic of Vietnam, the Vietnamese diaspora, and various sociopolitical issues related to the Vietnamese American community. Beyond his immediate academic duties, Dr. Nguyen also serves on the Board of Director for the US-Vietnam Research Center, the Boat People SOS Center for Community Advancement, and offers consulting and grant writing services to Vietnamese American non-profit organizations.

events.title: Film Screening: Taming the Garden
events.description: With astonishing cinematic style, Taming the Gardentracks the surreal uprooting of ancient trees from their Georgian locales. With each removal, tensions flare between workers and villagers. Some see financial incentives—new roads, handsome fees—while others angrily mourn the loss of what was assumed to be an immovable monolith of their town's collective history and memory. With a steady and shrewdly observant eye, Salomé Jashi documents a single man's power over Earth's natural gardens: how majestic living artifacts of a country's identity can so effortlessly become uprooted by individuals with no connection to the nature they claim as their own.

events.title: Georgian Cinema Now Symposium—Activism in Authoritarian Times: The Republic of Georgia as a Case Study
events.description: Free and open to the public, this symposium offers an invaluable introduction to the current political and cultural context in the Republic of Georgia. Guest speakers will offer a range of perspectives, from analyzing the political situation under the current Georgian Dream government to sharing experiences from the field as activists on the frontlines fighting for civil liberties, especially freedom of speech and LGBTQ+ rights. We will hear from journalists, media commentators, cultural historians, teachers, and independent filmmakers on the challenges and threats they face as a result of the Georgian government's introduction of the Foreign Agent Law—censorship, arrests, trials, and imprisonment—and parallels with broader global threats to democracy. The symposium will feature two panels, "Modern Georgia's Political History" and "Reports from the Field by Georgian Independent Filmmakers." In between, we will screen two recent documentaries on the impact of the current authoritarian government.

events.title: [UC Berkeley campus premiere] A Job in the Shade: The Emily Vasquez Story
events.location: Chevron Auditorium, International House (2299 Piedmont Avenue, Berkeley, CA)
events.description: About the Film This inspiring documentary chronicles the extraordinary life of Judge Emily Vasquez, the first Latina appointed in 2001 to the Sacramento County Superior Court in its history. Through intimate interviews with family members, friends, colleagues, and mentees, A Job in the Shade explores Judge Vasquez's remarkable journey from the agricultural fields of California to the courtroom. The film highlights a lifetime of service, leadership, and mentorship while demonstrating how education can transform lives and expand opportunities for future generations. Through her strength of character, hard work, and keen intellect, Judge Vasquez defied the odds. Judge Vasquez has made it look easy with her many accomplishments but her many achievements did not come easy (not when you one of the first and come from humble beginnings). Her parents were poor, immigrant farmworkers from Mexico. As a child, she lived in labor camps and worked in the fields when school was not in session to help supplement the family income. She spent her early years living in tents and one-bedroom shacks with everyone, including her parents sleeping in the same room as her siblings. The bathroom was an outhouse. From her childhood in California's Central Valley, working alongside her poor farmworker parents, to her groundbreaking legal career, Judge Vasquez's story is one of resilience, determination, and the transformative power of education.Presented by:UC Berkeley Division of Equity & Inclusion Latinx Thriving Initiatives The Spencer Group In partnership with:University Development and Alumni Relations (UDAR) UC Berkeley College of Letters & Science Cal Alumni Association

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. The Magnes generates new knowledge and understanding of Jewish cultures with and for its academic and public audiences through its collections-based exhibitions and programs. events.title: Film Screening: English Teacher and Bakhmaro 2050
events.description: Georgia's movement to teach English to schoolchildren is the backdrop for this beautifully observed documentary about an English teacher, Bradley Nelson from South Africa, and his experiences in a remote Georgian village, Sajijao. There he encounters both the warmth of the local community, and some resistance to the "linguistic revolution" as a national initiative. A finely drawn portrait of a critical moment in Georgia's development as an independent nation in the post-Soviet era. Before construction begins on a major housing complex in Bakhmaro, a resort town in western Georgia that travelers visit for the special healing properties of the air, filmmaker Anka Gujabidze observes life as it is. Employing superimpositions and dissolves, this documentary portrait ruminates on the changes that will come with construction and what will be lost.

events.title: Film Screening: An Incomplete Day in the History of Georgia 10.06.93.
events.description: Derived solely from video recordings of Georgian parliamentary proceedings on June 10, 1993, when Eduard Shevardnadze was the head of state, An Incomplete Day in the History of Georgia presents the debate surrounding the introduction of Georgia's national currency coupon to replace the Russian ruble. Members of parliament voice their concerns from the floor, questioning the resolutions presented by the vice prime minister and president of the National Bank. How should the country's leaders proceed in light of domestic challenges such as starvation, fuel shortages, budget shortfalls, and rapid inflation? Viewed with hindsight, this document from the early days of Georgian independence reminds us how fragile the democratic process can be.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Free Bakry-Emery Calculus
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Martin Peev, University of OxfordWe prove a free probabilistic Bakry-Emery criterion for the Poincare Inequality and Logarithmic Sobolev Inequality. Our approach relies on a noncommutative extension of the Carre du Champ operator and its iteration to the setting of Free Probability. I will show how one can formulate a positive curvature condition in terms of direct formulae involving th potential of a Gibbs state. I will then present how one can employ these abstract curvature conditions to prove a (non-universal) free poincare Inequality and a Logarithmic Sobolev Inequality in this setting. I will particularly stress where classical methods have to be adapted in order to accommodate the tensorial nature of the free derivative. This talk is based on joint work with Ajay Chandra and Masha Gordina.
