events.title: Dissertation Talk: Graph Database Repair
events.description: Graph databases support applications ranging from question answering to digital twins, but errors in them can undermine downstream applications. Although schema validation can detect these errors, it cannot determine the correct repair, and existing repair systems are difficult to evaluate systematically. This dissertation talk presents a unified framework for generating controlled schema violations and using them to diagnose and compare repair systems. It also introduces an LLM-based agentic repair system that selectively provides access to an external corpus. Together, these contributions provide controlled methods for evaluating graph repair and studying when external evidence is useful.

events.title: Ashok Prasad: Cell Shapes and Cytoskeletal Networks: Morphological Analysis of Cellular Identity
events.description: Cell morphology offers a powerful and relatively underutilized lens for understanding cell state and behavior. While transcriptomic and proteomic profiling have revolutionized our capacity to characterize cells, quantitative morphological features can provide complementary insights into cell state and function. In this talk, I will present some of our work demonstrating that cells can be robustly classified using microscopy images and morphological metrics, explore some of the links between cell and nuclear morphology and discuss our current efforts to develop morphological representations of the actin cytoskeleton and other dynamic polymer networks using simulations. This work contributes to a broader vision of morphology-based phenotyping and modeling as a bridge between structure and function in living systems.Division(s): INFORMAL SEMINAR

events.title: TAC Seminar - Pranav Nagarajan (Caltech)
events.description: Title: Black Holes in Wide Binaries from Gaia: Tests of Formation ModelsAbstract:Gaia astrometry has opened a new window on compact object binaries, leading to the discovery of three non-interacting black holes with low-mass stellar companions in au-scale orbits. The extreme mass ratios of these wide binaries challenge standard isolated binary evolution models. From hierarchical triples to cluster dynamics, numerous alternative formation channels have been proposed for these "Gaia BHs." In this talk, I will show how survey data can be combined with targeted follow-up observations to constrain these theoretical models and understand how Gaia BHs form and evolve.Host: TBD

events.title: Pariroo Rattan | Technologies of Populism: The Moral Politics of Digitization in India's Informal Economy
events.description: A talk by Pariroo Rattan (https://sociology.northwestern.edu/people/faculty/visiting/pariroo-rattan.html), Postdoctoral Fellow in Science in Human Culture in the Department of Sociology at Northwestern University, that examines why marginalized street vendors in India continue to embrace Aadhaar and digital payments despite their shortcomings, arguing that these technologies foster a powerful sense of political belonging and direct connection to the nation-state.Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Sai Balakrishnan (https://ced.berkeley.edu/people/sai-balakrishnan), Associate Professor of City & Regional Planning, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Mon, September 28, 2026 TIME: 12:30-2 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: On FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) —————-About the talk: Why do marginalized citizens in India continue to embrace biometric identification and digital payment technologies even when these systems routinely fail to deliver their promised economic inclusion? Digital India is a flagship policy of the Government of India to foster "economic growth combined with social inclusion." Central to Digital India is the Aadhaar card, a biometric identification now distributed to over 1.3 billion Indians, and a real time mobile payment technology, Unified Payments Interface (UPI), that has significantly replaced cash transactions. Technological promises to improve governance and economic opportunities are often not fully realized and create new sources of friction, especially for citizens in the informal economy such as street vendors. Nevertheless, many street vendors regard digital identification and payments as signs of economic and national progress. Why does there continue to be faith in techno-utopia even when its promises fall short, and what can this tell us about the nature of contemporary populist politics? Through interviews, archival work, discourse analysis and ethnographic research with street vendors in Delhi from 2020–2024, I argue that digital technologies acquire political force for marginalized citizens not simply through coercion or what they enable materially, but through the political relationships they establish between marginalized citizens and the nation-state. While the bureaucratic state was historically built as an instrument for advancing national development and extending citizenship rights, contemporary populist politics increasingly represents bureaucratic mediation itself as an impediment to democratic responsiveness and national progress. I use technology to illuminate some of the core tensions in the moral relations, state obligations, and forms of political belonging that constitute the foundations of citizenship in contemporary India.About the Speaker:Pariroo Rattan (https://sociology.northwestern.edu/people/faculty/visiting/pariroo-rattan.html) is a Weinberg College Postdoctoral Fellow in Science in Human Culture and the Department of Sociology at Northwestern University. She will also be teaching at the Department of Anthropology at Northwestern. Pariroo is a recent PhD graduate from Harvard University, where she was a long-standing Fellow at the HKS Science, Technology and Society (STS) program and received a secondary field in Music. Her doctoral dissertation is titled "A Marketplace for Populism: The Moral Politics of Digitization in India's Informal Economy" and studies the relationship of the digital economy with mediating state institutions and nation-building in India, through an ethnography of street vendors in New Delhi using digital biometric ID Aadhaar and payment system Unified Payments Interface. She also works comparatively on citizen resistance to legal data regulation regimes across the US, EU and China. Apart from digitization, Pariroo is writing about topics relating to the law such as the politics of evidence in the Harvard affirmative action lawsuit, and on the acoustic and sound politics of the urban economy. Her work has been supported by the Wenner Gren Foundation, Weatherhead Center for International Affairs at Harvard, and the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society among others, and has recently been published by the Economic and Political Weekly. _________________ Event made possible with the support of the Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/sarah-kailath-chair-memorial-lecture) Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952).PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking is not always easily available in Berkeley. events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Evyatar Tulipman: Bad metallicity in the semi-quantum regime of the Hubbard model
events.description: Bad metallicity in the semi-quantum regime of the Hubbard model Bad metals exhibit approximately T-linear dc resistivity beyond the Ioffe–Regel limit. That this behavior occurs in systems with radically different ground states suggests it is a generic manifestation of strong local correlations. We test this hypothesis in the infinite-U Hubbard model with small hole densities using exact diagonalization to compute thermodynamic and transport properties of finite clusters. Upon cooling, we find an intermediate temperature range, an electronic analogue of the "semi-quantum regime" of liquid helium, in which quantum effects produce a roughly T-independent compressibility, yet the resistivity is T-linear and exceeds the Ioffe–Regel limit. Entry into this regime is accompanied by the formation of quasi-local ferromagnetic "spin cages" around doped holes, regions that facilitate local quantum motion embedded in a fluctuating spin background, analogous to the transient crystalline cages thought to control incoherent transport in semi-quantum liquid helium. Remarkably, despite the simplicity of the model, the bad metal behavior found here resembles that seen in various material platforms. Speaker Bio: Dr. Evyatar Tulipman is a GLAM Postdoctoral Fellow and Zuckerman STEM Fellow at Stanford University. He received his Ph.D. in Physics from the Weizmann Institute of Science. His research combines analytical theory and numerical simulations to study anomalous transport in strongly correlated electronic systems, with a particular interest in high-temperature superconductors.

events.title: RTG Arithmetic Geometry, Number Theory and Representation Theory Seminar: Motivic Theta Lifting and Beilinson's Conjectures
events.description: Speaker: Linli Shi, ETH ZürichIn the Langlands program, theta functions are used as integral kernels to construct automorphic forms through theta lifting, and the Rallis inner product formula relates inner products of theta lifts to special values of L-functions. In the Kudla program, arithmetic theta functions with values in Chow groups are used to construct algebraic cycles through arithmetic theta lifting, while the arithmetic inner product formula relates the Beilinson–Bloch height pairing of arithmetic theta lifts to central derivatives of L-functions.I will describe a cohomological framework for constructing arithmetic theta functions and motivic theta functions with values in higher Chow groups. The motivic theta functions give rise to motivic theta lifts and provide a new construction of motivic classes beyond those arising from modular units. I will then explain an identity relating their Beilinson regulators to non-critical values of L-functions. This identity can be viewed as a Hodge–Deligne analogue of the Rallis inner product formula and provides evidence for Beilinson's conjectures.In the pre-talk, I will review classical theta lifting, the Rallis inner product formula, and their arithmetic analogues in the Kudla program, and explain the motivation for the motivic picture discussed in the research talk.This is joint work in progress with Wenxuan Qi, Liang Xiao, and Yichao Zhang.

events.title: Consumer Preference Modeling at Scale: A Generative Model for Cart Building (Srikanth Jagabathula, NYU)
events.description: Title: Consumer Preference Modeling at Scale: A Generative Model for Cart BuildingAbstract: How do customers build their online shopping carts across multiple product categories, and how do operational factors such as prices, delivery fees, and promotions influence their choices? Existing multi-purchase choice models in operations, marketing, and economics often overlook the dynamic and sequential nature of cart-building and struggle with scalability in real-world scenarios involving millions of customers and thousands of products. Machine learning models, while scalable, are often opaque and fail to capture problem-specific nuances. We leverage the latest developments in generative AI to bridge this gap by combining the scalability of machine learning with the structure of economic choice theory. We model a customer's cart building process as a sequential decision problem, in which the customer sequentially selects products based on their needs, preferences, and the operational context, which includes recommendations and promotions. Each customer is a reinforcement learning agent who sequentially selects products to maximize their overall reward. Using the observed basket purchase data as samples of expert demonstrations, we leverage techniques from inverse reinforcement learning and generative AI to infer the underlying reward function of the customer and train a generative model of customer purchase behavior. This model allows us to simulate individual customer cart purchases under various counterfactual settings. We implement our methods using a large dataset from a leading quick-commerce platform in India, comprising 8.5 million orders spanning 2000 product categories from 350,000 customers. Our model successfully scales to such large data sizes and predicts customer carts with a high degree of accuracy. Our model's structural insights reveal that customers strongly respond to free delivery over flat discounts of the same value, highlighting the behavioral characteristic of avoiding additional service fees. Our counterfactual analyses reveal how increasing the threshold for free delivery impacts cart value and product demand, with discretionary items like chips and longer shelf-life items like onions experiencing an increase in demand as thresholds rise.Bio: Srikanth Jagabathula is the Robert Stansky Research Faculty Fellow; Professor of Technology, Operations, and Statistics; and Academic Director of the Khubani BS in Business, Technology, and Entrepreneurship program at the NYU Stern School of Business. He was also a Visiting Associate Professor of Technology and Operations Management at Harvard Business School, and teaches operations management and AI/ML at the undergraduate, graduate, PhD, and executive levels. He holds a Ph.D. and S.M. in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from MIT, and his research has appeared in NeurIPS, the Journal of Machine Learning Research, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, Management Science, Operations Research, and Marketing Science. Recent work includes generative models of consumer shopping behavior, unstructured-text models for commodity-price forecasting, reinforcement learning for dynamic pricing, and a benchmark of 23 frontier AI models on the CFA Level III exam. He pioneered the use of large-scale choice models for operations problems, and has co-founded companies applying this work to pricing, recommendations, and supply-chain decisions. His honors include the NSF CAREER Award, the MSOM Young Scholar Prize, the Wickham-Skinner Early-Career Research Accomplishments Award, more than ten best-paper awards, NYU Stern's Distinguished Teaching Award, and recognition by Poets & Quants as a Top 40 Under 40 business professor. He serves as Department Editor at Management Science and as Associate Editor at Operations Research and Manufacturing & Service Operations Management.

events.title: Human Rights for Victims of Conflict in a Fragmenting World
events.description: Human Rights for Victims of Conflict in a Fragmenting World Monday, September 28, 3:30 – 5 pm Institute of International Studies, 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/NewAa5x9VL2jdDXV8) For too long, the field of international justice has been satisfied with "paper victories" - legal precedents and symbolic judgments that look good in a briefing but fail to manifest as tangible change on the ground. Systemic shifts are required for the human rights sector to remain effective in an increasingly volatile global landscape. To be truly victim-centered, human rights defenders need to shift their priorities away from in-principle victories to approaches that actually repair the harm survivors have experienced. Barrister Eva Buzo will discuss her work to shift the agency back to the survivors of conflict and displacement, ensuring they are the ones defining what justice looks like and what repair requires.

events.title: Seminar 271, Development: Jeanne Sorin - "Public Roads on Private Lands: Land Costs and Optimal Road Improvements in Urban Uganda"
events.description: Abstract: Cities in low-income countries need large investments in road infrastructure. Yet whether they pay off depends not only on potentially large benefits, but also on hard-to-measure and routinely ignored costs. I study the role of land acquisition costs in shaping the net returns to 114 km of implemented road improvements in Kampala, Uganda. Using two new surveys of real-estate brokers and landowners, I show that under compensation at the legal market rate these costs could have amounted to 40% of total project costs. The upgrades raised citywide net welfare substantially, but only because most land was acquired without compensation. Paying the legally mandated market value would have sharply reduced the gains, and even reversed them had public funds been sufficiently costly. Estimating a quantitative spatial model, I show that the fiscal wedge on land payments, which must be financed from scarce domestic funds, is highest where roads help most and distorts where it is optimal to build. The welfare-maximizing program under market-value compensation captures only 70% of the gains attainable without payment. The misallocation can be mitigated by donor financing of land or alternative compensation schemes like the claim-based rule the government adopted. The broader lesson is one of the second best: requiring full compensation to protect owners need not raise welfare when public funds are scarce, with implications for how road investments in fast-growing cities are designed, funded, and evaluated.

events.title: Lines of Control: The Hidden Politics of Soviet Ethnographic Maps
events.description: This talk is based on a collaborative digital mapping project that critically examines the interplay of erasure, power, and empire in Soviet-era ethnographic maps of the Caucasus. Using the 1959 census and ensuing maps as an example, Goff will discuss why these maps should be analyzed as argumentative sites rather than as illustrations of statistical data. How are maps representations of the concerns and subjectivities of Soviet mapmakers and how do the aesthetic qualities of maps complicate the historical narratives that we can tell? Speaker's Bio: Krista Goff is an associate professor of history at the University of Miami and co-editor of Kritika: Explorations in Russian and Eurasian History. She is the award-winning author of Nested Nationalism: Making and Unmaking Nations in the Soviet Caucasus and co-editor of Empire and Belonging in the Eurasian Borderlands. Goff is currently working on a new manuscript about the experience of World War Two in the Caucasus and the long life of war-related deportations, forced resettlements, and prosecutions.

events.title: Tanja Kortemme: "AI-guided design of de novo proteins: From new structures to programmable dynamics, protein networks, and cellular functions"
events.description: Methods from artificial intelligence (AI) trained on large datasets of sequences and structures can now "write" proteins with new shapes and molecular functions de novo, without starting from proteins found in nature [1]. Many protein functions - those critical for signal processing, energy conversion, and multistep catalytic transformations - require defined structural transitions between dynamically interconverting protein conformations. These functions are currently challenging to design de novo even with advanced AI models that are trained to predict and design static structures. I will describe our recent progress with (i) designing dynamic proteins [2] and (ii) developing advanced AI methods that can generate proteins with multiple conformational states and physically realistic paths between them. I will show recent results demonstrating the design of diverse, de novo protein conformational changes, suggesting that protein motions might be more designable than previously thought. Since suitable and large-scale experimental data on protein dynamics remain a critical bottleneck for developing improved models, I will describe how we are designing and experimentally characterizing hundreds of predicted protein conformational switches in high-throughput. Finally, I will discuss advances moving from design of bimolecular recognition to design of reaction networks. Exciting frontiers lie in constructing synthetic cellular signaling from the ground up using programmable de novo proteins [1]. References: [1] Kortemme T. De novo protein design - From new structures to programmable functions. Cell 187, 526-544, 2024. [2] Guo AB, Akpinaroglu D, Stephens C, Grabe M, Smith CA, Kelly MJS & Kortemme T. Deep learning guided design of dynamic proteins. Science 388(6749):eadr7094. 2025.

events.title: Physics Colloquium with Chiara Salemi: Tuning in to axion dark matter: how we search for an "invisible" particle with powerful magnets and quantum sensors
events.description: Tuning in to axion dark matter: how we search for an "invisible" particle with powerful magnets and quantum sensors Axions are one of the most compelling answers to the question of what makes up the majority of the matter in the universe: the dark matter. Detecting axion dark matter is a challenge, due to the particle's theorized tiny coupling to visible matter and its very low, unknown mass. To reach sensitivity to the best-motivated axion models, we are addressing these challenges with innovative experimental techniques and new technologies, working to increase signal strength as well as beat down the noise. Here I will discuss the work we are doing at Berkeley, developing technologies to enable future, large-scale detectors as well as building intermediate-scale experiments with unprecedented sensitivity.

events.title: AI & Disability: A Roundtable Discussion feat. Jeff Nagy, Renée Cummings, and Os Keyes
events.description: A History & Theory of New Media event with Jeff Nagy, Assistant Professor, Communication and Media Studies, York University; Renée Cummings, Professor of Practice, School of Data Science, University of Virginia, and Nonresident Senior Fellow and Co-Director, AI Equity Lab, Brookings Institution; and Os Keyes, Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Massachusetts, Lowell - Monday, September 28, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (http://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdsmOw4XW_mhfHzcHEg012STGGi9YE_lwF5AYv-7wTx4xVmJg/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=NzBtNDI4MWUzNzcwOXZucDA1N3R2M2MyZ2UgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - What does AI have to do with disability, and what is it doing to disability? This question undergirds a roundtable discussion featuring Jeff Nagy, Renée Cummings, and Os Keyes. In brief individual presentations, followed by a moderated discussion, these three experts in the field will tackle the question of AI and disability from a range of distinct and overlapping perspectives. Professor Nagy will examine the remaking of psychiatric disability in an AI era through the case of algorithmic depression diagnostics. Tracing a deep history of attempts to bring computing to bear on depression, he argues that the shift from clinic to program and platform, and the substitution of machine learning features for diagnostic criteria, are rewiring the political economy of diagnosis and overwriting disability identities. Through close reading of contemporary systems and the datasets they depend on, he reveals an emergent technopolitics of disability in action, one that operates at cross-purposes with disability community and activism. Professor Renée Cummings wil discuss what happens when automated systems become gatekeepers of opportunity for individuals with disabilities. Focusing on the data infrastructures governing healthcare, education, employment and public services, she exposes how incomplete datasets, inaccessible design, and reductive classifications can convert ableism into computational logic. Through the lens of data justice, she will confront the ethics of algorithmic exclusion: whose needs are recognized, whose experiences are misread, and who is excluded altogether. Centering accessibility, disability justice, and community expertise, Professor Cummings argues that disabled people must possess meaningful power to design, govern, challenge and—when necessary—refuse the systems shaping their lives. Finally, Dr. Keyes will ask what the history of computational psychiatry teaches us about the political economy of diagnostics.The role of AI in psychiatry is often framed as novel, and focused on improving efficiency and patient access to care. But neither is the case. AI has a long history in the upper echelons of psychiatry, as a field and a practice, and that history has consistently been entangled with broader political conflicts over who plays a role in shaping diagnosis and treatment., and under what conditions. Beginning with the start of computational diagnostics in the 1960s, he will trace out the history of how (and why) computational approaches to psychiatry have come in and out of vogue, arguing that the ultimate purpose of these diagnostic tools is to reshape the political economy of diagnosis and disability. About Jeff Nagy Jeff Nagy is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Communication and Media Studies at York University. He is a historian of computing and AI, currently focused on the intersection of AI development, the behavioral sciences, and disability. He holds a PhD in Communication from Stanford University. With the DISCO Network, he is a co-author of Technoskepticism: Between Possibility and Refusal (Stanford University Press, 2025). His research and writing have appeared in Parapraxis, n+1, New Media and Society, Technology and Culture, and elsewhere. About Renée Cummings Professor Renée Cummings is an internationally recognized AI governance leader, criminologist, public interest technologist, and public sector intelligence futurist whose work is helping shape how governments, institutions, and organizations prepare for the intelligence age. She is widely recognized as one of the leading global voices advancing responsible AI, trustworthy public sector AI, innovation governance, algorithmic accountability, and the governance frameworks required to strengthen public trust, democratic resilience, and institutional integrity. An award-winning AI innovator and internationally sought-after keynote speaker, Professor Cummings serves as Professor of Practice at the University of Virginia School of Data Science, where she teaches future leaders how to excel with AI and deliver AI excellence. She is also a Nonresident Senior Fellow and Co-Director of the AI Equity Lab at the Brookings Institution and serves as Co-Chair of the Global Academic Network at the Centre for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP), one of the world's leading organizations dedicated to AI governance, policy, and digital rights. About Os Keyes Dr. Os A. Keyes is a Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Massachusetts, Lowell. A widely published and award-winning scholar of everything from the history of medicine to critical approaches to Artificial Intelligence, their first book, Trans Science, is under contract with University of Washington Press. events.title: Five Years after the Youth Protests: The Thai Monarchy Strikes Back
events.description: Speaker: Pavin Chachavalpongpun (Professor, Center for Southeast Asian Studies, Kyoto University) This talk discusses the Thai monarchy's strategic response to the 2020 youth-led protests, which called for reforms to the royal family's place in national life. The speaker argues that King Vajiralongkorn did not merely seek to restore the status quo but executed a profound transformation which he terms 'overt power codification and defensive hyper- personalisation.' This shift converted informal influence into visible, legally codified, and personally commanded authority, entrenching absolute power within the constitutional framework to neutralize reformist momentum. Speaker bio: Pavin Chachavalpongpun is a professor at the Center for Southeast Asian Studies, Kyoto University. He is the chief editor of the online journal Kyoto Review of Southeast Asia, in which all articles are translated from English into Japanese, Thai, Bahasa Indonesia, Filipino, Vietnamese, Burmese and Khmer. Earning his PhD from the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London, Pavin is the author and editor of several books, including the upcoming Kings in the American Mirror: Two Centuries of U.S.-Thai Monarchy Relations (University of Hawai'i Press).

events.title: Naturalizing the Nation: Computational Perspectives on Canon, Nation, and Motif in Danish Golden Age Painting
events.description: This talk draws on preliminary and collaborative work situated within Rie Eriksen's PhD project, Re-Mapping the Golden Age: Computational Representations of Nature in 19th-Century Denmark. There will be a focus on on questions of canon formation, national style, and iconography in Danish Golden Age landscape painting (roughly 1800–1850), dividing the talk into three sections: Computational work on literary canons has already found measurable stylistic differences between canonical and non-canonical texts; however, painting has not had the same test. The first part of the talk asks whether canonical status leaves any comparable visual trace computationally, or whether it is better explained by institutional and curatorial history than by anything visible in the paintings themselves. The second part turns to the collection underlying this first analysis, showing that it is itself the product of a nationally motivated curatorial program and digitization practices. By creating a network of stylistic relationships, Eriksen tries to infer distinct levels of canonicity, and also raises a further question: what really makes a Danish landscape painting Danish? Can it even be separated from a Norwegian one? Does the distinction lie in the narrative of national romanticism itself? Finally, the talk narrows to a single recurring motif, the tree, tracing how one visual motif becomes closely bound to national identity over the course of the period. Across all three sections, computational analysis is treated as a complement to close reading/viewing rather than a replacement for it, and the results are always interpreted against established scholarship and historical contextualization in art history and nationalism studies.These studies are a part of the Golden Matrix project supported by grants from the Carlsberg Foundation (The Golden Array of Danish Cultural Heritage) and the Aarhus Universitetsforskningsfond (Golden Imprints of Danish Cultural Heritage).Rie Schmidt Eriksen is a PhD Fellow at the Center for Humanities Computing, Aarhus University, Denmark. Her research examines how representations of Danish nature and landscape became a central narrative in the construction of the Danish nation-state during the 19th century, drawing on literature, paintings, caricature, and newspapers. She is interested in how narratives take shape across different media and genres, and in the intersections between cultural symbols, storytelling, and perceived reality.

events.title: Synchro and SimTraffic for Signal Coordination
events.description: Description This four-session online course (4 hours per session) provides beginning-to-intermediate training in Synchro and SimTraffic software and the recently published Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) 7th Edition: A Guide for Multimodal Mobility Analysis (TRB 2022 and HCS7). Using a combination of interactive lecture, question and answer, and virtual computer lab, you will become proficient in the network coding and use of Synchro and SimTraffic for signal optimization and coordination projects. Working on a real-world multi-modal project, students will use Synchro to incorporate a Bing aerial background, add/modify roadways, input intersection geometrics, enter multi-modal traffic volumes (cars, trucks, pedestrians, and bicycles), and signal timings to replicate / validate existing operations for signalized and unsignalized intersections and roundabouts. Students will also use Synchro to evaluate and develop optimal signal timing plans that reduce delays, stops, congestion, fuel consumption, and greenhouse gas emissions. The seamless integration of Synchro with SimTraffic, a microsimulation software, will be used to evaluate intersection operations and compare the differences between "isolated - macro-level" Synchro and "network-wide - micro-level" SimTraffic analysis that is recommended for multi-modal, closely spaced intersections and congested corridors. Lastly, this course will teach you how to review and understand the potential differences in delay, level of service, and queuing analysis when using the empirical (Synchro) analysis or the micro-simulation (SimTraffic) analysis. Topics IncludeDetailed review of Synchro input requirements Developing a Synchro network for a real-world multi-modal project Analysis of signalized, unsignalized and roundabout intersections using Synchro Multi-modal vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle LOS using HCM 7th Edition Optimizing signal timings for a single intersection that is added to an existing corridor Optimizing signal timings for a group of intersections Seemless Integration of SYNCHRO with SimTraffic SimTraffic Model Calibration and Application What You Will Learn Using a real-world project in a virtual computer lab class setting, students will be able to interact with the instructor as they learn how to develop a network and use the Synchro and SimTraffic software. This includes incorporating a Bing aerial background, add/modify straight and curved roadways, inputting intersection geometrics and pocket lengths, entering multi-modal volumes (cars, trucks, peds, and bicyclists), and signal timings to replicate / validate existing operations analysis for signalized and unsignalized intersections and roundabouts. You will learn the steps used to optimize and coordinate a group of intersections to reduce delays, stops, congestion, fuel consumption, and greenhouse gas emissions. Lastly, you will learn how to review and understand the analysis results and the potential differences when using the empirical (Synchro) analysis or the micro-simulation (SimTraffic) analysis for signal coordination projects. The materials in this course are based on the following references:Transportation Research Board. Highway Capacity Manual, 7th Edition, 2022 CUBIC Transportation Systems. Synchro Studio 12 Traffic Signal Software -User Guide, 2024 Who Should Attend No prior experience using Synchro and SimTraffic is necessary. This course is designed for traffic engineers, planners, and technicians in both public agencies and private firms who engage in improving signal system optimization and coordination projects using the integrated Optimization Module in the Synchro software.

events.description: In her new book, Disabling Relations (https://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Ftupress.temple.edu%2Fbooks%2Fdisabling-relations&sa=D&source=calendar&ust=1788721620000000&usg=AOvVaw2AEfvc0GMN5Yf3xDPscb0e), Dr. Kazemi draws on thirteen years of ethnographic research, hundreds of interviews, and her own lived experience to invite readers to bear witness to the lives of disabled dissidents, veterans, and civilians in the aftermath of Iran's 1979 Revolution. Her analysis spans multiple sites of disablement and survival, including dissidents incarcerated and tortured by the Islamic Republic, veterans and civilians wounded in and by the Iran-Iraq War, survivors of state-sanctioned punitive limb amputation, and survivors of gender-based violence. Through the concepts of "wounding" and "disability consciousness," Kazemi theorizes disability as a historical process of becoming and remaining disabled through unequal social relations of power, while also examining how survivors make meaning of, negotiate, and resist the conditions of their disablement.

events.title: Robert G. Strand | Nordic Capitalism: Lessons for Realizing Sustainable Capitalism
events.description: Why do the Nordics consistently rank among the world's happiest, most prosperous, and most trusted societies? What lessons might the Nordics offer the United States at a moment when many people feel growing frustration and anxiety about the direction of American capitalism?Nordic Capitalism: Lessons for Realizing Sustainable Capitalism (2026, Cambridge University Press; open access:https://bit.ly/3MSvrOp (https://bit.ly/3MSvrOp)) by Robert G. Strand explores a simple but urgent idea: capitalism must be rooted in democracy if it is to support freedom, shared prosperity, and sustainability. Drawing on research, lived experience, and comparative analysis between the Nordics and the United States, Strand argues that the Nordic countries offer practical inspiration for reimagining capitalism in the twenty-first century. "Where democracy is in charge of capitalism, the people win. When capitalism is in charge of democracy, the oligarchs win. In this important book, Robert G. Strand shows how democracies can stay in charge. Nordic Capitalism explains that the Nordic nations can be a model for the US, and how democratic capitalism serves the many, not the few." — Robert B. Reich, Former U.S. Secretary of Labor and Professor Emeritus of Public Policy, UC Berkeley Dr. Robert G. Strand is the founding Executive Director of the Nordic Center at UC Berkeley and Executive Director of the Center for Responsible Business at Berkeley Haas, where he serves on the faculty. He is also Associate Professor at Copenhagen Business School. His research examines how Nordic societies have organized capitalism and how companies pursue responsible and sustainable business, with attention to applications for reimagining American capitalism. Before joining UC Berkeley in 2014, he served as Assistant Professor at Copenhagen Business School following a decade in corporate America with IBM and Boston Scientific. He received a Ph.D. in Corporate Social Responsibility from Copenhagen Business School, an MBA in International Business from the University of Minnesota, and a B.S. in Industrial Engineering from the University of Wisconsin. events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Science: Evidence from AlphaFold"
events.description: Abstract: We study how a frontier AI model affects scientific discovery by examining the release of the AlphaFold2 algorithm and its impact on structural biology and related fields of science. Structural biology is the field of science concerned with understanding the structure of proteins. Researchers in this field historically devoted substantial time and resources to experimentally solving three-dimensional protein structures. AlphaFold can predict these structures without running experiments. In July 2021, researchers gained access to hundreds of thousands of these AI-predicted structures virtually overnight. Yet, to date, we find that the rate of experimental structure determination has remained almost unchanged. Instead, researchers appear to use predicted structures to facilitate and complement experimental structure determination. Looking at downstream science that builds on protein structures, we find that basic research on proteins that had no structural information prior to AlphaFold increases by 23 to 32% relative to proteins that already had a structure, with the effects increasing dramatically over time. This represents a significant shift in the direction of research toward less-studied proteins. By contrast, the response of applied R&D, as measured by patents referencing those proteins, has been far more muted.

events.title: Seminar 221, Industrial Organization: Lucio Wasserman "Shrinkflation: What Happens When Package Sizes Change?"
events.description: JMC PracticeAbstract: Package sizes are one of the main features of consumer goods and one of the determinants of unit prices. However, they have received little research attention. This paper develops a method to identify size changes at scale, opening the door to systematic studies of this issue. We apply it to retail scanner data and show that size reductions are considerably more common than increases. Next, we estimate the size elasticities of demand over time using an event study approach. We find different dynamics in response to size increases and decreases. The demand response to size increases is immediate and stable over time. On the contrary, after size decreases, demand has a sluggish response: the size elasticity is smaller in the short term than in the medium term. An incentivized shopping experiment shows that individuals deviate from optimal behavior by responding less to size than to price, and provides evidence of attention as a mechanism. With the experiment, we test policy interventions, showing that the display of unit prices and of sizes more prominently can reduce welfare losses. On the other hand, size change labels can generate the opposite bias, with individuals responding to sizes more than what is optimal. We explain the empirical results with a dynamic demand that allows for inattention, paired with a supply model in which firms strategically advertise size increases but not reductions. Finally, using model-derived sufficient statistics, we evaluate the effect of inattention and of related policies on consumer surplus.Draft of the paper (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_dmfFkjdc4QwcMT6gSoWWerCMXLU5spC/view)

events.title: Too Close: Predicting Segmentation Behaviors of Beginning Readers from Coarticulatory Patterns in English and Spanish
events.location: 4215 - Berkeley Way West, and via Zoom https://berkeley.zoom.us/j/98016247113
events.description: This dissertation tests the premise that, for beginning readers, speech is the 'object of segmentation' (Schreuder and van Bon, 1989). I posit that one aspect of speech in particular—coarticulation as proxied by gestural overlap—is likely to influence segmentation performance: reduced coarticulation should enable segmentation, while greater overlap should make it more difficult. Using empirical evidence of gestural overlap from articulatory Phonetics, I make predictions about the segmentability of English and Spanish stimuli, both between and within languages. Participants were 472 TK – Grade 2 children from various educational contexts. Students were asked to segment a spoken word. Their responses received two scores: first sound isolation (0/1) and unitization (0/1), the latter denoting instances where the first two phonemes of a stimulus were identified as a single unit (e.g., /fl/ for flee). For each outcome, 12,388 responses were analyzed within a Generalized Linear Mixed Model (GLMM) framework that controlled for item- and person-side variables. Five out of six hypotheses were supported, pointing to a strong, predictable association between gestural overlap and segmentation performance. Specifically: 1) English clusters were more difficult to segment than Spanish clusters; 2) English items starting with vowels followed by sonorants (e.g., eel) were more difficult than their Spanish counterparts and English equivalents with obstruent codas (e.g., eke); 3) English and Spanish singleton onsets did not differ in difficulty; 4) voiced-plosive clusters were more difficult than unvoiced-plosive clusters in both languages; 5) fricative clusters were easier to segment than plosive clusters in both languages. Taken together, these results suggest that the speech code is indeed what participants operate on during a phoneme segmentation task. These findings are discussed within the context of broader literature on theory-development, reading instruction, and assessment.

events.title: My Favorite Expanders
events.description: Expander graphs are sparse graphs for which, whenever you split the graph into two parts, the number of edges going between the parts is proportional to the size of the smaller part. There are extremely simple, strongly explicit expander families whose analysis requires only a tiny bit of group theory. This fact is perhaps not so widely known. In this lecture, Ryan O'Donnell will show some of these constructions/analyses, and also indicate how they can be used to get even stronger kinds of expanders, such as "super-expanders," and "non-sofic property (T) groups."Ryan O'Donnell is a Professor of Computer Science at Carnegie Mellon University. He received his BSc from the University of Toronto in 1999, and his PhD in applied mathematics from MIT in 2003, where he was advised by Madhu Sudan. His research interests include complexity theory, quantum computation, and spectral graph theory. He is the author of the book Analysis of Boolean Functions.Refreshments will be served at 3 p.m., before the event. The Richard M. Karp Distinguished Lectures were created in Fall 2019 to celebrate the role of Simons Institute Founding Director Dick Karp in establishing the field of theoretical computer science, formulating its central problems, and contributing stunning results in the areas of computational complexity and algorithms. Formerly known as the Simons Institute Open Lectures, the series features visionary leaders in the field of theoretical computer science and is geared toward a broad scientific audience. events.title: Student Harmonic Analysis and PDE Seminar (HADES): Many-body physics via second quantisation
events.description: Speaker: Maciej Zworski, UC BerkeleyThe purpose of the talk is to provide an introduction to basic aspects of second quantisation and its relevance to many body physics. It will be done from a perspective of a non-expert with the principal source being the appendix by Kevin Stubbs to the Lecture Notes with Zhongkai Tao \url {https://math.berkeley.edu/~zworski/Notes_279.pdf}. I will introduce quantum many body Hamiltonians, switching then to an abstract formulation using the fermionic Fock spaces, and eventually writing those Hamiltonians in that language. That will lead to the formulation of the Hartree–Fock minimisation problem. Creation and annihilation operators will play a central role and I will explain how, in some settings relevant to condensed matter physics, they can be operator valued distributions. The talk provides some (optional) background for a Wednesday talk in the Spectral Theory Seminar.

events.title: Book Talk with Nicole Gonzalez Van Cleve (Brown University) – Crime Fictions: How Racist Lies Built a System of Mass Wrongful Conviction
events.description: Join us for a lecture by Nicole Gonzalez Van Cleve (https://vivo.brown.edu/display/nvanclev) (Brown Sociology) on her new book Crime Fictions: How Racist Lies Built a System of Mass Wrongful Conviction (https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/711146/crime-fictions-by-nicole-gonzalez-van-cleve/) (Penguin Press, 2026). A description of the book from the Penguin Press website appears below. Copies of the book will be available for sale at the event. This event is sponsored by the Othering and Belonging Institute and the Center for the Study of Law & Society. **** Wrongful convictions have long been dismissed as rare exceptions to an otherwise well-oiled criminal justice machine. But, after years spent investigating the largest criminal courthouse in the nation, Chicago's Cook County, Dr. Nicole Gonzalez Van Cleve began to uncover a far more chilling truth. Wrongful convictions are not accidental, nor anomalous: There are at least hundreds of cases indicting innocent Black youth of crimes they didn't commit. Arresting and incarcerating kids is the point—the "evidence" is tailored to fit. In a suspenseful narrative account based on years of interviews, archival research, and the excavation of hidden documents, Gonzalez Van Cleve presents an ironclad "howdunit," illustrating the steps that our supposed system of justice takes to "find" criminals, coerce confessions, and bury evidence. A clear pattern emerges as Lee Hester, a disabled fourteen-year-old boy, is branded a "super predator" and convicted of killing his teacher. At just seven years old, Romarr Gipson is charged with a murder that is physically impossible for him to commit. Groups of boys like the Roscetti Four and Dixmoor Five are characterized as "wolf packs" in a pattern that connects them to the Central Park Five. These "crime fictions" are actively produced, perfected by police, enshrined in our legal records by the courts, and reinforced by the media. Placing the exonerated boys at the center of their own story, Crime Fictions is a devastating, systemic account that leaves us to wonder just how many innocent souls have been claimed by the racist lies police tell.

events.title: Joint Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics with Seminar 281, International Trade and Finance: Pete Klenow - "Misallocation versus Inequality"
events.description: Joint Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics with Seminar 281, International Trade and Finance. Abstract: A stream of research contends that input misallocation takes a toll on aggregate productivity. If this is true, then why does it persist? One answer could be that policies to mitigate misallocation exacerbate inequality. We explore this possibility using data on Indian manufacturing firms and households in a model with both heterogeneous firms and workers. We focus on size-dependent misallocation given the ample evidence for size-dependent policies in India. We find that abandoning such policies would boost aggregate manufacturing productivity by 1-4%, but would also raise the skill premium and overall inequality because larger firms employ more skilled workers and earn more profits for their owners. We estimate that size-based reforms could lower consumption-equivalent welfare on the order of 9%. This suggests removing misallocation may be unpopular because it worsens consumption inequality

events.title: David Szanton | India's Mithila Painting: Home, Rituals and Traditions
events.description: A talk by David Szanton (https://ethnicartsfoundation.com/about/), President of the Ethnic Art Foundation (EAF) and Former Executive Director of International and Area Studies, UC Berkeley, drawing on his newly edited volume, India's Mithila Painting (https://uwapress.uw.edu/book/9780295753225/indias-mithila-painting/), co-edited with Paula Richman. The presentation will examine the long-term transformation of Mithila painting from a domestic ritual practice into a distinctive indigenous art form characterized by an expanding repertoire of themes, styles, and subjects. Through an illustrated discussion, Szanton will consider the work of contemporary practitioners, focusing on the ways in which established visual forms and stylistic conventions are adapted to address immediate social, cultural, and political concerns. He will also discuss a significant turning point in the late 1960s, when paper became an important medium for Mithila artists, facilitating new modes of production, circulation, and artistic experimentation. The talk will further explore the diversity of artists and stylistic approaches that have emerged over subsequent decades, while highlighting the important role of the Ethnic Art Foundation in supporting artists and advancing the recognition and wider appreciation of Mithila painting.Event moderated by Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Tue, Sept 29, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ——��—–About the Book: Since at least the fifteenth century, Hindu women in the Mithila region of northern India have been painting images of deities, flora and fauna symbolizing fertility and prosperity, and floor designs that sacralize sites for ritual within their homes. Their artwork remained ephemeral since its plant-based colors faded over time. In response to an extended drought that led to widespread crop failure in the 1960s, the Indian government's All India Handicraft Board provided high-quality paper to the women of Mithila to test the income-generating possibilities of transferring wall and floor artwork to a new medium. The unique Mithila aesthetic, novel compositions, and precise linework won enthusiastic buyers in New Delhi and abroad. The small number of women painters expanded across the ranks of the social hierarchy and even included a few men. They developed individual styles and depicted novel subjects such as village history, their own life stories, the tsunami in Sri Lanka, social justice, protecting trees, and changing social norms. Major international museums now house Mithila collections, and individuals around the world own paintings. This volume, the first to present an up-to-date analysis of the history and practitioners of Mithila painting, includes contributions from Mithila artists, anthropologists, art historians, historians of Indian religions and specialists of visual culture, gender studies, and translation studies.About the Speaker:David Szanton (https://ethnicartsfoundation.com/about/) is an American anthropologist renowned for his extensive work in South Asian studies and education policy. Beyond his roles at the Social Science Research Council (SSRC) and the University of California, Berkeley, Szanton has collaborated with several esteemed institutions. He has authoredMithila Painting: The Evolution of an Art Form(2007) andMany Visions, Many Versions: Art from Indigenous Communities in India(2017). In 1971, he served as an assistant to Howard G. Schaller in the Ford Foundation's Southeast Asia office, contributing to the foundation's initiatives in the region. In 1980, Szanton co-founded the Ethnic Arts Foundation (EAF), a nonprofit organization dedicated to promoting and supporting Mithila art—a traditional women's art form from the Mithila region of India and Nepal. As president of the EAF, he has been instrumental in fostering cross-cultural understanding and appreciation through the arts. David's enduring commitment to anthropology, education, and the preservation of indigenous art forms underscores his significant contributions to these fields. events.title: A Conversation on Compassion and AI with Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Kailash Satyarthi
events.description: Kailash Satyarthi is a Nobel Peace Prize laureate and founder of the Satyarthi Movement for Global Compassion. For over four decades, he has dedicated his life to championing the freedom, dignity, and dreams of the world's most vulnerable, transforming moral conviction into large-scale, systemic change. His leadership has shaped international norms, national legislation, and global movements committed to justice, equity, and human dignity. ​Satyarthi is the architect of the Global Campaign for Education and led the movement that helped secure the Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act in India in 2009. He also founded GoodWeave International, pioneering child labor-free certification and promoting ethical supply chains. ​In his latest book – Karuna: The Power of Compassion – Satyarthi challenges the idea that compassion is passive. Grounded in deep awareness of ourselves and others, compassion can compel individuals to transform entrenched systems. It is this disruptive power of compassion that Satyarthi seeks to bring to the dialogue on AI: a call to steer away from potential catastrophe and toward the service of humanity. ​Hosted by the UC College of Computing, Data Science, and Society, in collaboration with the Satyarthi Movement for Global Compassion (https://satyarthimovement.org/?utm_source=luma) and Arete Youth Academy (https://areteyouthacademy.org/?utm_source=luma). ​Discussion to follow. Panelists include: ​Stuart Russell, professor of computer science, UC Berkeley ​Jennifer Chayes, dean, UC Berkeley College of Computing, Data Science, and Society ​Rose Niousha, Ph.D. student in computer science, UC Berkeley ​Kailash Satyarthi, Nobel Peace Prize Laureate and founder, Satyarthi Movement for Global Compassion

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Thomas Farber
events.description: Describing America's deeply unsettling current politics, at age eighty-one Thomas Farber (English) explores personal accountability, impending second childhoods, mortality, and the hunger for immortality. Weighing the functions of satire and the meaning of art, his short takes illuminate, debunk, commiserate, and celebrate by rejoinder.Reckonings (El León Literary Arts/Manoa Books, 2026) is framed by two insights: no one chooses to be born, and no one can help being what they are. Reckoning with democracy in crisis, aging and mortality, his career, the role of the writer, and the fate of books, Farber reflects on endings with curiosity, honesty, wit, and compassion. Reckonings is the latest in a series of remarkable creative memoirs he has written over the past decade, coming to terms with life and its limits. Farber is joined by Sam Otter (English). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: PMB Seminar with Rebecca Lamason | Dissecting the cellular landscape of host-pathogen interactions
events.description: Intracellular bacterial pathogens must navigate and remodel the host cell to survive, replicate, and spread. My lab investigates these interactions using two pathogens with distinct strategies: the obligate intracellular, tick-borne pathogen Rickettsia parkeri and the foodborne pathogen Listeria monocytogenes. We take a multidisciplinary approach, combining cell biology, microbiology, genetics, and biochemistry with tool development, to investigate the host and bacterial factors that regulate pathogenesis. Today, I will describe how these approaches have revealed unexpected host machinery acting at the bacterial surface, and how these interactions influence pathogen dissemination.

events.title: Tobias Rees: What was intelligence?
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. Wednesday, September 30, 2026 Time: 12:00pm Location: 101 Weill hall Speaker: Tobias Rees Affiliation: Limn (https://www.limn.ai/) (founder and CEO) Join via Zoom: https://berkeley.zoom.us/j/92645313112 (https://berkeley.zoom.us/j/92645313112)

events.title: Kristin Pauker | Cultural Snapshots and Cultural Transmission of Bias
events.location: Berkeley Way West (2121 Berkeley Way), Room 1102
events.description: Institute of Personality and Social Research ColloquiumKristin Pauker, Professor of Psychology, University of Hawai'i at MānoaCultural Snapshots and Cultural Transmission of Bias Researchers have long argued that culture plays a role in shaping and creating individual biases. But how do we examine how culture transmits bias to and among individual minds? This talk presents cultural snapshots as a methodology uniquely suited to (a) capture the cultural patterns typically encountered by individuals in their natural ecologies and (b) examine how perceiving those patterns—in their natural ecologies—influences individuals. I will present an introduction to the cultural snapshots method and its theoretical background, and focus on recent work that has used this approach to demonstrate how cultural patterns of nonverbal behavior in popular children's television contribute to the cultural transmission of bias and the erosion of U.S. children's interracial relationships in middle childhood. Kristin Pauker is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Hawai'i and director of the ISP lab (https://manoa.hawaii.edu/isplab/). Her work explores how environments and culturally-shaped theories about race impact basic social perception, social interactions, and stereotyping in childhood and throughout development. Dr. Pauker's research spans both Social and Developmental Psychology and has been widely published in academic journals (e.g., Science, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Developmental Psychology) and featured in the media (e.g., New York Times, New York Magazine, Time Magazine). She has been the recipient of a Board of Regents' Medal for Excellence in Research and a Board of Regents' Medal for Excellence in Teaching from the University of Hawai'i, and her work has been supported with over $1 million in combined support from the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation.If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Ore Carmi [Tel: 510-642-5050; Email: orecarmi@berkeley.edu] with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Spectral Theory Seminar: Hartree–Fock coercivity for twisted bilayer graphene
events.description: Speaker: Maciej Zworski, UC BerkeleyAbstract: Hartree–Fock (HF) minimisation is considered as an easier version of finding many body ground states. The coercivity is then a soft replacement of a, typically much desired and rarely known, spectral gap. I will address this problem in the setting of twisted bilayer graphene (a background on its specific model will be provided) where the non-interacting Hamiltonian exhibits topologically non-trivial perfectly flat bands. In a discrete model Becker, Lin and Stubbs identified the HF minimisers as projections to simple flat bands determined by their Chern numbers, and we reproduce this result in the easier continuous model stressing its topological origins. We then prove the coercivity which comes from a new mechanism, the difference of Chern numbers between the flat bands. The talk is based on a joint paper with Kevin Stubbs.

events.title: (Vamsi Mootha) Mapping the Powerhouse: From Human Disease to Evolutionary Origins - Charting the Mitochondrial Proteome Across the Tree of Life
events.description: Allan C. Wilson Memorial LecturesMitochondria are central to cellular energy metabolism and arose through a singularendosymbiotic event ~2 billion years ago. Human mitochondria retain a vestige of theirbacterial ancestry – a compact mtDNA encoding just 13 proteins – while the remaining~1,100 proteins are nuclear-encoded and imported. Both genomes operate in concert toensure normal physiology, and defects in either can underlie human disease.In Lecture II, I will widen our lens to explore mitochondrial diversity across theeukaryotic tree of life. I will present integrated experimental and computationalstrategies to map the mitochondrial proteomes of highly diverged eukaryotes. Usingthese data, we reconstruct the lineage-specific gain-and-loss events that shape extantmitochondria and infer the ancestral mitoproteome of the Last Eukaryotic CommonAncestor (LECA). We envision this work laying the foundation for an emerging field ofcomparative mitochondrial biology.Division(s): Department of Molecular & Cell Biology

events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - California Agriculture and the Seeding of Silicon Valley
events.description: In the years immediately following World War II, California's Santa Clara Valley was an agricultural breadbasket to the world. A mere 30 years later, the Santa Clara Valley would be known as 'Silicon Valley', and would be the most technologically productive region on the planet. This transition from an agricultural economy to an urbanized, technological economy came to be seen as aberrational, or even an object of nostalgia. But in fact, the midcentury period of rapid suburban development out of an agricultural landscape laid the foundation for the housing and labour markets that came to characterize the contemporary Silicon Valley. This talk will discuss how the years following the Second World War set the stage for what Silicon Valley would become today. It argues that the roots of Silicon Valley's current housing and labor system were based in the agricultural regime of the immediate post-World War II period and the subsequent Cold War economy. Jeannette Estruth is an Assistant Professor of History at Santa Clara University and a Faculty Associate at the Harvard Berkman- Klein Center for Internet and Society. Estruth's writing has appeared in the Washington Post, The Drift, Urban History, IEEE Annals of the History of Computing, the Business History Review, and Enterprise and Society, among others. She is currently completing her book manuscript, "Think Different: Silicon Valley Activism and the Making of Modern American Politics," which explores the history of social movements, the technology industry, and ideological formation in the United States.

events.title: MBN Seminar: The surprising functions of adipocyte extracellular vesicles
events.description: Dr. Clair Crewe, Assistant Professor, Cell Biology & Physiology, Washington University School of MedicineTitle: The surprising functions of adipocyte extracellular vesiclesSummary: Adipose tissue (AT) protects other tissues from lipotoxicity during overnutrition by storing lipids and releasing adipokines that regulate systemic metabolism. In obesity, AT becomes dysfunctional, leading to ectopic lipid deposition, inflammation, insulin resistance, and oxidative stress that contribute to diseases such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. From the discovery of leptin almost 30 years ago we have come to appreciate the robust role that adipokines have in inter-organ crosstalk to regulate metabolism in physiology and pathophysiology. Recently, us, and others, have demonstrated a new language that adipocytes use to communicate with other organs, extracellular vesicles (EVs). This language is powerful as these membrane-enclosed vesicles can carry any macromolecule including miRNAs, RNA, or enzymes, resulting in robust functional modulation of receiving cells at all levels of regulation, transcription, translation, and signaling. In obesity, AT releases more EVs that can propagate inflammatory and insulin resistance signals. This talk will explore the unexpected and broad functions of adipocyte EVs and factors that regulate adipocyte EV signaling. We found that adipocyte-derived EVs participate in inter-organ signaling by transferring damaged mitochondria to the heart, which may modulate cardiovascular outcomes in obesity. At the adipose tissue level, we found adipocytes EVs can signal to surrounding cells to recruit mRNA to restore expression deficits. These findings highlight adipocyte EVs as surprisingly versatile signaling system that may fundamentally reshape how we think about adipose tissue communication across the body.

events.title: Neyman Statistics Seminar with Molei Tao: Scaling Diffusion Language Models
events.description: This talk will begin with a brief review of the classical continuous diffusion model, followed by variations that extend it to discrete data. Then a more technical presentation will be given to a first test-time-scaling method for diffusion language models that provably converges to a reward tilted distribution in polynomial complexity of sequence length. The method, MDM-VGB, is a discrete diffusion sampler that augments unmasking generation with principled reward-guided remasking. Its corresponding Markov Chain is carefully designed to ensure fast mixing, and consequently good scalability. Cases where there is advantage over autoregressive language models will also be described. Finally and time permitting, stochastic optimal control based RLVR methods for fine tuning diffusion models will also be discussed.

events.title: Michael Maltzan: Scales of the City | Architecture Lecture Series
events.description: Michael Maltzan founded Michael Maltzan Architecture, Inc. in 1995. His projects cross a wide range of typologies, from cultural institutions to city infrastructure. His notable projects include the Moody Center for the Arts at Rice University, MoMA QNS, Star Apartments, the Pittman Dowell Residence, the new Sixth Street Viaduct, MIT Vassar Street Residential Hall, the UCLA Hammer Museum, and the Winnipeg Art Gallery Inuit Art Centre. Maltzan received an MArch from the Graduate School of Design at Harvard University, as well as BFA and BArch degrees from the Rhode Island School of Design. He is a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects and received the 2016 AIA Los Angeles Gold Medal. He is a recipient of a 2012 American Academy of Arts and Letters Architecture Award and was inducted as a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters in 2023. He was elected to the National Academy of Design in 2020 and to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2026, and he currently serves on the Dean's leadership council at the Harvard Graduate School of Design and the Visiting Committee to the GSD. He was featured in the Canadian Centre for Architecture's 2019 film, What It Takes to Make a Home, delivered the 20th Annual John T. Dunlop Lecture for the Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University, and his work was named one of the 25 Best Inventions of 2015 by Time magazine. Maltzan's work has gained international acclaim for innovation in both design and construction. It has been recognized with five Progressive Architecture awards, 52 citations from local, state, and national chapters of the American Institute of Architects, the Rudy Bruner Foundation's Gold Medal for Urban Excellence, the Zumtobel Group Award for Innovations for Sustainability & Humanity in the Built Environment, a 2020 Best of the Millennium AIA LA Honor Award, the 2025 AIA California Maybeck Award, and the 2025 Cooper Hewitt National Design Award in Architecture. The firm and its projects have been widely featured in national and international publications and have been exhibited in museums worldwide, including the Museum of Contemporary Art Los Angeles, the Museum of Modern Art, New York, the Heinz Architectural Center, the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the Carnegie Museum of Art. The firm's work was selected for the 2006, 2018, and 2020 La Biennale di Venezia and is included in the permanent collections of the Carnegie Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the Art Institute of Chicago.

events.description: Anna Dziapshipa was born in Tbilisi to an Abkhazian father and a Georgian mother. As a child, her Abkhazian surname was initially associated with her grandfather's footballing success, but it has since become closely linked to the conflict that has kept the two nations in opposition since 1992. This situation had a profound effect on her childhood and identity, caught in the middle of two warring countries. In Self-Portrait Along the Borderline, the filmmaker returns to the Abkhazian family home built by her grandfather, located in a country that is off-limits to Georgian citizens and still not recognized by Georgia.

events.title: Are We Living in a 1938 Moment? How Autocracies Threaten the West
events.description: Are We Living in a 1938 Moment? How Autocracies Threaten the West Thursday, October 1, 12:30 – 2 pm *Lunchtime talk* Institute of International Studies 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/aJvKjMEtZbCn3H1JA)The warning signs of the 1930s feel alarmingly familiar today: nationalist rhetoric, revisionism, military rearmament, political polarization. The liberal order is eroding, autocracies are rearming, and the West appears weaker than at any point in decades. In this book talk, historian and security expert Dr. Moritz Pöllath argues that these patterns function as an early warning system for the present: a new authoritarian axis — Russia, China, North Korea, Iran — is forming, exploiting a strategic power vacuum to impose a world order beyond freedom and democracy. The years ahead may prove decisive: between 2027 and 2030, the world may decide whether it descends into a new global systemic conflict, with a possible attack on Taiwan as its most dangerous flashpoint. Moritz Pöllath is an Assistant Professor of Public History at Ludwig Maximilian University Munich, where he teaches courses on the History of Democracy, US History, the Cold War, and history teaching methods for secondary schools. He studied Diplomatic and Military History at Hawaiʻi Pacific University and American History at the University of Cologne. His first book, Out-of-Area? NATO and Decolonization in Africa and Asia 1949–1961 (2017), explores the roots of NATO's global security policy during the early Cold War; his second book (habilitation), Narrating Freedom: Challenges to American and German Master Narratives in the 21st Century, was completed in 2023. He has held visiting professorships at the University of Leipzig and was previously a visiting scholar at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a fellow of the Cold War Studies Program at Harvard University and the University of Udine.

events.description: Please RSVP to attend (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScBDQrjMuo76n6pZySYpqe58aLn5PGOzcfC-UsmeoIXwLOYeg/viewform?usp=publish-editor). Join the Banned Scholars Project and A Counter-Imaginary in Authoritarian Times for a conversation with scholars Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor and Sarah Haley. Responding to the move to reduce Black feminism to an analytic, Taylor and Haley will trace its genealogies and practices as a guide for political struggle. How can the tools of Black feminism and the legacy of radical Black left feminists inform resistance in our current moment and authoritarian times?Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor writes and speaks on Black politics, social movements, and racial inequality in the United States. ​She is author Race for Profit: How Banks and the Real Estate Industry Undermined Black Homeownership, published in 2019 by University of North Carolina Press. Race for Profit was a semi-finalist for the 2019 National Book Award and a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize in History in 2020. She is a 2021 MacArthur Foundation Fellow. Her earlier book From #BlackLivesMatter to Black Liberation won the Lannan Cultural Freedom Award for an Especially Notable Book in 2016. She is also editor of How We Get Free: Black Feminism and the Combahee River Collective, which won the Lambda Literary Award for LGBQT nonfiction in 2018, and co-editor with Colin Kaepernick and Robin D.G. Kelley of Our History Has Always Been Contraband: In Defense of Black Studies.Sarah Haley's research areas include African American and queer history, feminist historical methods, carceral history, and prison abolition. She is the author of No Mercy Here: Gender, Punishment, and the Making of Jim Crow Modernity. She organizes with Scholars for Social Justice and is director of the Institute for the Study of Sexuality and Gender at Columbia University.

events.title: Chases, clusters, and surfin' birds: Effects of group flight on locomotor biomechanics and energetics
events.description: Context matters in locomotion biomechanics, through direct effects such as differences in terrain or the environment altering the physics of locomotion, and indirectly when different contexts alter the underlying trade-offs between different approaches to movement. Group or collective movement represents one such context and here I use field recordings and laboratory experiments to explore how group interactions affect fundamental aspects of locomotor biomechanics and energetics in bird flight. Specific examples include tandem flights in Cliff Swallows, the cluster flocks of shorebird species across a range of body sizes, and an experimental wind tunnel examination of the energetics of European Starlings flying solo and in small groups. These specific examples demonstrate the importance of group movement context in bird flight while also suggesting similar context-driven changes in other organisms, in other environments, and during other behaviors.
