events.title: CCB Seminar: Markus Covert - The E. coli Whole-Cell Modeling Project: Accelerating Discovery via Comprehensive Biological Simulation
events.description: Abstract: Francis Crick first called for a coordinated worldwide scientific effort to determine a "complete solution" of the bacterium Escherichia coli. We have been working for some years now to complete a model of E. coli that takes into account all of the known functions of every well-annotated gene, in order to better understand and predict the behavior of this scientifically-relevant and industrially-significant model organism. Now that a majority of the annotated gene functions have been added to the model, our simulations have generated biological insights that change our perspectives about cellular biology and physiology. As examples, I will present our new findings regarding how metals are utilized in E. coli, as well as the effect of gene organization into operons, and the impact of engineering new gene content into the chromosome.Bio: Markus Covert is the Ram Shriram Chair and Professor of Bioengineering at Stanford University. Over the course of his career, his lab has generated several new exciting technologies to measure, analyze, and mathematically model the behaviors of individual cells. The lab is probably best known for constructing the first "whole-cell" computational model, which explicitly represents all known gene functions and molecules in a bacterial cell - an advance which was highlighted by the journal Cell as a highlight publication of the 40-year history of that journal. Markus is the author of the textbook Fundamentals of Systems Biology: from Synthetic Circuits to Whole-Cell Models. He has received several awards for his efforts to develop new technologies, in particular the NIH Director's Pioneer Award, and the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation Distinguished Investigator and Discovery Center awards. He has also consulted in industry, including on the scientific advisory board of Emerald Cloud Labs, and as an inaugural Ambassador at X Labs, (previously Google [X]). Finally, Markus has taught one of the most popular courses at Stanford for several years, an integrated "lecture, lab and lunch" course entitled Bon Appétit, Marie Curie! The Science of Haute Cuisine.

events.title: Ariel Bierbaum: Schools for Sale — Disinvestment, Dispossession, and the Promise of Reparative Planning in School Building Reuse | City & Regional Planning Lecture
events.description: Ariel Bierbaum (PhD in City & Regional Planning) shares her decade-long research into Philadelphia's public school closures and the afterlife of its public school buildings. She shows how school closures and reuses change the spatial and social arrangements of neighborhoods amid broader urban transformations and point to how planners and communities can envision new possibilities for public buildings.About Ariel Bierbaum is associate professor of urban studies and planning at the University of Maryland, a lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania, and affiliate faculty with UMD's National Center for Smart Growth and Maryland Transportation Institute. Her cross-disciplinary research connects urban studies, planning, and public education to examine how neighborhood, city, and regional policies interact to perpetuate inequality. She advocates for political action and collective resilience to advance educational justice and urban development. Bierbaum is co-author of Schools for Sale: Disinvestment, Dispossession, and School Building Reuse in Philadelphia (University of Chicago Press) and widely published in leading academic journals. She brings more than 25 years of experience in the nonprofit and public sectors, working across public policy, community development, and community arts. Bierbaum holds a PhD in City & Regional Planning from UC Berkeley, an MCP from MIT, and a BA from the University of Pennsylvania. This lecture is part of the Department of City & Regional Planning's fall lecture series.

events.title: Authors Meet Critics: "Demos: How the People Ruled Athens"
events.description: REGISTER (https://forms.gle/KddCT6ubaNBAkJXY8) Join us on October 1 for an Authors Meet Critics panel on the book Demos: How the People Ruled Athens, by Daniela Cammack, Assistant Professor of Political Science at UC Berkeley, with a courtesy appointment in the Department of Ancient Greek and Roman Studies (formerly Classics). Professor Cammack will be joined in conversation by James Porter, Distinguished Professor and Irving Stone Chair in Literature in the Department of Rhetoric at UC Berkeley, and Kinch Hoekstra, Chancellor's Professor of Political Science and Law at UC Berkeley. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Departments of Political Science and Ancient Greek & Roman Studies. The Social Science Matrix Authors Meet Critics (https://matrix.berkeley.edu/category/event-type/authors-meet-critics/) book series features lively discussions about recently published books authored by social scientists at UC Berkeley. For each event, the author discusses the key arguments of their book with fellow scholars. These events are free and open to the public.About the Book In ancient Greece, demokratia meant "rule by the people"—but what people, and how did they rule? Scholars have long argued that demokratia signified the rule of all adult male citizens over themselves. In Demos, Daniela Cammack counters this view by arguing that demokratia meant rule by the crowd that assembled when a public meeting was held. This crowd was the demos, which the Greeks distinguished from orators, generals, councilors, public benefactors, and other civic leaders. Drawing on literary and epigraphical evidence as well as the key theoretical insights of Aristotle and Hobbes, Cammack explains how constantly changing masses of ordinary ancient Greek men ruled while their leaders were ruled over. This political system relied on kratos, the power to prevail militarily, epitomized by the victories of the Athenian demos in civil conflicts around 508 and 404 BC. In peacetime, the superior strength of the demos revealed itself in large, frequently summoned crowds of ordinary citizens acting as policymakers, legislators, and (crucially) judges, who wielded great power over politicians. Aristotle characterized the years 403 to 322 as the era of "ultimate democracy," and it was during this period that the Athenians pulled off a feat unmatched by modern democrats: making use of talented and ambitious leaders without being ruled by them. By contrast, the Greeks called rule by elected office-holders "oligarchy." As people today lose faith in democratic institutions, Cammack's account prompts us to ask if we've been doing democracy all wrong—or even at all.PanelistsDaniela Cammack (https://polisci.berkeley.edu/people/person/daniela-cammack) is Assistant Professor of Political Science, affiliated with the Department of Ancient Greek and Roman Studies. She teaches broadly in the history of political thought and has particularly well-developed research interests in ancient Greek political thought, the history and theory of democracy, ancient and modern. and the topics of crowd power, deliberation, representation, and demotic sovereignty. She holds a B.A. in Modern History and English Literature (2002) from Oxford, an M.Phil. in Political Theory and Intellectual History (2005) from Cambridge, and a Ph.D. in Political Theory (2013) from Harvard, where her dissertation, Rethinking Athenian Democracy, won Harvard's Noxon Toppan Prize for the best dissertation in Political Science. Before moving to Berkeley in 2019, she was a Junior Fellow in Harvard's Society of Fellows and an Assistant Professor at Yale. Over the past decade, she has published numerous book chapters and articles in journals including Political Theory, The Journal of Political Philosophy, The Journal of Politics, and Classical Quarterly; she is also executive co-editor of History of Political Thought and associate editor of Polis, the Journal for Ancient Greek and Roman Political Thought. Her book, Demos: How the People Ruled Athens, will be published in January 2027 by Princeton University Press. A sequel, entitled Democracy: How the People Lost Power, is in progress and also under contract with Princeton. Kinch Hoestra (https://polisci.berkeley.edu/people/person/kinch-hoekstra) is Chancellor's Professor of Political Science and Law at UC Berkeley. He works on the history of political, moral, and legal thought, especially ancient, renaissance, and early modern political philosophy. Recent contributions to ancient political thought include "Athenian Democracy and Popular Tyranny," "Thucydides and the Politics of Necessity" (with Mark Fisher), and "The Liberties of the Ancients" (with Quentin Skinner). Another focus of Hoestra's research has been the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes (including studies of his theory of equality, obligation, democracy, tyranny, mixed government, natural law, and the rationality of justice); he co-edited The Oxford Handbook of Hobbes. Work that bridges these two areas includes "Hobbes and Aristotle on the Foundation of Political Science" (with Nicholas Gooding), "Hobbes's Thucydides", "Thucydides in the Renaissance and Reformation", and "The Melian Dilemma". From 1996 to 2007, he was a member of the Faculty of Philosophy at the University of Oxford, where he regularly taught graduate students in the Faculty of Classics and the Department of Politics and International Relations.James Porter (https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/james-porter) is Irving Stone Professor in Literature and Distinguished Professor in Rhetoric. His teaching and research has followed a few different trajectories. One is a study of Nietzsche's thought, early and late (Nietzsche and the Philology of the Future and The Invention of Dionysus: An Essay on 'The Birth of Tragedy' (both Stanford University Press, 2000). Another is a study of models of aesthetic sensation, perception, and experience in ancient Greece and Rome, which he explored in The Origins of Aesthetic Thought in Ancient Greece: Matter, Sensation, and Experience (Cambridge University Press, 2010; pbk. 2016). A continuation of this inquiry is The Sublime in Antiquity (Cambridge University Press, 2016; pbk. 2020), which received the C. J. Goodwin Award of Merit from The Society for Classical Studies (2017). A further strand is Jewish literary and critical thought in authors from Spinoza to Freud, Adorno, and Arendt. His most recent book is Homer: The Very Idea (University of Chicago Press, 2021; pbk. 2023), which captures some of his interest in classical reception studies. Current projects include Existence, Crisis, and Faith: Selected Essays and Letters by Rachel Bespaloff, a Cambridge Critical Guide to The Birth of Tragedy (co-edited with Michael Forster), and The Cynics: A Very Short Introduction. Dylan Riley (https://sociology.berkeley.edu/faculty/dylan-john-riley) studies capitalism, socialism, democracy, authoritarianism, and knowledge regimes in a broad comparative and historical perspective. His first book, The Civic Foundations of Fascism in Europe: Italy, Spain, and Romania 1870-1945 (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2010), argues that fascist regimes arose paradoxically on the basis of strong civil societies in the pre-fascist period. Reviewers have called this book "the most original and provocative new analysis of the preconditions of Fascism that has appeared in years", and "brilliant and courageous". A second book, How Societies and States Count: A Comparative Genealogy of Censuses (with Rebecca Jean Emigh and Patricia Ahmed in preparation for Palgrave), argues, against state centered accounts of official information that censuses work best where there is intense interaction between state and society. He has started a new project investigating the connection between the meaning and substance of democracy in interwar and post-war Europe. Riley has also published articles in the American Journal of Sociology, American Sociological Review, Catalyst, Comparative Studies in Society and History, Comparative Sociology, Social Science History, The Socio-Economic Review, and the New Left Review. He is a member of the editorial committee of the New Left Review.

events.title: Erin Schuman: Protein synthesis and degradation mechanisms and machines at neuronal synapses
events.description: The Department of Neuroscience and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute (HWNI) are delighted to announce the 2026 Carla & Corey Lectureship Series. This event, created through the generosity of co-founding directors of the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute, Dr. Carla Shatz and Dr. Corey Goodman, will bring outstanding neuroscientists to our campus to share their research and engage with our vibrant, interdisciplinary scientific community, spanning the full breadth of mind and brain science. This year's guest speaker will be Dr. Erin M. Schuman (https://brain.mpg.de/schuman), Professor and Director of the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research in Frankfurt, Germany, and soon-to-be Director of University College London Queen Square Institute of Neurology. The Schuman lab's long-standing research interest is the study of cellular mechanisms and neural circuits that underlie information processing and storage. The lab focuses on the molecular and cell biological processes that control protein synthesis and degradation in neurons and their synapses. The complex morphology of neurons, with most synapses located hundreds of microns from the cell body, presents a logistical challenge for the establishment, maintenance and modification of local synaptic proteomes. For her groundbreaking work on local protein translation in neurons and the establishment of its importance for brain development and plasticity, Dr. Schuman has been awarded the 2026 Kavli Prize in Neuroscience (https://www.kavliprize.org/bio/erin-schuman). The event will take place October 1, from 4-6pm at the David Brower Center, with a reception to follow. Join us for an inspiring afternoon of conversation and meaningful connections as we delve into the latest advances in neuroscience.

events.title: Mathematics Department Colloquium: The arithmetic of differential equations
events.description: Speaker: Daniel Litt, University of TorontoIn 1875 Fuchs asked for a criterion that determines when the solutions to an algebraic differential equation are themselves algebraic functions. Conjectural answers to this question have been given by Grothendieck and Katz, Ekedahl–Shepherd-Barron–Taylor, and Bost, in terms of the arithmetic of the differential equation's structure constants. I'll explain joint work in progress with Joshua Lam verifying these conjectures for a class of non-linear differential equations arising in algebraic geometry. This work is largely an excuse to try to better understand the arithmetic and geometry of algebraic differential equations and representations of fundamental groups of algebraic varieties.

events.title: Miroslav Krleza, "Foreword to Krsto Hegedusic's The Drava Valley Motifs" (NYS reading group)
events.location: Event held at Stanford (Berkeley carpool meets at Dwinelle Roundabout at 4pm)
events.description: The next session of the Berkeley-Stanford New Yugoslav Studies group is held on Thursday, Oct 1, at Stanford (Building 260, Room 252). The session will focus on the writings of Miroslav Krle��a, maybe the figure who looms largest in all of Yugoslav literature. Krleža laid a foundation for what Yugoslav culture would look like even before the founding of socialist Yugoslavia. Starting in the late 1920s, he entered into a spirited argument – now known as the "Conflict on the Literary Left" (Sukob na književnoj ljevici) – about the relationship between beauty, ideology, and political commitment in art. We'll read two texts by Krleža for next Thursday: First, we'll read an essay he wrote in 1933 as the Preface to the collection Podravski motivi(The Drava Valley Motifs) by the artist Krsto Hegedušić. An important statement of Krleža's views about art and socialism, this essay was also written against the Soviet program of "socialist realism." Secondly, we'll jump from the interwar period into the early years of socialist Yugoslavia, and read Krleža's Speech at the 1952 Writers' Congress in Ljubljana. This speech is a major historical document, as well as a pleasure to read: it's usually seen as the definitive public statement of socialist Yugoslavia's policy of variety and experimentation in the arts, the cultural equivalent of Yugoslavia's geopolitical non-alignment and split with both the Soviet Union and the capitalist world.* Note that this NYS session is taking place at Stanford (Pigott 252) at 6pm. Carpool from Berkeley meets at 4pm at the roundabout behind Dwinelle Hall. For readings and to join the NYS carpool, contact Djordje Popovic (dpopovic@berkeley.edu (mailto:dpopovic@berkeely.edu)). Contact person at Stanford: Dominick Lawton (dlawton@stanford.edu (mailto:dlawton@stanford.edu))

events.title: Panel Discussion: Water and AI
events.location: Anthropology and Art Practice Building, Room 120
events.description: The Water and AI panel brings together four speakers with different answers to a simple question: What is water? For Tiah Ross-Butner, a UC Berkeley student and enrolled member of the Yurok Tribe, water is family. For Sheena Conforti, a Stanford researcher who studies wastewater and public health, water carries information about community health. For Lance Legel, a UC Berkeley visiting scientist who uses AI to study ecosystems, water is a resource we need to understand more deeply. For Greg Niemeyer, a UC Berkeley professor and data artist, water is circulation. For Vivien Slagle, a UC Berkeley student studying art, anthropology, and law, water is a shared resource under competing demands from agriculture, data centers, and living systems. Water also helps make AI possible. Many data centers use water for cooling, and producing the electricity they consume can require additional water. Together, the panelists will explore how their cultures and practices shape the ways we understand and talk about water, and how these conversations can support sustainable water management. What is water? How can we talk across our differences? And where can we find common ground? This event is sponsored by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative.

events.title: Film Screening: Italianamerican and American Boy: A Profile of Steven Prince
events.description: Martin Scorsese's documentaries are like portals to his sources of inspiration, and Italianamerican takes us to the heart of the matter via a conversation with his parents. As his mother prepares meatballs, she and her husband tell the stories of their families' journeys from Sicily to Elizabeth Street, which speak volumes about the immigrant experience. American Boy is the realization of Scorsese's idea for a film in which "a man sits down, tells his story, and little by little you see an era emerge, a way of life, a way of surviving." He found the perfect subject in Steven Prince, a great storyteller, who played the gun dealer in Taxi Driver, a role for which he provided his own guns.

events.description: The Berkeley Tamil Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/berkeley-tamil-initiative) is pleased to present The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/tamilberkeley/uc-berkeley-conference-tamil-studies), a Tamil Studies conference exploring vaṭivam—form, shape, style, arrangement, and embodiment—as a way to understand how Tamil narratives are created, circulated, and transformed across literature, performance, visual culture, cinema, and digital media. More than a neutral vessel for narrative, vaṭivam offers a way to understand form as an aesthetic practice, a material structure, and a response to changing social worlds. Bringing together scholars working across literature, performance, visual culture, cinema, and digital media, the conference will examine how Tamil narrative forms have been made and remade across time. By placing premodern and modern materials in conversation, The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/tamilberkeley/uc-berkeley-conference-tamil-studies) asks how Tamil traditions can contribute to broader debates on form, media, and circulation, while remaining attentive to the histories, languages, and material contexts that shape Tamil cultural production. events.title: Defending Democracy Online Through Social Media: Deep Fakes and Our Cognitive Security, with Alexa Koenig
events.description: Digital technologies are rapidly transforming how people live their lives, including their access to information. Social media and smartphones are affecting both the creation and consumption of news — trapping consumers in information "silos" that obscure alternate points of view — while deep fakes are threatening the quality of information found online. All of this raises significant risks for the functioning of our democracy. Dr. Alexa Koenig will discuss this new information environment, some of the challenges it poses for democracy — including our sense of cognitive security — and opportunities for uncovering the truth in this digital age.About the Speaker Dr. Alexa Koenig is faculty director of Berkeley's MacArthur-Award Winning Human Rights Center; co-founder of U.C. Berkeley's Investigations Lab; and a research professor at Berkeley Law, where she focuses on the role of new and emerging technologies in human rights research and investigation.

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Frequency Synthesis for Integrated FMCW Sensing and Communication
events.description: Frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) radar is an attractive solution for wireless sensing of distance and velocity, enabling fine resolution and simple receiver design. The critical determinant of the performance of an FMCW radar system is the linear FM "chirp" used as both the transmitted signal and the frequency-translator of received echos. In particular, chirp nonidealities, including FM nonlinearity and phase noise, create artifacts in the intermediate frequency (IF) spectrum which directly constrain the signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio (SNDR). In this talk, I will present the two-phase "chart & chirp" method of one-shot, in situ voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) tuning curve estimation and learning ("chart") with on-demand predistortion ("chirp") for all physically realizable chirp parameters. Using a cycle-counting frequency-to-digital converter (FDC) in the "chart" phase and an integrating digital-to-analog converter (QDAC) providing linear voltage interpolation in the "chart" phase, this architecture produces optimally linear chirps via linear least-squares estimation (LLSE). Analysis and simulation of the FM and phase errors of generated chirps in the time- and frequency-domains reveal deterministic links between chirp nonlinearity and artifacts in the IF spectrum, including ghost targets and spectral smearing. Remarkably, these results demonstrate the possibility for poor IF SNDR in spite of low RMS FM error and phase noise, and I will discuss the modulation parameters necessary for high IF SNDR and accurate target detection.

events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Thrinadh Dasyam & Christina Schuler, Intel | How Do You Find a Bug in a Billion-Transistor Chip?
events.description: Abstract: Modern System-on-Chip (SoC) designs contain billions of transistors and integrate processors, memory controllers, high-speed interfaces, security engines, and many other complex components. With this level of complexity, how do engineers find a tiny design bug before the chip is manufactured? This presentation introduces the fascinating world of Design Verification (DV) and explains how engineers verify complex semiconductor designs before they become physical silicon. Using practical and student-friendly examples, we will walk through the journey from a design specification to test planning, simulation, stimulus generation, checking, coverage, and finally debugging failures. We will also discuss how technologies such as SystemVerilog, UVM, assertions, emulation, and automation help engineers uncover difficult bugs hidden inside increasingly complex SoCs. Thrinadh Dasyam, Bio: Thrinadh Dasyam is a Design Verification Engineer at Intel with more than 21 years of experience in semiconductor design verification and validation. His experience spans ASIC, SoC, and FPGA verification, including System Verilog/UVM, verification planning, functional coverage, emulation, and complex SoC debug and triage. He has also held engineering leadership roles and enjoys mentoring and sharing his industry experience with the next generation of engineers. At UC Berkeley, TD will present "How Do You Find a Bug in a Billion-Transistor Chip?", introducing students to the challenges and techniques behind verifying today's complex semiconductor designs. Christina Schuler, Bio: Christina Delgadillo Schuler brings over a decade of multifaceted experience at Intel Corporation, where she currently serves in Human Resources as a Campus Talent Acquisition based at the Folsom site. Through her 11 years at Intel, Christina has supported Sales & Marketing and Executive Leadership teams before pivoting her expertise to university recruitment. A former collegiate student-athlete, high school and college coach, and educator, Christina brings a uniquely supportive approach to mentoring students, guiding career discovery, and preparing emerging talent for meaningful careers at Intel.

events.title: Welfare Effects of Information Provision on Environmental Externalities | Zac Pond
events.description: Job Market PresentationAbstract Information provision is frequently used to motivate prosocial behavior, yet its impacts on welfare are rarely measured. I study these impacts by combining a signaling model with a series of randomized experiments on personal carbon emissions. The model generates predictions for how information provision can directly affect consumer welfare by altering the relationship between emissions and inferred altruistic type. I implement three interventions, two that provide participants with private information about their emissions and one that publicly reveals them, and measure their welfare effects with an incentive-compatible willingness to pay elicitation. The private information interventions are positive-sum in consumer welfare, whereas public recognition is negative-sum. Nevertheless, 16 to 25 percent of participants pay to avoid receiving private information. Under public recognition, relatively high emitters incur significant utility losses while relatively low emitters receive no gains. I use these estimates to compare the social efficiency of different forms of information provision on externalities.

events.title: Composition Colloquium: Nicholas Isherwood
events.location: Morrison Hall Room 125, UC Berkeley Campus, 94720
events.description: Oct 2: Nicholas Isherwood (MORRISON)TITLE: TESSITURA: VOCAL REGISTERSCONCERT: 8pm CNMATBIO: The Franco-American bass Nicholas Isherwood did musical, literary and theatrical studies at Oberlin College (B.A. in French Literature, B.M. in voice with Richard Miller), The Actors Centre in London and the Ecole des Hautes Etudes (D.E.A. in Musicology). An eclectic artist, Isherwood has sung medieval music with Joel Cohen, baroque music with William Christie, the Magic Flute at the Salle Pleyel, Wagner's Meistersinger with Zubin Mehta, several world premieres by Karlheinz Stockhausen and an evening at the Knitting Factory with Steve Lacy. His interest for contemporary music has led him to work with composers such as Sylvano Bussotti, Elliot Carter, George Crumb, Mauricio Kagel, György Kurtág, Olivier Messiaen, Giacinto Scelsi, Karlheinz Stockhausen and Iannis Xenakis as well as the leading composers of younger generations. He has performed both the Bach and Gubaidulina St. John Passions with Helmuth Rilling and improvised with Joëlle Léandre, Steve Lacy, David Moss and Sainkho Namtchilak. Isherwood has sung on five continents, including the greatest theaters in Europe and the United States (Ravinia, Tanglewood, the Disney Hall, La Scala, the Teatro dell'Opera in Rome, Covent Garden, the Châtelet, the Théatre des Champs Elysées, the Philharmonie, the Royal Festival Hall, the Concertgebouw, the Biennale in Munich, all three Berlin opera houses, the Moscow Conservatory, the Konzerthaus in Vienna, the Salzburg Festival, the Aix Festival, etc.) and with world class orchestras and ensembles (London Philharmonic, RAI Orchestra, the Philharmonic Orchestra in Paris, the London Sinfonietta, the SWR Orchestra, the Ensemble Intercontemporain, the Ensemble Modern, the Arditti and Diotima Quartets, etc.) Isherwood has recorded 70 CDs for labels such as Erato, Naxos, NEOS, Stockhausen Verlag and Harmonia Mundi. He has participated in films with Stockhausen, Aperghis and Frize for Arte, the WDR and the INA. In addition to his work as a singer, he has directed contemporary music theatre (SMIO in Orléans, Sons d'Hiver, Parvis St. Jean in Dijon, Teatro Regio in Torino, Stuttgart Opera, Tadashi Suzuki's theatre in Togamura, Deutsche Oper Berlin, etc.) and taught master classes in 5 languages on the French Art Song (USC, UdK), Olivier Messiaen (cnsmd in Paris), baroque singing (Cal State LA) and contemporary singing (Salzburg Mozarteum, ARIAM, UdK in Berlin, Munich Conservatory, Milan Conservatory, etc.), given lectures (Harvard, USC, Penn, Stanford, Berkeley, Freie Universität Berlin, IRCAM, etc.) and composed several pieces for voice (2 commissions from the DRAC and one from Art Zoyd). Nicholas Isherwood has taught at numerous universities in the United States, as well as the Ecole Normale de Musique and the Conservatoire National Supérieur in France, the UdK in Berlin and the Hochschule für Musik in Munich. He has published a book, "The Techniques of Singing" (Bärenreiter, 2013), as well as three peer reviewed articles (LIM, the Journal of Singing, Vox Humana). He is professor of singing at the Conservatoire du Pays de Montbéliard and professor of contemporary singing at the Conservatorio di Santa Cecilia.

events.title: Roundtable: Transportation Opportunities and Priorities for a New California Governor
events.description: ITS Berkeley will present a roundtable discussion in Transportation Opportunities and Priorities for California at 3 p.m. in the Bauer Wurster Hall Auditorium on Oct. 2, 2026.Join the Institute of Transportation Studies for an engaging discussion on the most pressing mobility challenges facing California's next governor. Our panelists will dive into what's working, what needs fixing, and the policies required for the future of transportation.Topicsthe panel will cover include:Solving the transportation funding crisis.How do we get riders back on transit?Enhancing EV market share and the challenges and opportunities of self-driving cars.Linking land use, climate goals, and how much we drive. Moderator: Egon Terplan, Senior Policy Advisor, ITS Berkeley Senior Fellow Panelists: Ken Alex, Director of Project Climate at UC Berkeley Scott Moura, UC Berkeley Civil and Environmental Engineering Professor and Partners for Advanced Transportation Technology Director Susan Shaheen, UC Berkeley Civil and Environmental Engineering Professor and Transportation Sustainability Research Center Director Laura Tolkoff, SPUR Transportation Policy Director Bios:Ken Alex is the Director of Project Climate at the University of California, Berkeley, focusing on the most promising climate solutions and moving them more quickly to policy and scale. From 2011 to 2018, Ken was a Senior Policy Adviser to Governor Jerry Brown, Director of the Governor's Office of Planning and Research, and Chair of the Strategic Growth Council, focusing on climate, energy, environment, and land use issues. Before joining the Governor's Office, Ken was the Senior Assistant Attorney General heading the environment section of the California Attorney General's Office, and the co-head of the Office's global warming unit. From 2000 to 2006, Ken led the California Attorney General's energy task force, investigating price and supply issues related to California's energy crisis. Ken is a graduate of Harvard Law School and holds a B.A. in political theory from the University of California at Santa Cruz. Scott Moura is a Professor in Civil & Environmental Engineering, Director of the Energy, Controls, & Applications Lab (eCAL), and Faculty Director of PATH. He received the B.S. degree from the University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA, and the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, in 2006, 2008, and 2011, respectively, all in mechanical engineering. From 2011 to 2013, he was a Post-Doctoral Fellow at the Cymer Center for Control Systems and Dynamics, University of California, San Diego and a Visiting Researcher at the Centre Automatique et Systèmes, MINES ParisTech, Paris, France in 2013. His research interests include control, optimization, and AI for batteries, electrified vehicles, and distributed energy resources. Susan Shaheen is a professor in Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of California, Berkeley. She also co-directs the Transportation Sustainability Research Center of the Institute of Transportation Studies (ITS)-Berkeley and is the director of the UC ITS' Resilient and Innovative Mobility Initiative. Throughout her more than 25-year career, Shaheen has focused on sustainable transportation technologies, environmental/energy policy, behavioral understanding and environmental impacts. She is recognized as a leading international expert in innovative mobility strategies and was among the first to research and write about the changing dynamics in several areas, including shared mobility and autonomy. Her research focuses on electrification and alternative fuels, innovative mobility strategies, behavioral dynamics and public policy as it relates to sustainable transportation and social equity. Shaheen earned a Ph.D. from UC Davis and a M.S. from the University of Rochester. She is a member of the Transportation Research Board's (TRB) Executive Committee – serving as chair in 2021 and vice-chair in 2020 – and the California Transportation Foundation Board since 2022, where she serves as co-chair of the Scholarship Committee. Shaheen received the 2017 Roy W. Crum award from TRB for her distinguished achievements in transportation research. Egon Terplan is CA FWD's Regionalism Fellow. In that role he researches and writes about opportunities to strengthen and improve California's system of regional economic development and planning. He has served as an advisor and consultant to CA FWD since 2022. He is concurrently a Senior Fellow at UC Berkeley's Institute of Transportation Studies where he studies and writes about the future of transit, downtowns, and cities. He continues to maintain a portfolio of external clients focused strategy and policy advisory services. Prior to 2022, Egon was the Senior Advisor for Economic Development and Transportation within the Governor's Office of Planning and Research and the California Strategic Growth Council. In that role he helped launch and manage "Regions Rise Together" a Governor's initiative which resulted in the creation of the Community Economic Resilience Fund (now California Jobs First) and the Regional Early Action Planning Grants 2.0. Egon received a Master of City Planning from UC Berkeley's College of Environmental Design and graduated Phi Beta Kappa from Swarthmore College in Pennsylvania. He has been a visiting professor and lecturer at UC Berkeley, Stanford University, the University of San Francisco, and San Jose State University. From 2021 to 2023 he held the Robert S. Cornish Endowed Chair of Regional Planning and Lecturer in City & Regional Planning at UC Berkeley. Laura Tolkoff is SPUR's transportation policy director. She believes that a sustainable transportation system is the scaffolding for a society that cares for the environment, that embraces public life, and that is healthier, more just, and more prosperous. In addition to overseeing SPUR's transportation portfolio, her areas of focus include public transit, land use integration, project delivery, governance change, and interregional coordination. Laura has worked for SPUR since 2015 in various roles, overseeing several strategic local and regional initiatives and was SPUR's first San José policy director from 2015 to 2017. Prior to joining SPUR, Laura held a senior role managing the energy and environment program at Regional Plan Association (RPA) in the New York Metropolitan area during and after Hurricane Sandy. She spearheaded federal, state, and regional reforms and worked in coalition to launch a federal design competition that brought over $1 billion to local climate resilience projects. Laura earned a Master's degree in urban and environmental policy and planning from Tufts University and a Bachelor's degree in media studies from the University of California at Berkeley. She is an American Leadership Forum senior fellow and was named to Mass Transit magazine's "Top 40 under 40" in 2019.

events.title: "Anti-Muslim Racism and Genocide" Featuring Prof. Sherene Razack (UCLA)
events.location: 3335 Dwinelle Hall (Level C) University of California Berkeley, CA 94720-2550
events.description: Event Description: This presentation examines anti-Muslim race-making and the question of Palestine; it explore how the figure of the Muslim is transformed into a racial rather than an exclusively religious figure in the colonial imaginary. Speaker bio: Sherene H. Razack is a Distinguished Professor and the Penny Kanner Endowed Chair in the Department of Gender Studies, UCLA. She is an interdisciplinary critical race and feminist scholar whose work engages several fields including Sociology, Legal Studies, Gender Studies, Ethnic Studies, American Studies and Political Science. With a central focus on racial violence, she explores how imperialism, colonialism, capitalism and patriarchy interlock to produce and sustain a racially structured world where racialized populations are marked as disposable and subjected to an unrelenting violence. She is the founder of the Racial Violence Hub, a virtual network of scholars (Racialviolencehub.com). Her books and publications examine settler colonialism, colonialism, neo-colonialism and global white supremacy with a particular focus on the gendered effects of anti-Indigenous, anti-Black, anti-Asian and anti-Muslim racism as they operate in law. Her two most recent books are: Nothing Has to Make Sense: Upholding White Supremacy Through Anti-Muslim Racism (2022) and Dying from Improvement: Inquests and Inquiries into Indigenous Deaths in Custody (2015).

Strand A: Building Lessons for Real World Competence Collaborate, Innovate, Invigorate: Next-level Lessons for every classroom. Invigorate your teaching this year! This strand is for all language teachers who want to take their instruction to the next level, whether beginning or experienced. You will collaborate to develop lessons that focus on teaching in the target language with comprehensible input, guided practice, grammar in context and formative assessment for all levels of proficiency. You will build a complete Lesson over time while learning and practicing strategies to implement immediately. Prerequisite: an open mind, curiosity, and a desire to grow. Build a thematic unit grounded in authentic materials that reflect real language and culture. You will learn how to design a unit that aligns with UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), AP themes and CA World Languages Standards while integrating global competence, social justice, and social-emotional learning. Using backward design, you'll craft essential questions, Can-Do statements, and assessments that support meaningful communication across all modes—creating immersive, relevant learning experiences that connect students to the real world and help them grow as confident, culturally aware language users. events.title: Film Screening: Band of Outsiders
events.description: Would-be tough guys Franz (Sami Frey) and Arthur (Claude Brasseur) have little better to do than drive around Paris and act out scenes from B movies. But when they team up with Franz's English-class crush, wide-eyed Odile (Anna Karina), to plot a burglary, they stumble into the gap between playacting and reality. Jean-Luc Godard said, "It is not the people who are important, but the atmosphere between them." The atmosphere arises not only from the actors' interplay—their dance in a café and their sprint through the Louvre are among the most memorable and joyous moments in Godard's cinema—but also from Raoul Coutard's exquisitely bleak cinematography and Michel Legrand's jaunty, melancholy score.

events.title: Roadway Geometric Design in California
events.description: Description This dynamic three-day, in-person course provides a deep dive into the principles and best practices of roadway geometric design in California. Built for professionals looking to strengthen or refresh their roadway design knowledge and expertise, the course begins with the latest transportation planning perspectives and emerging multimodal design philosophies that prioritize safety, mobility, and accessibility for all road users. Students will work directly with the industry's most essential design resources, including the Caltrans Highway Design Manual (HDM), the AASHTO Greenbook, PROWAG, the 2026 California MUTCD, and other key state, federal, and local guidelines. Through real world examples, students will learn how to apply geometric design principles to evaluate constraints, solve design challenges, and develop context sensitive solutions for various design projects. This fast-paced, interactive course blends expert instruction, case studies, group problem solving, and hands-on exercises modeled on real projects. Students are expected to have prior knowledge of or experience with geometric design of roadways, and familiarity with the HDM, AASHTO, and CA MUTCD. Key Topics IncludeGeometric Design Basics & Planning Context Modern Design Philosophy for All Users Design Standards & Guidance (HDM, AASHTO, NACTO, PROWAG, CAMUTCD) Traffic Operations: LOS, Capacity, and VMT Roadway Segment Design (Cross Sections, Profiles, Drainage, Superelevation) Horizontal & Vertical Curve Design Sight Distance Fundamentals (Stopping, Passing, Intersection, Ped/Bike) Intersection Design (Radii, Turn Pockets, Curb Ramps, Signals, Roundabouts) Bikeway Design (Class I-IV Facilities) Pedestrian Facilities Design & Accessibility (ADA/PROWAG) Temporary Traffic Control & Work Zone Design Freeway Design Elements (Interchanges, Merge/Diverge, Mainline) What You Will Learn Students will gain a strong understanding of the principles and best practices of geometric design across multiple roadway functional classes, along with the external factors that influence design decisions. Who Should Attend This course is intended for transportation engineers and technicians who have some basic prior knowledge of or experience with geometric design of roadways, as well as for those more experienced who seek a refresher course. events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: On the generator problem for $W^*$-bundles
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Ben Hayes, University of VirginiaWe give an explicit example of a $W^*$-bundle $M$ over a compact, metrizable space $K$, which has each fiber $M_p$ a $\textrm {II}_1$-factor with separable predual, and which satisfies the following negation of the generator problem : given any finite family $a_1,\cdots , a_n\in M$ of continuous sections, there is a $p\in K$ (depending upon that family) so that $a_{1,p},\cdots ,a_{n,p}$ together with $N_p$do not generate $M_p$. as a von Neumann algebra. More generally, if $N$ is a sub-bundle of $M$ with the property that each fiber is hyperfinite, or has a Cartan, or is generated by two commuting diffuse subalgebras, or has diffuse central sequence algebra, or is generated by a single sequential commutation orbit, then given any finite family $a_1,\cdots ,a_n\in M$ of continuous sections, there is a $p\in K$ (depending upon that family) so that $a_{1,p},\cdots ,a_{n,p}$ together with. $N_p$ do not generate $M_p$. We discuss implications for the generator problem for von Neumann algebras: e.g. there is no "continuous" way to take countably many generators for a tracial von Neumann algebra with separable predual and produce a single generator, at least if such a procedure works for all von Neumann algebras simultaneously.

events.title: CSLS Speaker Series: Losing the Law: How Legal Polarization Threatens American Democracy (Princeton University Press, 2026)
events.organizer: Center for the Study of Law and Society
events.description: featuring Deborah Pearlstein, Director, Program in Law and Public Policy and Visiting Professor in Law and Public Affairs, Princeton UniversityAbstract: The norms that have separated law from politics in America are eroding, making government by constitutional democracy increasingly hard to sustain. Losing the Law tells the story of how we came to this precarious moment. This powerful, persuasively argued book describes how a decades-long revolution in professional culture and legal thought is fueling the nation's authoritarian slide. It also offers essential guidance on what we can do to change course, not just by crafting institutional reforms but by resetting professional incentives and popular beliefs about the power and limits of the rule of law in constitutional governance. Looking behind the well-recognized politics of red and blue, Deborah Pearlstein charts the independent rise of "legal polarization"—a growing divide between lawyers and judges who believe there should be a difference between law and politics and those who no longer do. Drawing on original interviews and archival research, a close reading of American law and legal thought, and a sobering accounting of recent events, she unearths the conservative legal movement's foundation-shifting secondary effects as it established a new career pipeline from law school to judgeship, promoted partisan loyalty above professional responsibility, and popularized legal theories in irreconcilable conflict with long-settled understandings of how law worked. From the early role of unitary executive theory in kneecapping major post-Watergate reforms to originalism's inevitable rejection of precedent, Pearlstein traces how legal polarization has supercharged democratic backsliding under Trump 2.0. An urgent call to action by one of today's foremost legal minds, Losing the Law lays out the complex task ahead for those committed both to understanding the depth of the current crisis and to reestablishing sustainable constitutional governance in the years ahead. events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Johannes Lischner: Controlling the interaction of light with nanomaterials: from twisted multilayers to plasmonic nanoparticles
events.description: Controlling the interaction of light with nanomaterials: from twisted multilayers to plasmonic nanoparticles Nanoscale materials exhibit fascinating light-matter interactions: in twisted multilayers, bound electron-hole pairs called excitons are trapped by the moiré superlattice potential and in metallic nanoparticles collective charge density oscillations called localized surface plasmons give rise to enormous light absorption cross-sections which can be harnessed in optoelectronic devices. In my talk, I will describe how these phenomena can be understood and controlled using atomistic quantum-mechanical modelling approaches. First, I will describe the optical signatures of charged defects in two-dimensional semiconductors. Then, I will discuss quadrupolar excitons in twisted trilayer materials. Finally, the generation of highly energetic electrons and holes (also known as hot carriers) from the decay of localized surface plasmons in metallic nanoparticles will be analyzed. Speaker Bio: Johannes is a Professor in Theory and Simulation of Materials in the Department of Materials at Imperial College London. He is also the Director of the MSc in Advanced Material Science and Engineering and Imperial's director of the Thomas Young Centre for Theory and Simulation of Materials and Molecules. He obtained a Ph.D. in Physics from Cornell University in 2010. Before joining Imperial in 2014 as a Royal Society University Research Fellow, he was a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley and Lawrence Berkeley National Lab. His research is focused on electronic excitations in complex materials. Recently, his group has developed novel methods to model excited states in twisted bilayers of two-dimensional materials, such as twisted bilayer graphene and twisted homo- and heterobilayers of transition metal dichalcogenides. Other areas of interest include hot carrier generation in nanoplasmonic materials and simulating core and valence electron spectroscopies via the GW and GW cumulant approach or the Delta-SCF method.

events.title: RTG Arithmetic Geometry, Number Theory and Representation Theory Seminar: Purity of Motivic Cohomology in Mixed Characteristic
events.description: Speaker: Arnab Kundu, SLMathMotivic cohomology is a cohomology theory that can be defined internally within Grothendieck's category of motives. Voevodsky developed this theory for smooth varieties, demonstrating its deep connections to algebraic cycles and algebraic K-theory. However, its behaviour in mixed characteristics remains less well understood. Building on recent advances by Bachmann, Elmanto, Morrow, and Bouis, in joint work with Bouis we establish a purity result over deeply ramified bases. I will also discuss an application of this result to p-adic Hodge theory.

events.title: Distributionally Robust Newsvendor on a Metric (Vineet Goyal, Columbia University)
events.description: Title: Distributionally Robust Newsvendor on a Metric Abstract:We consider a fundamental generalization of the classical newsvendor problem where the seller needs to decide on the inventory of a product jointly for multiple locations on a metric as well as a fulfillment policy to satisfy the uncertain demand that arises sequentially over time after the inventory decisions have been made. To address the distributional-ambiguity, we consider a distributionally robust setting where the decision-maker only knows the mean and variance of the demand, and the goal is to make inventory and fulfillment decisions to minimize the worst-case expected inventory and fulfillment cost (where the expectation is taken over the worst case choice of distribution with given mean and variance). We present a significant generalization of the classical result of Scarf (1958) and give a policy with strong theoretical guarantees as well as good practical performance while maintaining the simplicity and interpretability of the solution in Scarf (1958). In particular, our policy first identifies a hierarchical clustering of the locations, and assigns a "virtual-underage cost" for each cluster. Our inventory solution ensures that for each cluster, the total inventory in the cluster is at least as large as the inventory level suggested by Scarf's solution for the virtual-underage cost if the cluster was a single point. We present a worst-case performance guarantee for our policy and also demonstrate that the policy performs well in practice. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm with provable performance guarantees. (This is joint work with Ayoub Foussoul)Bio: Vineet Goyal is a Professor in the Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research, and the Chair of the Center of Financial and Business Analytics at the Data Science Institute at Columbia University. He received his Bachelor's degree in Computer Science from Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi in 2003 and his Ph.D. in Algorithms, Combinatorics and Optimization (ACO) from Carnegie Mellon University in 2008. Before coming to Columbia, he spent two years as a Postdoctoral Associate at the Operations Research Center at MIT. He is interested in the design of efficient and robust data-driven algorithms for large scale dynamic optimization problems with applications in revenue management and healthcare operations. His research has been continually supported by grants from NSF and industry including NSF CAREER Award in 2014 and faculty research awards from Google, IBM, Adobe and Amazon.

events.title: Itay Budin: "The private life of lipids: small chemical changes that shape cell membranes"
events.description: Abstract: Our lab investigates how – and why – cells control the composition of their lipid membranes. In this talk, I will focus on our efforts to uncover how lipid composition is controlled in intracellular membranes and describe emerging biophysical models to explain its chemical diversity in cells. I will first highlight recent studies that demonstrate how surprisingly small modifications to lipid molecules drive membrane function. In the other, we uncovered how the shape of phospholipids – described by their spontaneous curvature – is a biophysical parameter that drives habitability and is actively maintained by distinct pathway in lipid metabolism. I will then focus on new chemical biology approaches we have developed to map phospholipids in cell membranes and determine factors that control their trafficking. A key advance has been the use of fluorogenic dyes in biorthogonal labeling reactions to enable compartment- and leaflet-specific detection of phospholipid pools. These tools allow cell biologists to interrogate lipid trafficking at ever-greater spatial details.

events.title: Physics Colloquium with Derek Jackson Kimball: New twists in searches for exotic fields with spin-dependent sensors
events.description: New twists in searches for exotic fields with spin-dependent sensors Nature has provided many hints that our best current theoretical models of the universe are missing important constituents. These undiscovered constituents could include exotic ultralight bosons such as axions. Many well-motivated theories predict that such fields interact with the intrinsic spins of ordinary particles, producing extremely feeble torques that might be detected with sensitive spin-based quantum sensors. Some of the most distinctive (and possibly largest) signals may originate from astrophysical sources. The Global Network of Optical Magnetometers for Exotic Physics Searches (GNOME) is a worldwide array of time-synchronized, magnetically shielded spin sensors designed to identify correlated signals from exotic fields of astrophysical origin. GNOME is now being upgraded from atomic magnetometers to noble-gas comagnetometers, which suppress magnetic-field noise and significantly improve sensitivity to exotic interactions with nuclear spins. The newest search targets for GNOME are signals from black hole scalar sirens. If ultralight spin-0 bosonic fields exist, spinning black holes can grow surrounding clouds of these scalars via superradiance. If the scalars interact with one another, the black holes can continually emit scalar waves. Summed over the expected hundreds of millions of isolated black holes in the Milky Way, these sources could produce a persistent signal up to two orders of magnitude larger than conservative expectations for bosonic fields created in the early universe. Detecting a black hole scalar siren signal would simultaneously reveal the existence of exotic scalar fields and illuminate the otherwise hidden population of isolated black holes in our galaxy. Finally, our research group is developing a novel type of spin-dependent sensor: a levitated ferromagnetic gyroscope (LFG). This mesoscopic object combines strongly correlated spins, mechanical isolation, and controllable quantum dynamics, offering a promising route toward even more sensitive measurements of exotic spin-dependent interactions. Speaker Bio: Derek F. Jackson Kimball's research uses techniques of experimental atomic physics for precision tests of the fundamental laws of physics. In particular, his research focuses on searches for exotic interactions that may have a connection to dark matter. Prof. Jackson Kimball is the Scientific Coordinator of two international collaborations using atomic magnetometers and nuclear magnetic resonance to search for interactions of ultralight bosonic dark matter fields with nuclear spins: the Global Network of Optical Magnetometers for Exotic physics searches (GNOME) and the Cosmic Axion Spin Precession Experiment (CASPEr). Prof. Jackson Kimball also works on the Search for Non-Interacting Particles Experimental Hunt (SNIPE Hunt), a multi-institution collaboration that uses magnetometers located in quiet magnetic environments to search for oscillating magnetic fields arising from the conversion of ultralight bosonic dark matter (axions and hidden photons) into photons. Another experimental focus is the development of a levitated ferromagnetic gyroscope (LFG), a new type of spin-dependent sensor. Prof. Jackson Kimball was awarded his Ph.D. in 2005 from the University of California at Berkeley under the mentorship of Prof. Dmitry Budker. Afterwards, he joined the faculty of California State University ��� East Bay where he has mentored over 90 undergraduate students in his research laboratory and has published three books and over 100 research papers. Three of his students have been awarded NSF Graduate Research Fellowships. Prof. Jackson Kimball was the 2020-21 Chair of the American Physical Society (APS) Topical Group on Precision Measurements and Fundamental Constants (GPMFC), chaired the 2023 Atomic Physics Gordon Conference, is the 2027 chair of the APS Apker Award Committee for undergraduate research in physics, and is presently serving as Secretary-Treasurer of APS's Division on Atomic, Molecular, and Optical Physics (DAMOP). He was named California State University – East Bay's Outstanding Professor in 2012, elected a fellow of the American Physical Society in 2018, received the Spitzer Distinguished Science Faculty Award in 2019, and in 2022 won the American Physical Society's Prize for Faculty Research at an Undergraduate Institution.

events.title: Decision Making with AI: Think Better, Choose Smarter (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) We are rapidly heading into an AI-driven future. At first, we feared it might cost us jobs, but now we see the bigger risk: it could cost us our judgment. When we outsource our thinking to fast answers, we lose the ability to ask better questions. To be ready for this future — to truly empower it — we must strengthen our uniquely human potential: clarity, critical thinking, and decision-making. That's what this workshop is about. In this interactive, hands-on session, participants will learn how to frame better decisions — before they ever open a chatbot. Using a practical tool called the Decision Framing Canvas, they'll work through a real business case and discover how to define decisions as real, actionable choices (not just goals or problems). At every step, participants will collaborate with AI — not to skip the thinking, but to deepen it. They'll use AI to challenge assumptions, expand options, and uncover what might be missing. This workshop helps participants take back control of their thinking in an AI-saturated world. It's not about better prompts — it's about better minds. Participants will walk away with a repeatable method to make smarter, clearer decisions in their daily work — and a deeper understanding of how to use AI not just as a tool, but as a thinking partner. No technical background required. Just bring your brain, your curiosity, and your favorite LLM (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc).Learning Outcomes: –Use the Decision Framing Canvas to define complex decisions as actionable choices between real options clearly. –Collaborate with AI to challenge assumptions, uncover blind spots, and expand decision options before jumping to solutions. –Learn key principles for working effectively with AI as a thinking partner — and apply them immediately to real decision-making scenarios.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as this virtual workshop date draws near.

events.title: Failure by design: The California energy crisis and the limits of market planning
events.description: With Georg Rilinger, Assistant Professor of Technological Innovation, Entrepreneurship, and Strategic Management, MIT Sloan School of Management The Western U.S. energy crisis was one of the great financial disasters of the past century. The crisis began in April 2000, when price spikes started to rattle California's electricity markets. Decades later, some blame economic fundamentals and ignorant politicians, while others accuse the energy sellers who raided the markets. In Failure by Design, sociologist Georg Rilinger offers a different explanation, one that focuses on the practical challenges of market design. The unique physical attributes of electricity made it exceedingly difficult to introduce markets into the coordination of the electricity system, so market designers were brought in to construct the infrastructures that coordinate how market participants interact. An exercise in social engineering, these infrastructures were intended to guide market actors toward behavior that would produce optimal market results and facilitate grid management. Yet, though these experts spent their days worrying about incentive misalignment and market manipulation, they unintentionally created a system riddled with opportunities for destructive behavior. Join us at BESI for this talk as Rilinger illuminates the California energy crisis and develops a broader theoretical framework for thinking about markets as the products of organizational planning and the limits of social engineering.Register Now (https://forms.gle/NGwAc9WuQseojhox9) About the speaker Georg Rilinger is an assistant professor of economic and organization sociology at MIT Sloan School of Management, where he holds the Fred Kayne Career Development Professorship. His research examines organizational, cultural, and political reasons why technocratic expertise — from Nobel Prize-winning market designers to financial regulators — so often fails to prevent market failures, drawing on archival research, interviews, and ethnographic methods. He is the author of Failure by Design: The California Energy Crisis and the Limits of Market Planning (University of Chicago Press, 2024), which won the Viviana Zelizer Prize for Best Book in Economic Sociology. His work has appeared in the American Journal of Sociology, Socio-Economic Review, Theory and Society, and others.

events.title: How to Survive Authoritarianism: A Russian's Phrasebook for Everyday Life in America
events.description: How to Survive Authoritarianism: A Russian's Phrasebook for Everyday Life in America Thursday, October 6, 12:30 - 2 pm Lunchtime Talk Institute of International Studies, 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/yD8LTQaNvyDeTDCa6)How to Survive Authoritarianism (https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324098799) offers Americans the tools needed to face the threat of authoritarianism today—from a country that's been surviving it for a century. Across the globe, far-right extremists are gaining power as checks and balances between branches of government dissolve at alarming rates. Author and activist Maria Kuznetsova and researcher Dan Storyev - who grew up in 2000s Russia when Vladimir Putin was tightening his grasp on the country and suffocating civic life - share the language that allowed them to talk about authoritarianism and to subvert it. Friends of Kuznetsova and Storyev's began asking what life was like in Russia, most having never experienced a dictatorship but increasingly worried they were about to learn. In attempting to answer their friends' questions of "How do you overcome fear of the state?" and maybe the most harrowing, "When is it too late?," Kuznetsova and Storyev draw upon their own experiences and the broader cultural memory of Russia to explore the basics of how authoritarian structures are built, and how ordinary people can resist. How to Survive Authoritarianism offers one hundred Russian idioms and turns of phrase for this purpose, from "apparatchik" to "samizdat." Some, like "power vertical," coined by Putin, give name to a hyper-centralized form of government with a top-down hierarchy of power. Others are more playful, like mnogohodovochka ("master plan"), used to deride bizarre, misguided state measures. Taken together, they make up the vocabulary we need to understand what is really taking place in our current moment and offer a roadmap to what might still lie ahead. In Russia, the dual reality of the truth, and what is called the truth by the government, has been the law of the land for generations. Over the years, a vernacular of double-speak emerged, one that helped everyday people make sense of how illiberalism makes itself known in daily life.

events.title: Lily Beckett | Poems on the London Underground (and Beyond)
events.description: Since 1986, Poems in the Underground has enabled commuters on London to randomly encounter poetry – classic and contemporary, British and international – while traveling on the tube, via poster cards slotted in the carriage advertising spaces. In conversation with Professor Eric Falci, Lily Beckett's talk will explore the history, development, and impact of Poems on the Underground as a public poetry project. Founded by Judith Chaiken (a native New Yorker), the idea for the project arose in the middle of Thatcher's premiership, a political moment characterised by an ideological turn away from the public and towards the private. Since its founding, the project has continued, uninterrupted, for 40 years, and has inspired multiple spin-off schemes abroad, with poetry being installed on transit systems in cities like Dublin, Paris, and New York. Adopting a socio-poetic angle, this talk offers Poems on the Underground as a prompt for further considering the value of poetry in public spaces. What does poetry do for the 'travelling public' of modern cities – whether in the 1980s in Britain under Thatcher, or today, anywhere in the world, in the age of AI?Lily Beckett is undertaking a PhD in Comparative Literatures and Cultures at the University of Bristol. She is currently a visiting scholar at UC Berkeley's Institute of European Studies. Her thesis investigates the connections between intermedial poetics and radical politics in the latter decades of the 20th century, across a range of global contexts. Before Bristol, she completed her master's degree in Comparative Literature at King's College London, and her undergraduate studies in Classics and English at Oxford University. She recently appeared on Soho Radio to discuss the lasting relevance of the 18th century poet William Blake, and her research papers can be found (or are forthcoming) in the academic journals Interfaces and Women's Studies.Eric Falci is a professor in the Department of English. He is the author of three books: Continuity and Change in Irish Poetry, 1966-2010 (2012); The Cambridge Introduction to British Poetry, 1945-2010 (2015); and The Value of Poetry (2020), as well as a number of essays on Irish and British poetry. With Paige Reynolds, he co-edited Irish Literature in Transition, 1980-2020 (2022). He is the series editor of Cambridge Elements in Poetry and Poetics, and the editor of the Cambridge History of Irish Poetry, scheduled to be published in 2026. He is also the author of a book of poetry, Late Along the Edgelands (2019). His research focus concerns the problem of form in twentieth and twenty-first century poetry. He teaches classes on modern Irish and British literature, and poetry.

events.title: Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics/Monetary Economics: "A Macroeconomic Model of the Cross-Section of Currencies"
events.description: Abstract: We study the cross-section of currencies using a macroeconomic model with heterogeneous countries, segmented asset markets, and risk-averse financial intermediaries. The model admits a two-factor structure of bilateral exchange rates. The factors combine global business cycle shocks and financial shocks that reprice the business cycle risk. Countries' exposures to these factors are heterogeneous and depend on their reliance on commodity exports and dollar asset holdings. We estimate the resulting factor structure empirically and use it to quantify the model. Our results indicate substantial heterogeneity in the drivers of dollar exchange rates across countries. Economies with high commodity exposure or low dollar holdings are risky, and their exchange rates fluctuate in response to global output and risk shocks. The exchange rates of countries with low commodity incidence and high dollar assets are less volatile, and their fluctuations are mostly determined by idiosyncratic local shocks.

events.title: Amara Ali | Beyond Delhi and Lucknow: The Lives of Urdu in Twentieth-Century Kashmir
events.description: A talk by Amara Ali, (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) Lecturer in Urdu, Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, that examines twentieth-century Kashmir as a distinctive center of Urdu literary culture through the evolution of Shia marṣiya.Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Tue, October 6, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————- ABSTRACT The history of Urdu has largely been told through its major centers, Delhi and Lucknow, with other regions positioned as peripheral recipients of a tradition formed elsewhere. This talk turns to Kashmir to complicate that geography, taking the twentieth century as its focus. This was a period in which Kashmir developed its own robust institutions of Urdu literary production and appreciation, from madrasas and administrative offices to mushāʿira gatherings and radio broadcasts. Multilingualism has long been part and parcel of Kashmiri intellectual and cultural life, with different languages holding prominence in different periods: Sanskrit, then Persian, and eventually Urdu. To trace how this played out in the twentieth century, the talk turns to Kashmiri Shia marṣiya, a devotional genre, and its jadīd (modern) forms, which register this movement between languages and make visible Kashmir's own productive engagement with Urdu. SPEAKER BIOAmara Ali (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) is a Lecturer in the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies. Her research centers on the interplay of Urdu, Hindi, and Kashmiri literary traditions and Islam in South Asia. Her doctoral dissertation provides a literary examination of the Kashmiri marsiya (an elegiac poem), analyzing how this local form articulates a unique Kashmiri aesthetic, while remaining in critical dialogue with the broader Urdu, Persian, and Arabic literary traditions. Earlier, she completed her master's studies at the University of Cambridge, focusing on the celebrated Urdu poets Mirza Ghalib and Faiz Ahmed Faiz.Event Poster TBA —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Zionism in Translation: Encounters in the German-Hebrew Archive
events.description: n her new book, Zionism in Translation: Encounters in the German-Hebrew Archive, Na'ama Rokem investigates written exchanges by a range of literary twentieth century authors, including Hannah Arendt, Gershom Scholem, Yehuda Amichai, Ludwig Strauss, Erich Auerbach, Walter Benjamin, Leah Goldberg, Peter Szondi, Paul Celan, and Tuvia Ruebner. This remarkable bilingual archive encompasses not only letters but also drafts, reviews, and other ephemeral documents. Written in German and Hebrew, these documents were sent to and from Jerusalem, primarily in the decades following 1948. The writers at the center of Rokem's study contend with the genocidal violence that brought the rich historical relation between German and Hebrew to a seeming end. They also grapple, in different ways, with the new reality in Israel/Palestine in the wake of the founding of the State of Israel and the Palestinian Nakba. The bilingual conversation that crosses over between German and Hebrew in these letters thus centers around the question of Jewish fate in the twentieth century and is immersed in negotiations about Jewish nationalism, the Zionist movement, and the possibilities of Jewish poetry. In the space between German and Hebrew, Rokem argues, the protagonists of her study articulate forms of ambivalence and doubt that remain absent from their published writings. In this book presentation, Rokem will discuss forms of belonging and resistance that emerged in relation to the Zionist movement throughout the twentieth century, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of Jewish nationalism and its discontents.To register for this event, please click this link. (https://forms.gle/5p6thMQDtfz5LarP8)Na'ama Rokem teaches Hebrew and Comparative Literature at the University of Chicago, where she has served as director of the Joyce Z. and Jacob Greenberg Center for Jewish Studies and as chair of the Department of Comparative Literature. Zionism in Translation: Encounters in the German-Hebrew Archive (University of Chicago Press, 2026) is her second book. Her first book, Prosaic Conditions: Heinrich Heine and the Spaces of Zionist Literature, was published by Northwestern University Press in 2013. It uses the case of the reception and translation of the works of German-Jewish poet Heinrich Heine to argue that prose - as a figure of thought, a mode and a medium - played an instrumental role in the literary foundations of the Zionist revolution. Currently, she is working as one of the co-editors of the forthcoming Volume IV.2 of the Critical Edition of the Complete Works of Hannah Arendt (https://hannah-arendt-edition.net/index.html?lang=en) (Essays and Short Writings on Jewish Politics) and starting a new research project on Zionism and pedagogy. Rokem has been involved in a number of collaborative projects, including The Quest for Modern Language: Between the Mediterranean and the Black Sea (https://neubauercollegium.uchicago.edu/research/the-quest-for-modern-language-between-the-mediterranean-and-black-sea-1820-1948#:~:text=This%20is%20a%20collaborative%2C%20multidisciplinary,19th%20and%20early%2020th%20centuries.), and Translation Networks and the Stakes of Comparison: Convergences and Crossings Between Arabic and Hebrew (https://neubauercollegium.uchicago.edu/research/translation-networks), both sponsored by the Neubauer Collegium on Culture and Society at the University of Chicago, and the Oak Woods Cemetery (https://www.oakwoodsproject.org/) project, a public history initiative that uses a historic cemetery in Woodlawn as a site for teaching, programming, and researching the history of the South Side of Chicago, with a particular interest in the complexly intertwined histories of African Americans and Jews in the city. This project has received funding from the NEH, the Mellon Foundation, and the Women's Board at the University of Chicago. ��� If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in these events, please contact Jennifer Lipscomb at jlipscomb@berkeley.edu (mailto:jlipscomb@berkeley.edu?subject=Accommodation%20Needed%20for%20CJS%20Event) with as much advance notice as possible. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Diego Pirillo
events.description: The Atlantic Republic of Letters (Pennsylvania, 2026) offers an alternative intellectual history of early America. Focusing on Benjamin Franklin's Philadelphia, the book frames Euro-American colonialism as an intellectual enterprise, established not only through military and economic means but also through books, ideas, and cultural institutions. Through extensive archival research, Diego Pirillo (Italian) brings together two interconnected histories. First, he recovers the place of British America in the cosmopolitan world of the Republic of Letters, studying the communication system that facilitated the transatlantic circulation of knowledge. Second, he shows that knowledge was weaponized in the effort to survey and control North America. While fashioning themselves as independent and cosmopolitan scholars, Franklin and his associates were in fact deeply tied to political power and tailored their ideas to the needs of their patrons. They served as agents of empire and helped to devise and put into practice the colonial project. Not only were books, libraries, and cultural institutions funded by the wealth created by the slave trade and the expropriation of Indigenous land, but, as Pirillo argues, the very taxonomies and classification systems that Euro-American scholars devised directly shaped the colonial enterprise. The Atlantic Republic of Letters illuminates the relationship among books, intellectuals, and colonial governance, and explores the ways in which knowledge circulated and shaped conquest. Pirillo is joined by Brian DeLay (History). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.description: Leo Martinez is an assistant professor in the Division of Epidemiology at the UC Berkeley School of Public Health. He studies the epidemiology of tuberculosis and other infectious diseases, with a focus on how social, biological, and programmatic factors shape who becomes infected, who develops disease, and who experiences long-term health consequences. Dr. Martinez uses epidemiologic, statistical, and quantitative approaches to study tuberculosis transmission and prevention in high-burden settings and among populations at elevated risk, including children, people living with HIV, people with diabetes, and incarcerated populations. Much of his work centers on early-life risk factors for pediatric tuberculosis, the role of nutrition and growth in tuberculosis risk, tuberculosis transmission in congregate settings, and the relationship between tuberculosis and chronic disease outcomes. His research is highly collaborative and is conducted with colleagues and public health partners in the United States and globally, including in South Africa, Kenya, Brazil, China, and Indonesia. Through these partnerships, his work aims to produce evidence that can inform tuberculosis prevention policy, improve screening and treatment strategies, and reduce disparities in tuberculosis burden. Prior to joining UC Berkeley, Dr. Martinez was a faculty member in the Department of Epidemiology at the Boston University School of Public Health.
