events.title: Nina Miolane: Science of Intelligence Seminar Series
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. events.title: The Loft Hour: Mark Minch-de Leon + Latanya d. Tigner
events.description: Elevate your lunch break with The Loft Hour, a year-long series that invites Berkeley Arts faculty to riff on their work over lunch, in an informal conversation moderated by an ARC-affiliated faculty member. The year will kick off in October with welcoming Mark Minch-de Leon (Associate Professor, Film & Media) and Latanya d. Tigner (Assistant Professor, Dance) in conversation with Tadiwa Madenga (Assistant Professor, English). Mark Minch-de Leon is an Associate Professor in the Department of Film & Media. He was most recently an Associate Professor of Indigenous studies in the Department of English at UC Riverside where he also directed the California Center for Native Nations. His current research focuses on Indigenous anticolonial resistance and its relation to communism and anarchism, radical conceptions of community and understandings of violence, and Indigenous theories and practices of aesthetics and media-making before, beyond, against, and after settler life. His recently published book, Indigenous Inhumanities: California Indian Studies After the Apocalypse looks at the anticolonial, nonvitalist dimensions of California Indian intellectual and cultural resurgence in the wake of destruction. His publications include Race and the Limitations of 'the Human' in After the Human, and Atlas for a Destroyed World: Frank Day's Painting as Work of Nonvital Revitalization in Native American and Indigenous Studies. Professor Minch-de Leon received his AA in Liberal Studies from Butte Community College, his BA in Philosophy from CSU Chico, and his PhD in Rhetoric with an Emphasis in Gender, Women, and Sexuality from UC Berkeley. He is a member of the Susanville Indian Rancheria and co-founder of the California Indian Studies and Scholars Association. Latanya d. Tigner, a longtime member and administrator of Oakland's esteemed Dimensions Dance Theater, Inc., holds a B.A. in Physical Education/Dance, a Master's in Arts Administration, and is certified in the Yanvalu Level 2 of Talawa Technique™, the first American to do so. Her time with Dimensions includes studying Guinea, Senegalese, South African, Cuban, Haitian, modern, and jazz dance, as well as performing multidisciplinary contemporary works anchored in African diasporic dance and the African American experience. Latanya's research-based choreographic work has afforded her the opportunity to serve as co-artistic director of the renowned San Francisco Ethnic Dance Festival from 2018-2021, as well as led to the creation of Dancing Cy(i)phers in 2019. Latanya became a lecturer for TDPS in 2016 after leading the dance program at Contra Costa College for eight years. In 2018, she developed the course African Dance Presence in Hip Hop, based on her Here We Go Again workshop developed in 2014 that unfolds her research and "movement line" pedagogy. In Spring 2021, she received The Michael Mansfield and Randy Sweringen Social Justice Award for Artistic Excellence in Creating a More Equitable and Inclusive World. Latanya has commissioned works for Dimensions Dance Theater, Black Choreographers Festival, Robert Moses' Kin, UC Berkeley, Mills College, and has presented work in SF Ethnic Dance Festival, CubaCaribe, and Mabina Dance Festival (Congo-Brazzaville). She has also choreographed for SF Shakespeare, Oakland Theater Project, Lorraine Hansberry Theater, Cal Shakes, Contra Costa College, Li Smith's Victorious, and co-choreographed Delina Brooks' An Open Love Letter to Black Fathers. She received best choreography nominations in theater in 2017 and 2025. Her new work, Reclaiming the Void, will premiere in collaboration with the creator of the Talawa Technique, Dr. Thomas Talawa Presto. She has presented workshops at Collegium of the African Diaspora Dance (CADD), International Association of Black in Dance (IABD), California Dance Education Association (CDEA), National Dance Education Organization (NDEO), Intangible Roots at USC, Show and Prove at UC Riverside, University of the West Indies (Barbados), and in Paris. She has also served as a member of the Hewlett Foundation's Arts Education Task Force, a board member for the California Dance Education Association, and as an advisor for Alliance for California Traditional Arts' Taproot Initiative. Latanya currently serves on the board of directors for the Alliance for California Traditional Arts. Tadiwa Madenga is a scholar of African and Black diasporic literature, gender and sexuality, and print cultures. Her research is concerned with the relationship between literature and sexuality which she traces through 20th and 21st century African book fairs and their subgenres: keynotes, book stalls, magazines, poetry. Across her academic and creative projects, her reading practice centers archival work and site specificity as critical methods for literary analysis. These interests converge in her current research project which focuses on the emergence of African queer literature and politics through the Zimbabwe International Book Fair. The book fair was a preeminent destination for African literature and arts throughout the 1980s and 1990s, but it also became notorious for staging public debates around race and homosexuality. By examining how the book fair functioned as a contested site that codified the limits and possibilities of sexual freedom, the project also reconsiders what genres and spaces are imagined to be the foundational subjects of African literary studies and Black queer studies. Madenga's research has been supported by various fellowships and grants at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences, the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs, the Center for Black, Brown, and Queer Studies, and the Hutchins Centre for African and African American Research at Harvard University.

events.title: Enemies in Agreement: Political Volatility and the Design of Arms Control
events.description: Enemies in Agreement: Political Volatility and the Design of Arms Control Wednesday, October 7, 3:30 to 5 pm Institute of International Studies, 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/T9JoQxrtVy2JcxvP6) Why do adversaries sometimes cooperate to restrain their military competition? Why do they design arms control agreements with intrusive verification in some cases but rely on minimal transparency in others? Amidst ongoing international competition, arms control remains rare despite potential mutual benefits, and agreements vary dramatically in their approaches to monitoring. Jane Vaynman will discuss her book, Enemies in Agreement: Political Volatility and the Design of Arms Control (https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/politics-international-relations/international-relations-and-international-organisations/enemies-agreement-political-volatility-and-design-arms-control?format=HB&isbn=9781009486507/resources#description). The book reveals how uncertainty from domestic political changes — such as leadership transitions or social unrest — can enable arms control. It identifies two paths to agreement: during periods of uncertainty, states that previously relied on informal understandings hedge by establishing lightly-monitored agreements, while those that anticipated deception take calculated risks through agreements with intensive verification. Through comprehensive data analysis and rich case studies, Jane Vaynman challenges conventional wisdom about uncertainty in international relations while offering insights for policymakers. As states confront challenges from nuclear competition to emerging technologies, understanding when arms control becomes viable is more vital than ever. Dr. Jane Vaynman is an Assistant Professor of Strategic Studies at the School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS) at Johns Hopkins University. Dr. Vaynman's work focuses on security cooperation between adversarial states, the design of arms control agreements, and the effects of technology on patterns of international cooperation and competition. From 2022-2024 she served a senior advisor in the Bureau of Arms Control, Deterrence, and Stability at the U.S. Department of State. Her prior academic appointments include the Department of Political Science at Temple University and the Elliott School of International Affairs, George Washington University. She was also previously a Lightning Scholar at Perry World House at the University of Pennsylvania, a Stanton Nuclear Security Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, and a Fulbright Fellow at the Carnegie Moscow Center. Dr. Vaynman received her Ph.D. in political science from Harvard University and B.A. from in international relations from Stanford University.

events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - Experiments in Art and Geography
events.description: In this lecture, Trevor Paglen presents a framework for thinking about what happens when artistic practice and geographic method are fused together. Drawing on his work on mass surveillance, computer vision and AI, psyops, and neuroscience, Paglen will discuss art-making not simply as a means of representing geographic research, but as a geographic research method in its own right. Artistic practice can function as a form of fieldwork: a way of investigating landscapes, infrastructures, technologies, and institutions while developing new forms through which to understand them. Paglen will explore how this hybrid practice creates opportunities for collaboration across disciplines and produces forms of knowledge that do not fit neatly within conventional academic or artistic categories. The talk argues that occupying a position neither fully within art nor geography can generate questions, methods, objects, and ways of seeing that neither discipline could produce on its own. Trevor Paglen is a multidisciplinary artist whose practice explores technology, infrastructure, and perception across exhibitions, publications, and public projects worldwide. A MacArthur Fellow and 2026 LG Guggenheim Award winner, he holds advanced degrees from UC Berkeley and the Art Institute of Chicago.

events.title: California Spotlight: Wealth & Poverty
events.description: REGISTER California is one of the wealthiest states in the country, yet it also faces persistent poverty, stark economic inequality, and some of the highest costs of living in the nation. These tensions raise fundamental questions about who benefits from California's economic growth and why so many residents struggle to achieve economic security. This panel brings together leading scholars to examine the forces shaping wealth and poverty across the state. Drawing on research spanning inequality, affordability, economic mobility, and social policy, the discussion will explore the roots of California's economic divides, how they are reproduced across generations, and what is at stake for families, communities, and the future of the state. This panel will feature David Grusky, Edward Ames Edmonds Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, and Professor of Sociology at Stanford; Marianne Page, Professor of Economics and Director of the Center for Poverty Research at UC Davis; and Samuel Trachtman, Senior Researcher at the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative at UC Berkeley. Evan White, Executive Director of the California Policy Lab at UC Berkeley, will moderate. This event is co-sponsored by the Goldman School of Public Policy, the Institute for Research on Labor and Employment, the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative, and the Opportunity Lab.PanelistsDavid Grusky (https://grusky.people.stanford.edu/) is Edward Ames Edmonds Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, Professor of Sociology, Senior Fellow at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, Faculty Fellow at the Center for Population Health Sciences, Faculty Director of the Stanford Center on Poverty and Inequality, and coeditor of Pathways Magazine. He is a member of the National Academy of Sciences and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, a corecipient of the 2004 Max Weber Award, the founder of the Cornell University Center for the Study of Inequality, and a former Presidential Young Investigator. His recent books are Inequality in the 21st Century (with Jasmine Hill, 2017), Social Stratification (with Kate Weisshaar, 2014), Occupy the Future (with Douglas McAdam, Robert Reich, and Debra Satz, 2012), The New Gilded Age (with Tamar Kricheli-Katz, 2011), and The Great Recession (with Bruce Western and Chris Wimer, 2011).Marianne Page (https://mepage.faculty.ucdavis.edu/) is a Professor of Economics (https://economics.ucdavis.edu/) and a founding director of the Center for Poverty Research at UC Davis (http://poverty.ucdavis.edu/). She is a Research Associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research and member of the Institute for Labor Economics. She currently serves as a Co-Editor of the Journal of Human Resources, and recently completed a term serving on Governor Newsom's Council of Economic Advisors. She is an expert on policies promoting intergenerational mobility and equality of opportunity for children in the United States. Her research has appeared in economics journals including the Quarterly Journal of Economics, the American Economic Review. and the Journal of Labor Economics, and has been funded by the National Science Foundation, National Institutes of Health, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.Sam Trachtman (https://besi.berkeley.edu/people/samuel-trachtman/) is a senior researcher at the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative (BESI), where he leads the research program on the political economy of California. Sam completed his Ph.D. in political science in 2021 at UC Berkeley, where he honed skills in quantitative methods and policy-engaged empirical research. He has published widely in academic journals including American Political Science Review, Climatic Change, Governance, Legislative Studies Quarterly, Nature Energy, Public Opinion Quarterly, and Perspectives on Politics.Evan White (https://capolicylab.org/staff/evan-white/) co-founded the California Policy Lab, which generates research insights for government impact. Through hands-on partnerships with government, CPL performs research across issue silos and builds the data infrastructure necessary to improve programs that millions of Californians rely on. Since 2017, CPL has helped conduct 300+ projects with 75+ agency partners. As Executive Director, Evan leads the Lab's Berkeley site and authors reports on household finance, migration, and poverty. Prior to joining CPL, Evan served as Senior Advisor to the first Director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Evan also served as Director of Fair Housing for northern California's largest fair housing nonprofit. He holds a joint degree in Law and Public Policy from UC Berkeley.

events.title: Disasters of Biblical Proportions: Reimagining the Ten Plagues in the Age of Covid and October 7
events.description: The biblical story of the ten plagues, the series of disasters sent against Pharaoh and the Egyptian in order to compel them to free the Israelites, introduced into collective imagination a connection between disaster and justice. In this presentation, StevenWeitzman will explore how Jews, Christians and Muslims have reimagined the biblical story to make sense of the disasters and injustices of their own age, focusing on how the story has been reshaped in the wake of the traumatic events and protests that have unfolded since October 7, 2023.To register for this event, please click this link.Steven Weitzman serves as the Ella Darivoff Director of the Herbert D. Katz Center for Advanced Judaic Studies at the University of Pennsylvania as well as the Abraham M. Ellis Professor of Semitic Languages and Literatures in the Department of Religious Studies. His previous academic roles include directing Stanford's Taube Center for Jewish Studies. Recent publications include The Origin of the Jews: the Search for Roots in a Rootless Age; the coedited Princeton Companion to Jewish Studies; Disasters of Biblical Proportions: the Ten Plagues Then, Now, and at the End of the World (the basis of this talk); and The Jews: a History, co-written with John Efron and Matthias Lehmann and now in its fourth edition.

events.title: ERG Colloquium Series Fall 2026: Josh Apte
events.description: Description: More than 50 years after the Clean Air Act, Americans breathe far cleaner air, yet people of color and overburdened communities still breathe more pollution than everyone else. Why does unequal air persist while overall air quality improves? Drawing on recent results from hyperlocal field measurements and model simulations, I will present evidence on key drivers of air pollution disparities. With a view towards identifying solutions, we'll explore how targeted, place-based interventions could prove decisive in providing cleaner, more equitable air for all. Bio: Joshua Apte is associate professor of Environmental Engineering and Environmental Health Sciences at University of California, Berkeley. His group uses a combination of air quality models and field measurements to understand sources, processes and impacts that affect air quality from the neighborhood to global scale. Apte earned his MS and PhD in Energy and Resources (2008, 2013) from UC Berkeley.

events.title: (Screening) No Monastery, No Village | Voices from the Roof of the World
events.description: In recognition of the devastating mud flood that struck Nepal's Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems on August 26, claiming thousands of lives, ISAS will screen a documentary about a remote Himalayan village (located in Limi Valley of Humla District, northwestern Nepal) with an eleventh-century Buddhist monastery at its center confronting the threat of a catastrophic glacial flood. Produced in 2024, the documentary examines the accelerating effects of climate change on Himalayan glaciers and the resulting dangers of glacial erosion, instability, and flooding. It therefore offers a timely perspective on the environmental conditions underlying the recent tragic flooding. Directed by climate activist and filmmaker Tashi Lhazom (https://nepalclimatehub.org/climate-champions/thasi-lhazom), the film is part of the series Voices from the Roof of the World (https://www.aku.edu/vrw/Pages/home.aspx), produced by Aga Khan University in collaboration with Shanta Nepali Productions.Running time: 28 minutes. Watch the trailer HERE (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wDBhThOUHjk). The screening will be followed by a moderated conversation with Tashi Lhazom, who will join us remotely. Dr. Ran Ran (https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=oSdIhKQAAAAJ&hl=en) 冉冉, a Senior Research Fellow at the School of Government, Shenzhen University and currently based in Stanford and Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer), Assistant Professor of History will serve as discussants. The discussion will be moderated by Alexander von Rospatt (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/alexander-von-rospatt), Professor of Buddhist and South Asian Studies and Director of the Group in Buddhist Studies at UC Berkeley. The event is FREE, but reservations are required. Please reserve your seat HERE (https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_avDi1InTQXCrNjCAA9SkjQ) ————–DATE: Wed, October 7, 2026 TIME: 5:30-7 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall REGISTRATION: The event is FREE but registration is required. Please register HERE (https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_avDi1InTQXCrNjCAA9SkjQ) ———��—- ABOUT THE DOCUMENTARY High in Nepal's remote Limi Valley, the village of Halzi is home to around 500 people whose lives revolve around the 11th-century Waltse Rinchenling Buddhist Monastery, the spiritual and cultural heart of the community. But just a few kilometers upstream, a rapidly melting glacier poses an existential threat. A previous glacial flood has already caused destruction, and scientists warn that another could wipe out both the village and the monastery. The film follows residents as they confront an impossible choice: leave their ancestral home for safety, or remain to protect a sacred way of life rooted in faith, memory, and place. Through the experiences of villagers including monk Sonam Dhondup and yak herder Pema Dolma, the documentary explores the tension between devotion and survival, revealing how climate change is not only transforming a Himalayan landscape but also threatening an entire cultural world. Running time 28 minutes. See the trailer HERE (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wDBhThOUHjk) ABOUT THE DIRECTORTashi Lhazom (https://nepalclimatehub.org/climate-champions/thasi-lhazom) is a prominent youth climate advocate working at the intersection of climate action, gender equality, indigenous rights, and political and climate literacy. She has spoken at grassroots, national, and global platforms, and is a co-founder of two civil society initiatives. With the wide range of hats that Tashi wears, she is also a filmmaker that harnesses the power of storytelling to promote generational change in delivering climate justice. "No Monastery, No Village" is her directorial debut based on the nexus of climate change and cultural heritage of indigenous people. As an academician, she covers climate diplomacy and politics. She holds an undergraduate degree from Hindu College, University of Delhi. She specializes in Climate Politics. ABOUT THE DISCUSSANTDr. Ran Ran (https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=oSdIhKQAAAAJ&hl=en) 冉冉 is a Senior Research Fellow at the School of Government, Shenzhen University. Her research interests include comparative environmental politics, climate change and climate justice. Prior to joining Shenzhen University, Dr. Ran was an Associate Professor at Renmin University of China. She earned her Ph.D. from the University of Duisburg-Essen in 2009 and subsequently held a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of Southern California from 2009 to 2010. Dr. Ran's research has been published in journals including the Journal of Environmental Policy & Planning, The China Quarterly, and the Journal of Cleaner Production, among others. Her current book project examines how strong state capacity in authoritarian systems produces both effective environmental outcomes, blame politics and environmental injustice, particularly for vulnerable rural communities. Her 2015 book examined the paradox of the "environmental policy implementation gap" in China's local authoritarian environmentalism. Dr. Ran was selected as one of the "Chinese Highly Cited Researchers in Political Science" by Elsevier from 2021 to 2025 EVENT POSTER TBD —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Tang Music in Contemporary China: Sensing Artistry Through Time
events.description: Tang Music in Contemporary China: Sensing Artistry Through Time October 8 Keynote Lecture (125 Morrison Hall) October 9 (125 Morrison Hall) October 10 (Hertz Hall)— F (https://events.berkeley.edu/live/files/54-tang-music-in-contemporary-china)ull program available here (https://events.berkeley.edu/live/files/57-tang-music-in-contemporary-china) ��� The resplendent court-entertainment music of the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE), born from cultural exchange along the early Silk Road, has always loomed large in histories of Chinese music. But in today's China, reconstructive performances of this music have begun to assert its place �� as living, breathing performance art — in concert halls and social media feeds, too. This conference brings together scholars and performers from across the world, including leading and emerging experts from China, to present, evaluate, and propel forward global scholarly and artistic discourse on Tang music in the contemporary world. Papers will explore the material culture of the Silk Road, early notations and musical instruments, techniques of historical reconstruction and performance, and the place of historical music and dance in contemporary Chinese society. Three leading ensembles from China and the United States will give live performances of Tang music and dance, followed by a roundtable discussion bringing scholarship and performance into critical dialogue.

events.title: Coffee with the Librarian: Resources, Strategies & Hidden Treasures for Research on Latin America and the Caribbean
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.location: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies | 2334 Bowditch Street, Berkeley
events.description: Event Description Are you a graduate student researching Latin America? Join us for coffee, snacks, and an informal conversation with Liladhar Pendse, UC Berkeley's Librarian for the Caribbean, Latin American and Latinx Studies Collections. In this session, Dr. Pendse will share practical strategies for finding books, articles, archival materials, primary sources, and other resources for research on Latin America. We'll explore how to make the most of Berkeley's library collections and databases — including search strategies that can help you move beyond the first page of results and uncover resources you might otherwise miss. Dr. Pendse will also offer a preview of a new library research guide on Black presence in Latin America, currently in development. The guide brings together resources for researching Black histories, communities, cultures, and experiences across the region. Because Latin America encompasses such a vast and diverse geographic area, the guide is very much a work in progress — but students will get an early look at what is already available and learn how to use these resources in their own research.Bring your research questions! This is an opportunity to learn about library resources while getting advice tailored to the questions and topics you are pursuing.SpeakerDr.Liladhar Pendse is UC Berkeley's Librarian for the Caribbean, Latin American and Latinx Studies Collections, as well as the Librarian for Slavic, East European, and Central Asian Studies Collections. He works to strengthen UC Berkeley's holdings, support students and scholars conducting research across these regions, and help connect researchers with the library's extensive print, digital, archival, and primary-source collections. Dr. Pendse holds an MA in Latin American Studies, an MLIS, and a Ph.D. in Information Studies from UCLA.

events.title: Author Larissa Lai: Echolocating Asian Canadian Studies: A Poethical Method for the Long COVID Moment
events.description: At the height of the COVID pandemic, the bat emerged from the Wuhan wet market as a racializing figure entangled with tropes of infection and consumption, re-activating late 19th century associations of Asians with disease. This essay reclaims the bat, both as a figure and as an existing animal, to consider how to engage with Asian Canadian Studies in this historical moment. Both racial and state formations are impossible to claim in essentializing or nationalist ways, and yet, "Asian Canadian" remains a productive location from which to do the work of both community building and critique. This talk considers phenomenological and poethical approaches to cultural embodiment, with a particular focus on the bat's ability to orient itself in flight by echolocation. Echolocation can be used to consider three possible moments of inception for Asian Canadian Studies - the 1910s, the 1970s, and the 1990s. It can also be used to consider the field's relationships with Indigenous Studies, Black Canadian Studies, Asian American Studies, and Queer and Gender Studies.Larissa Lai is the author of nine books including The Lost Century, The Tiger Flu, Salt Fish Girl, and Slanting I, Imagining We: Asian Canadian Literary Production in the 1980s and 1990s. Recipient of the Jim Duggins Novelist's Prize, the Lambda Literary Award, the Astraea Award, and the Otherwise Honor Book, she has also been a finalist for the ACQL Gabrielle Roy Prize for Literary Criticism, the Books in Canada First Novel Award and the Governor General's Award. She is currently the Richard Charles Lee Chair of Chinese Canadian Studies at the University of Toronto. Born in California, Professor Lai grew up in Newfoundland. She received her BA from the University of British Columbia, her MA from the University of East Anglia, and her PhD from the University of Calgary.

events.title: Cycads, Wild Black Peppers, and Amazonian roots: the role of plant specialized chemistry at three different scales
events.description: Specialized metabolites play critical roles in plant evolution and ecology, yet most of what we know about this rich and diverse organic arsenal comes from foliar tissues and local scales. As chemical ecology is being transformed by higher-resolution instrumentation and novel machine-learning approaches for data processing and analysis, scientists have ventured into larger-scale studies (geographically, environmentally, and phylogenetically). Furthermore, a more "holistic" understanding of plant chemistry has highlighted key differences in the likely mechanisms driving the evolution of chemical diversity across plant tissues. In this talk, I will present three research projects that highlight the role of plant specialized metabolites across different scales (from local to regional). This project also highlights fundamental trade-offs and constraints on phytochemical arsenals across plant tissues (leaves, roots, and seeds).

events.title: Symposium on Trans Negativity
events.location: 315 Wheeler Hall (Maude Fife Room), UC Berkeley, and The Lab, 2948 16th St, San Francisco
events.description: Trans negativity names a negative relation to trans life, as it presents itself in the devaluation of trans people across contemporary discourses, the withholding of rights and care, and the mobilization of suffering in public policy and anti-gender movements. At the same time, trans negativity also names an exciting turn within trans thought that, drawing on debates that have shaped queer theory for over two decades, refuses to be edifying and instead embraces the bleak, dissociative, and antagonistic. This symposium seeks to engage various senses of the negative and to elaborate its implications for trans study. Gathering scholars and artists working across psychoanalysis, aesthetics, theory, and political history, our program takes on negativity as an occasion for collective thought and practice.Program:Thursday, October 8, 4 - 5:30 pm Maude Fife, 315 Wheeler Hall, UC Berkeley. Grace Lavery presents her new book Personal Demons, in conversation with Jessy Nyiri and Ava Kim.Friday, October 9,9.45am - 6 pm Maude Fife, 315 Wheeler Hall, UC Berkeley. Paper presentations and panel discussions with Cameron Awkward-Rich, Salar Mameni, Jack Halberstam, Zakiyyah Iman Jackson, Roshanak Kheshti, Joshua Falek, Eva Hayward, Jessy Nyiri, Damon Young, Lieks Hettinga, Ava Kim, Willa Smart, Hil Malatino, Ianna Hawkins Owen, Julian Kevon Kamilah Glover, aeryka hollis-o'neil, Eric Stanley, Chris Lee.Saturday, October 10, 1 - 3 pm The Lab, 2948 16th Street, San Francisco. Jack Halberstam and artist Leila Weefur in conversation, preceded by a reading by Cameron Awkward-Rich. The Trans Negativity symposium is organized by Be Schierenberg and Simon(e) van Saarloos and sponsored by the Center for the Study of Sexual Culture (CSSC), the Center for Race and Gender, Othering & Belonging Institute, the Center for Interdisciplinary Critical Inquiry (CICI), Arts Research Center, the Townsend Center for the Humanities, the Trans Student Wellness Initiative (TSWI), The Big C, Asian American and Asian Diaspora Studies, Gender & Women's Studies, and the Departments of Rhetoric, German, and English at UC Berkeley.To stay up to date about the program, please register here. events.title: 2026 Gerald D. Feldman Lecture | Reckoning with the Past in Germany and the United States: The Case for Thinking Comparatively about Reparative Justice
events.description: German atonement for the Holocaust has been widely hailed by the international community as a paragon of national reckoning, and over the last decade, African American intellectuals such as Ta-Nehisi Coates have explicitly invoked Germany as a useful model in their calls for Americans to confront the legacy of slavery and other forms of state-sanctioned racism. In this lecture, Rita Chin, will trace the complicated, fraught 80-year process by which Germans have dealt with the Nazi past, focusing on developments and debates in the Federal Republic. She will consider the specific ways in which the German case is instructive for Americans seeking to pursue redress but also explore how Germany's vaunted memory culture has become fossilized such that it has sometimes become a stumbling block for a German society struggling to respond to contemporary challenges. Thinking comparatively about how to reckon with legacies of state-sanctioned racial harm, oppression, and violence not only presents Americans with a concrete template for imagining what reparative justice might look like, Chin suggests, it may also help Germans acknowledge the shape-shifting aspects of racism and perhaps even rethink some of the outdated aspects of their memory culture. Rita Chin, Louise A. Tilly Collegiate Professor of European History and Associate Dean of Social Sciences of the Rackham Graduate School at the University of Michigan, is a historian of modern Europe with particular expertise in immigration and human mobility, race and ethnicity, and colonialism and post-colonialism. Trained in European cultural and intellectual history, she has sought to apply these modes of inquiry to her ongoing interest in how difference and diversity have shaped the very terms of modern Germany and Europe more generally. Her research and writing have been supported by the SSRC, the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, the ACLS Burkhardt Fellowship for Recently Tenured Scholars, the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, and the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation. events.title: Matthew Shutzer | Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis
events.description: A talk by Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer), Assistant Professor of History, on his new book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis (https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691265919/until-the-last-ton?srsltid=AfmBOorxSc-xwrFM8YrmGZbYMJ4vEm3ZcucGahHadYBaRZA9ySGhXWds), a panoramic historical account of India's ascent in the global fossil economy. Event moderated by Sharad Chari (https://geography.berkeley.edu/professor-sharad-chari), Associate Professor of Geography, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, Oct 8, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————–About the Book: India is today one of the world's largest producers and consumers of fossil fuels, driving new investments in the global fossil economy and achieving record-breaking levels of coal extraction at home. As the planet burns from climate change, this entrenchment of fossil fuel dependence has left many searching for how we arrived at this point. Until the Last Ton provides a sweeping new appraisal of this planetary dilemma, uncovering how India became part of an emerging fossil capitalism that continues to shape the present. Matthew Shutzer recasts the origins of the fossil economy by showing how European industrialization unleashed a global search for fossil energy in the colonial world. Placing India at the center of this history, Shutzer traces how the highland forests of eastern India became early frontiers for global coal investment, transforming this landscape into the largest site of imperial overseas coal production across a century of colonial rule. At the heart of these shifts was a legal framework of subterranean property, which redefined local relations of land ownership and social power, while tying the growth of India's fossil economy to the progressive ecological destruction of the forest frontier. Following these dynamics into the postcolonial period, Until the Last Ton reveals the enduring impacts of colonial property on independent India's energy history, shedding new light on postwar struggles for energy development and resource sovereignty, as well as the violent conflicts over mining dispossession that have haunted India's economic ascent in an age of climate crisis.About the Author:Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer) is Assistant Professor of History at University of California, Berkeley. He is an environmental historian of South Asia. His research and teaching focus on the place of the environment in global history, with particular attention to fossil fuels, agriculture, forests, climate change, and environmental politics. His work also connects global environmental history to histories of law, capitalism, post-colonial development, the earth sciences, and photography. His book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis, is the first history of fossil fuels in colonial and post-colonial South Asia. It traces India's rise as a world-leading fossil economy in the twentieth century and examines the processes of empire, capitalism, and agroecological change that shaped this transformation. The book moves beyond the prevailing focus in the environmental history of energy on production and consumption, offering instead a longer-term perspective on land, subsurface property rights, geological knowledge, and mining conflicts. In doing so, it reveals the central role of agrarian development in shaping India's trajectory of fossil fuel dependence. Shutzer is currently working on a second book project examining climate change and the making of the Third World after 1945. Before joining the History Department at UC Berkeley, Shutzer taught as an Assistant Professor in the Department of History at Duke University. He previously served as a Junior Scholar at the Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies at Harvard University and as an S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup Fellow in Natural Resource Economics and Political Economy in the Department of Geography at UC Berkeley. He has also worked as a researcher on several projects related to the implementation of India's Forest Rights Act in western Odisha. Along with Rebecca Herman, Rebecca McLennan, and Bernadette Perez, Shutzer is one of the faculty conveners of the Berkeley Workshop on Environmental History, based in UC Berkeley's Department of History. events.title: The Significance of Postcolonial Fascism in Cold War Korea
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Sungik Yang (Arizona State University) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: The years after Korea's independence from Japanese colonial rule in 1945 were a time of extreme crisis that opened a space for fascist ideologies and discourses to gain ascendancy. In response to national division and political polarization and violence, there arose a heavily nationalist ruling discourse that openly promoted the supremacy of the homogeneous ethnic nation above all competing forms of identity while rejecting core tenets of Western liberalism, containing strong parallels with fascist ideologies in Europe and Japan. Furthermore, this hegemonic discourse pervaded Korean political culture for decades, helping to prop up authoritarian regimes in the country until the 1980s. This discourse, which I call "transcendent nationalism," was a product of the intersection of Korea's postcolonial and Cold War conditions. It sought to overcome Cold War divisions through an embrace of the Korean nation while maintaining colonial-era suspicions of Western capitalist modernity. Ultimately, the fascistic aspects of South Korea's post-1945 political culture reveals the liminal position that Koreans found themselves in during the Cold War, being pulled into the U.S.'s anticommunist orbit but expressing discomfort with American political and cultural hegemony. In addition, postcolonial Korea emerges as an intriguing case study to better understand the nature of fascism as a political discourse promoting an alternative form of modernity that rejected those of capitalist liberalism and communism. By analyzing how fascism took root in a postcolonial nation-state after World War II, we can also gain an understanding of fascism's enduring appeal in global politics even today. Speaker Bio: Sungik Yang is an assistant professor of history at Arizona State University. He is a political and intellectual historian of modern Korea, focusing on political ideology, nationalism, democracy, and historical memory. His forthcoming book is titled Nation Transcendent: Postcolonial Fascism in Cold War Korea.

events.title: Glenn T. Seaborg Memorial Lectures in Inorganic Chemistry
events.description: Erwin Reisner, Professor of Energy and Sustainability, University of CambridgeSolar Chemical TechnologiesInspired by the blueprint of photosynthesis, creating synthetic systems for the direct conversion of sunlight into sustainable fuels has long been a defining ambition of chemistry. While decades of research have been spent on developing solar water splitting catalysts to produce green hydrogen, recently a new generation of photosynthesis-inspired architectures capable of directly converting sunlight, carbon dioxide and carbon waste streams has emerged. This advance has been made possible by developing and integrating metal complex and biological catalysts with semiconductor materials and electrodes, together with the engineering of bespoke devices. This lecture will first introduce functional mimics of photosynthesis, which couple semiconductor light absorbers with immobilised (bio)catalysts to achieve solar-driven carbon dioxide fixation alongside water oxidation to oxygen. Next, an alternative strategy will be presented that replaces the challenging water oxidation reaction by the oxidation of waste biomass and plastics. This concept, termed solar reforming, simultaneously improves reaction thermodynamics, enhances overall rate of catalysis, and creates economic value through oxidative valorisation while simultaneously generating clean fuel. The ongoing demonstration of outdoor solar plastic reforming at the kilogram and square-metre scale illustrates the growing potential of this approach as a practical route towards circular solar-powered manufacturing. The lecture will close by giving an overview of emerging frontiers in integrated solar chemistry, including atmospheric CO₂ utilisation, advanced light-management strategies, and solar-powered cascade catalysis for selective chemical organic synthesis. Together, this presentation aims to provide a compelling vision for a new generation of solar technologies that combine carbon capture, plastic and biomass waste valorisation, and renewable chemical manufacturing in integrated, scalable systems. More information: https://www-reisner.ch.cam.ac.uk/

events.title: Critical Conversations: Transforming the Field of Black Studies with Selina Makana
events.description: Materialist Nationalism: Challenging the Heroic Masculinist Rendering of the Nation Nation building exists in an uneasy and fraught relationship with women. On the one hand, nations revere women for their social reproductive labor. In twentieth-century Africa, nationalist movements deployed the figure of "Mama Africa" to galvanize the masses for the fight for independence. On the other hand, women and girl women's bodies were used as battlefields in wars and political repression in the colonial and postcolonial period, albeit in different ways. This lecture focuses on Selina Makana's new book, Beyond the Battlefield: Women and the Nation in Twentieth-Century Angola (https://www.ohioswallow.com/9780821426739/beyond-the-battlefield/), to examine the meanings and complexities of Angolan women's lived experience of war and militarism and reveal the extraordinary means by which they contend with and contest the politics of the nation. Selina Makana is an Assistant Professor of African history at the University of Memphis. Her research and teaching interests focus on African history, gender and militarism, and African diaspora studies. Her first monograph, Beyond the Battlefield: Women and the Nation in Twentieth-Century Angola (Ohio University Press, 2026), probes the relationship between women, war, and nationalist politics in Angola. She is currently working on her second book project Paranoia and Pathology in the Colony: Hygiene, Health, and Colonial Governance in Early Twentieth-Century Angola, that examines the entwined histories of public health and colonial governance in Angola. She has published articles in Meridians: Feminism, Race, Transnationalism; Gender and History; and The Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African Women's History.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Jared Shaw, Professor, UC DavisStereoselective Synthesis with Rhodium Carbenes and NitrenesLow-valent reactive intermediates of carbon and nitrogen—namely, transition-metal complexes of carbenes and nitrenes—display diverse and powerful reactivity in the synthesis of complex organic molecules. Our group has focused on rhodium carbene complexes derived from substrates that lack electron-withdrawing groups. The diminished electrophilicity of these intermediates imparts exceptional functional group tolerance, enabling the construction of architecturally complex organic frameworks. The development of new methods and their application to the synthesis of a variety of heterocycles, including several natural products, will be presented. In parallel, analogous transformations involving rhodium nitrenes have been employed to generate complex heterocycles. The discovery of the first five-membered aromatic heterocycles featuring point chirality within the ring will be described, along with discussion of their distinctive structural characteristics.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Yuan T. Lee Lecture in Physical Chemistry
events.description: Toshi Suzuki, Professor, Kyoto UniversityReaction Dynamics in Solution Probed by Ultrafast PhotoemissionChemical reaction dynamics in aqueous solution have traditionally been studied using optical methods such as absorption, emission, and scattering spectroscopy. In this talk, I will describe our efforts to follow chemical reactions in solution in real time by detecting photoelectrons emitted from the surface of an aqueous solution—that is, by exploiting the photoelectric effect. At first glance, such measurements might appear to provide information only on processes occurring at the liquid surface. In practice, however, they also yield important insights into chemical reactions taking place in the bulk liquid. Furthermore, by combining photoelectron spectroscopy with infrared spectroscopy in a complementary manner, it becomes possible to track both changes in electronic states and accompanying changes in molecular structure. I will illustrate this approach mainly through examples involving nucleobases.

events.title: Indranil Chakravarty | The Power of Intercultural Dialogue: Octavio Paz between Mexico and India
events.description: A talk by Indranil Chakravarty (https://indrachakra.com/), film historian, screenwriter, and author, based on his new book, The Tree Within: Octavio Paz's Years in India (https://0235947a.streak-link.com/C3VGHy6fX8I10Qk1JABJW9Rn/https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.com%2FTree-Within-Mexican-Laureate-Octavio%2Fdp%2F0143471651%2F%3F_encoding%3DUTF8%26pd_rd_w%3DF95xZ%26content-id%3Damzn1.sym.4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%253Aamzn1.symc.5a16118f-86f0-44cd-8e3e-6c5f82df43d0%26pf_rd_p%3D4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%26pf_rd_r%3DVR6CA1607Z5S9X17FJWB%26pd_rd_wg%3Dvlupw%26pd_rd_r%3D12aba704-4be6-41aa-b6f0-8da866b68464%26ref_%3Dpd_hp_d_atf_ci_mcx_mr_ca_hp_atf_d), that explores how Octavio Paz's years as Mexico's ambassador to India transformed his personal life, poetry, philosophy, and understanding of cultural exchange.Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor of Global Modern Art and South and Southeast Asian Art, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley.The Tree Within (https://www.amazon.com/Tree-Within-Mexican-Laureate-Octavio/dp/0143471651/?_encoding=UTF8&pd_rd_w=F95xZ&content-id=amzn1.sym.4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%3Aamzn1.symc.5a16118f-86f0-44cd-8e3e-6c5f82df43d0&pf_rd_p=4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631&pf_rd_r=VR6CA1607Z5S9X17FJWB&pd_rd_wg=vlupw&pd_rd_r=12aba704-4be6-41aa-b6f0-8da866b68464&ref_=pd_hp_d_atf_ci_mcx_mr_ca_hp_atf_d) is the enchanting story of Octavio Paz's passionate love-affair with India where he served as Mexico's ambassador in the 1960s. Immersing himself in the country's rich cultural life and contemplative traditions, Paz travelled widely, forged deep friendships with some of India's finest minds, and produced several of his most inspired poetry and essays. It was here that he met the love of his life and experienced what he called his 'second birth'. In this richly textured and erudite work, Chakravarty reconstructs the inner journey of the poet by delving into multilingual archives, declassified diplomatic files, personal letters, and intimate interviews. Blending biography, cultural history, and literary criticism, The Tree Within is a luminous testament to the enduring alchemy between India and the world through one of the greatest writers of the 20th century.Indranil Chakravarty (https://indrachakra.com/) has taught film history and screenwriting over two decades at film institutes in India and abroad, and has made several documentaries. He studied at Presidency College (Calcutta), Escuela Internacional de Cine y TV (EICTV) in Havana, and earned PhD from Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand. He has published extensively in international research journals about biopics, literary biography and cosmopolitanism. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Diana Martinez
events.description: During US colonial rule in the Philippines, reinforced concrete was used to the near exclusion of all other building materials. In Concrete Colonialism (Duke, 2025), Diana Martinez (Architecture) examines the motivations for and lasting effects of this forgotten colonial policy. Arguing that the pervasive use of reinforced concrete revolutionized techniques of imperial conquest, Martinez shows how concrete reshaped colonialism as a project that sought durable change through the reformation of environments, colonial society, and racialized biologies. Martinez locates the origins of this material revolution in the development of Chicago, highlighting how building this urban center atop exceptionally challenging geology made it possible to transform diverse global ecologies. She details how the material's stability, plasticity, strength, and other qualities served the shifting imperatives of the US colonial regime, playing a central role in defending territory, controlling disease, and constructing monuments to nation and empire. By describing a world irreversibly remade, Martinez urges readers to consider how colonialism persists — in concrete forms — despite claims of its conclusion. Martinez is joined by Matthew Shutzer (History). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: PMB Seminar with Gautam Dantas | Understanding, Predicting, and Remediating Perturbations to Host-Microbe Interactions
events.description: Antibiotics can acutely and persistently compromise microbiome stability and resilience, enabling enhanced colonization of pathogenic microbes, and loss of host-beneficial functions from depleted commensals. We interrogate resistome, taxonomic, and functional dynamics of microbiota of humans, animals, soils, and built-environments via high-throughput functional metagenomic selections, whole metagenome and transcriptome sequencing, and isolate phenotyping and whole genome sequencing. We use these datasets to model and predict the impact of various biotic and abiotic perturbations on the transmission and evolutionary dynamics of diverse microbiomes and their resistomes across time and habitats, through application of generalized linear mixed models and machine learning algorithms. By integrating community-level analyses of microbiome perturbation and response, with mechanistic analyses of novel microbial resilience functions, we are improving the accuracy and sensitivity of genomics-based methods for diagnosing and treating pathogens and their resistance properties in the clinic and maintaining or rescuing healthy microbiome states.

events.title: Cheyenne Tretter: Private Arms, Public Consequences: Rethinking Arms Competition and War in the Age of U.S. Defense Industry Privatization
events.description: Events Add to Calendar iCal / Outlook The post-Cold War transformation of the U.S. defense industry has fundamentally altered the dynamics of global arms competition and the connection between arms racing and the risk of war. Cheyenne Tretter argues that increasing levels of privatization have transformed U.S. arms production by shifting arms racing from an episodic to a continuous phenomenon, and that this shift increases the risk of war by creating information problems that hinder adversaries’ ability to assess each other’s capabilities and intentions. To evaluate this argument, Tretter constructs a large-N dataset of U.S. weapons systems from 1900 to the present, with each system coded by domain, level of private involvement, and whether its development or modernization was initiated during a period of heightened tensions or relative peace. This dataset demonstrates a structural break: pre-1991 arms development clustered around crises and intense rivalries, whereas post-1991 development occurs continuously. Complementing this, qualitative case studies of Cold War missile racing, Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and U.S.–China competition in the Taiwan Strait test whether privatization increases the likelihood of war initiation, and further examine how privatization influences wartime adaptation.

events.title: Time as Space
events.description: This lecture is part of the Howison Lectures in Philosophy series hosted by the Graduate Division. About this Lecture Augustine says, in Book 11 of his Confessions: "What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to him who asks, I know not." He never says anything like that about space. Nobody ever says anything like that about space. And (indeed) the thought that there is something infinitely deeper and more mysterious about the question of time than there is about the question of space is all over the place in the history of western philosophy. And all of this suggests that an understanding of time as space, or as somehow reducible to space, or as somehow emerging from space, might represent a significant advance in our understanding of the world. And I want to argue here that an offhand remark at the end of an old paper by D. C. Williams – a remark that gestures in the direction of a far more radical and less familiar version of what is often referred to as the "spatialization" of time in the modern physical project – contains the kernel of an understanding like that.About David Z. AlbertDavid Z Albert is the Fredrick E. Woodbridge Professor of Philosophy at Columbia University in New York City. He has written extensively on various issues at the foundations of physics – particularly on the foundations of quantum mechanics and the direction of time. He received his Ph.D. in theoretical physics from the Rockefeller University in 1981, and his books include Quantum Mechanics and Experience, Time and Chance, After Physics, and A Guess at the Riddle. He is currently at work on a book about relationalism.

events.title: Aaron Gitler: Granulin loss and TMEM106B risk converge on lysosomal C-terminal fragment pathology in frontotemporal dementia
events.description: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is the second most common cause of dementia after Alzheimer disease. Mutations in GRN, which encodes progranulin, are a major cause of FTD. Common genetic variants in the TMEM106B gene modify risk of FTD and the effect is especially strong in GRN mutation carriers. Intriguingly, in GRN mutation carriers, being homozygous for the protective TMEM106B haplotype seems to confer near lifetime protection against FTD. Despite the strong genetic link between GRN and TMEM106B, how these two genes interact mechanistically has remained unresolved. Recent studies have revealed that a C-terminal fragment of TMEM106B forms amyloid fibrils and accumulates in the brains of older individuals and patients with neurodegenerative disorders, including FTD. How the production of this fragment connects to granulin deficiency is also unknown. Using lysosome immunoprecipitation, we show that granulin deficiency drives the accumulation of the TMEM106B C-terminal fragment within lysosomes in Grn-knockout mice and GRN-null human iPSC-derived neurons. Recombinant progranulin supplementation reduced TMEM106B C-terminal fragment accumulation. Isogenic neurons carrying the TMEM106B risk allele displayed allele-dose-dependent fragment accumulation that was reversible by progranulin. Structural and genetic analyses demonstrated that TMEM106B dimerization stabilizes the protein and limits C-terminal fragment formation. These findings define a lysosomal pathway linking granulin deficiency to TMEM106B C-terminal fragment accumulation and explain how protective TMEM106B alleles can confer resistance to FTD, even for GRN mutation carriers.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: The neural basis of cuttlefish camouflage and social behavior
events.description: All animals form internal neural representations of the external world that guide their behavior. Cuttlefish, coleoid cephalopods related to octopus and squid, perform visually driven adaptive camouflage by dynamically altering the color, pattern, and texture of their skin to create an approximation of their surroundings – a process directly controlled by the brain. Thus, cuttlefish perform a remarkable sensorimotor transformation: they recreate what they see on their skin, generating a motor output that approximates the sensory input itself. In addition to camouflage, cuttlefish use their dynamic skin to communicate with conspecifics using a series of innate skin patterns that reveal the animal's internal state. We are using the cuttlefish skin behaviors to understand how the physical properties of the visual world are represented by patterns of neural activity in the brain, and how this representation is transformed into an approximation of the physical world on the skin. We have performed a series of experiments to develop the dwarf cuttlefish, Ascarosepion bandense, as a model to investigate the neural basis of camouflage and social communication. We have sequenced the genome, developed gene editing techniques, completed a 3D brain atlas, developed camouflage and social behavior paradigms, examined dwarf cuttlefish behavior in the wild, and adapted miniscopes for underwater imaging. Furthermore, we recently succeeded in generating transgenic cuttlefish that express genetically-encoded calcium indicators in the brain, permitting the live imaging of neural activity. We are now using these technologies to simultaneously record neural activity and measure behavior to uncover how visual information is deconstructed in the brain, and then reconstructed into an image of the physical world on the skin.

events.title: Magdalena Ugarte: Rethinking the Normative — Settler State Planning, Indigenous Law, and Grounded Legal Pluralism | City & Regional Planning Lecture
events.description: Planning theory widely acknowledges that planning is inherently normative. Yet Western values, ethical frameworks, and visions for the future continue to shape everyday planning practice. The deep connection between planning and Western law is crucial: it often labels planning practices that challenge Western definitions of property, public interest, land use, and decision-making authority as illegal. Territorial conflicts between settler nation-states and Indigenous peoples illustrate these tensions. Drawing on years of community-engaged research with Indigenous communities in Chile, Magdalena Ugarte explores these disputes as clashing legal orders. By centering Indigenous law and land relations, we can reimagine planning in settler colonial contexts — shifting from the domination of Western law to practices rooted in legal pluralism. About Magdalena Ugarte is an associate professor in the School of Urban and Regional Planning at Toronto Metropolitan University, where she teaches planning theory, public policy, social and community planning, and studio. Her work examines the relationship between planning, settler colonialism, and other forms of racialized dispossession, as well as how communities persistently excluded from planning plan for themselves. She is currently involved in collaborative, community-based research projects that focus on Indigenous planning in Chile and Black-centered, Black-informed planning practices in Canada. She is also leading curricular changes that seek to advance racial justice and Indigenous rights in planning education. This lecture is part of the Department of City & Regional Planning's fall lecture series.

events.title: Translation in the Qing Poetic Imaginary | Lecture by Nathan Vedal
events.description: This talk, introducing a forthcoming monograph (Translation, Emulation, and Manchu Literary Culture), will consider the institution of a Manchu translation program in the elite Hanlin Academy. A subset of literati at the Hanlin Academy, a training ground for officials and court scholars who passed the civil service exam at the highest level, underwent a three-year program of Manchu study culminating in a final translation exam. Knowledge of Manchu gained at the Hanlin Academy, while primarily intended for bureaucratic purposes and court scholarship, is also evident in the deployment of multilingual literary effects in Chinese poetic compositions. Within Qing literary-intellectual culture, the juxtaposition of Chinese and Manchu yielded a productive venue for literary creation and self-fashioning. Speaker Bio:Nathan Vedal is an associate professor in the Department of East Asian Studies at the University of Toronto, specializing in Chinese intellectual and cultural history. He received his undergraduate degree from the Curtis Institute of Music and his PhD in Chinese history from Harvard University. His first book, The Culture of Language in Ming China: Sound, Script, and the Redefinition of Boundaries of Knowledge (Columbia University Press, 2022), won the Morris D. Forkosch Prize from the Journal of the History of Ideas.

events.title: Munis D. Faruqui | Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold
events.description: Please join us for a special book launch celebrating Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/aurangzeb-alamgir-and-the-mughal-empire/A6421F92BBEEBA78238E75F4D636E7C0), the new work by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director of the Institute for South Asia Studies and Professor of South and Southeast Asian Studies at UC Berkeley. In this compelling reassessment, Professor Faruqui offers a fresh and nuanced account of Aurangzeb's reign, illuminating the ambitions, conflicts, and political pressures that shaped the Mughal Empire at a pivotal moment in its history. The conversation will be moderated by Abhishek Kaicker (https://history.berkeley.edu/abhishek-kaicker), Associate Professor of History at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, Oct 15, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall ————– ABOUT THE BOOKAurangzeb 'Alamgir (r. 1658–1707) was the last of the so-called 'great' Mughal emperors. He remains a controversial historical figure: castigated for religious intolerance and placed at the centre of a narrative of Mughal decline by some; considered a great Muslim hero by others. In this richly researched exploration of Aurangzeb 'Alamgir's life and times, Munis D. Faruqui contests such simplistic understandings to unearth a more nuanced picture of the emperor and his reign. Drawing on a large and varied archive, Faruqui provides new insights into the emperor's rise to power, his administrative and religious policies, and the role of the imperial eunuchate and harem. By unpicking the complex dynamics of a long reign, from Aurangzeb 'Alamgir's accession to the last weeks of his life and his eighteenth-century memorialisation, this remarkable new history cuts through the many myths that have obscured the extraordinary life story of Emperor Aurangzeb 'Alamgir. SPEAKER BIOMunis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/) is a historian and the holder of the Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies. His focus is on the Muslim experience in South Asia, especially during the Mughal period. His books include Princes of the Mughal Empire, 1504-1719 (Cambridge University Press, 2012), Expanding Frontiers in South Asian and World History, co-edited with Richard Eaton, David Gilmartin and Sunil Kumar (Cambridge University Press, 2013), and Religious Interactions in Mughal India, co-edited with Vasudha Dalmia (Oxford University Press, 2014). His most recent book is titled Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold (Cambridge University Press and Juggernaut Press, 2026). He is co-editor-in-chief, along with Ali Anooshahr, of the Journal of Mughal Studies. In 2014, Dr. Faruqui was one of three faculty recipients of UC-Berkeley's Distinguished Teaching Award. The award recognizes teaching that "incites intellectual curiosity in students, engages them thoroughly in the enterprise of learning, and has a lifelong impact." Dr. Faruqui is the current Director of both the Institute for South Asia Studies and the Global, International & Area Studies unit. In addition to the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, Dr. Faruqui is affiliated with the Department of History and the Department of Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures. events.title: Glenn T. Seaborg Memorial Lectures in Inorganic Chemistry
events.description: Erwin Reisner, Professor of Energy and Sustainability, University of CambridgeSemi-artificial Photosynthesis using Formate Dehydrogenase Semi-artificial photosynthesis interfaces biological catalysts with synthetic light absorbers to overcome the inherent limitations of both artificial and natural photosynthesis. Furthermore, this emerging approach can also unlock novel reaction pathways and chemistries with significant technological potential and thus provides new opportunities that are currently not available in solar fuels or algae research. This presentation will summarise our progress in integrating the redox enzyme formate dehydrogenase into bespoke hierarchical 3D electrode scaffolds, photoelectrodes and semiconductor powders. Specifically, formate dehydrogenase immobilised on electrodes enables catalytic CO₂ reduction to formate with electrochemical reversibility and can thus operate at very low overpotential with high selectivity. The design principles for the integration of formate dehydrogenase in bespoke synthetic 3D electrode scaffolds and a detailed analysis of the biocatalyst-material interface will be presented. The understanding of the biotic-abiotic interface ultimately allows for the rational wiring of the biocatalyst into photoelectrochemical and photocatalytic systems for the solar synthesis of fuels and chemicals. Overall, the lecture aims to demonstrate that formate dehydrogenase should be considered as unique model electrocatalyst for CO₂-to-formate conversion in solar catalysis as it enables performance currently not achievable by synthetic catalysts. A recent review on this topic is available: Liu et al., Chem. Rev., 2026, 126, 8034–8088 (https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.6c00095).

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Risk Appetite and Monetary Transmission"
events.description: Abstract: We construct a new high-frequency measure of changes in risk appetite around Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings. Fed policy actions and communication have substantial effects on risk appetite, consistent with the literature on the risk-taking channel of monetary policy. Most of the variation in asset prices and risk appetite is unexplained by conventional interest-rate surprises, which points to an important role of risk appetite in monetary transmission. Proxy SVARs with two separately-instrumented monetary policy shocks—a risk-free rate shock and a risk appetite shock—show the empirical importance of this channel. Risk appetite shocks have large, significant, and theory-consistent effects on inflation, output and employment. By contrast, the effects of risk-free rate shocks become insignificant or switch signs as soon as a risk-appetite shock is included in the VAR setup. Our evidence suggests that monetary transmission works primarily through risk asset prices and risk appetite. Standard estimation of monetary transmission based solely on interest-rate surprises misses most of these effects for two main reasons: First, the impact of interest-rate policy on asset prices is time-varying and state-dependent. Second, central bank communication can affect risk appetite and asset prices in ways that go beyond changes in the expected policy path.

events.title: Jürgen Dinkel | All remains in the Family: A History of Inheritance in the US and Europe Since 1800
events.description: Over the next 25 years, Americans will inherit more than $100 trillion. Economists anticipate a "great wealth transfer" from the Baby Boomer generation to their children and grandchildren. At the same time, this enormous wealth will be distributed extremely unevenly throughout society. While a select few will inherit vast fortunes, many will inherit little, nothing at all, or even debt. This raises questions with renewed urgency—questions that have been debated in the transatlantic world since the American and French Revolutions: Who should receive a deceased person's estate? Who counts as family? Who should decide how an estate is distributed? How can the unequal distribution of inherited wealth be justified, and how can the rights to private property and equal opportunities be reconciled? In his lecture, Jürgen Dinkel traces the history of inheritance in the US and Europe since 1800. He demonstrates how governments, families, and individuals repeatedly negotiated the transfer and distribution of estates, thereby also renegotiating kinship relations, the bonds between the individual, the family, and the state, as well as the legitimization of wealth inequalities within their societies. Ultimately, this lecture contributes to the new histories of capitalism, the family, and the state, arguing that Euro-American societies from the 19th to the 21st century are fundamentally structured around inheritance and the family. Jürgen Dinkel is Professor of Modern and Global History at the University of Leipzig. His research focuses on the history of colonialism and decolonization, the Global South in World Politics, and European social history. His most recent publications include: Acknowledgments: The History of Academic Gratitude, in Bulletin of the German Historical Institute, Washington D.C. 76 (Fall 2025); "'The Rich Uncle from America': Transnational Inheritance Transfers between the United States, Germany, and Russia, 1840s–1980s," Law and History Review (2025); and "The Non-Aligned Movement: The Role of Diplomacy in Third-worldism and the Global South," in Oxford Handbook on the History of the Global South (Oxford UP, 2025). events.title: PMB Seminar with Adam Steinbrenner | Seeing like a plant: immune recognition and signaling by cell surface receptors
events.description: Plants sense extracellular cues through several hundred cell surface receptors. The most rapidly evolving group of receptors is the leucine-rich repeat receptor-like proteins (RLPs), which transduce immune signals as a bipartite receptor complex with the adapter SOBIR1. In recent years many new examples of immunogenic patterns detected by specific RLPs have been described, highlighting their versatility as immune sensing modules. I will discuss unique features of the RLP family that mediate recognition and signaling functions. For recognition, RLPs encode an extracellular island domain, which allosterically couples ligand binding to co-receptor recruitment. For signaling, RLPs lack a kinase domain typical of most receptors, but the short cytoplasmic tail domain can encode signaling through different defense pathways. For both recognition and signaling functions, I will describe new insights from our study of Inceptin Receptor (INR), which detects caterpillar-derived peptide elicitors and evolved 28 mya in a single subtribe of legumes. Since both island and tail domains are small (~10-60 aa) shared features of all RLPs, they may represent modular, editable handles to engineer plant immune systems.
