events.title: Esha Niyogi De | Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia
events.description: A talk by Esha Niyogi De (https://wp.ucla.edu/person/esha-niyogi-de/), Senior Lecturer in UCLA's Writing Programs, on her new book, Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia (https://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/?id=p088285) (University of Illinois Press, December 2024). The book uncovers the overlooked histories of women who worked as producers, directors, performers, and "star-authors" across the film industries of India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. De examines how these women used stardom, collaboration, and creative labor to cross geographic, institutional, and gendered boundaries, claim greater authority over filmmaking, and challenge the structures that often obscured their contributions to South Asian cinema. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies, UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Thu, November 19, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOK This book talk delves into previously submerged histories and hidden voices of women directors and film entrepreneurs from Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India. Drawing on neglected archives and rare field interviews with filmmakers and fans, Esha tells a comparative story of women's creative authority and entrepreneurial labor in selected film industries of South Asia��industries and markets that share languages, arts, and geopolitical rifts. Using "transborder" to refer not only to territorial borders but also to institutional and conceptual ones, her story dwells on two eras of women's cinema in this postcolonial region. In the era of the "star-authors" (50s-90s), female stars in Dhaka, Lahore, and Kolkata perform personas ambiguously to access infrastructures and direct fiction films that breach sexual and national borders. In the era of the "woman director" (2000s), even though opportunities appear to burgeon across the region, women negotiate transnational borders that take less obvious forms of brand-making and censorship. The talk will include rare footage from fiction films made by Kohinoor Akhtar Suchanda, Babita, Nargis Akhter (Bangladesh), Shamim Ara (Pakistan), and Kanan Devi (India). SPEAKER BIOEsha Niyogi De (https://wp.ucla.edu/person/esha-niyogi-de/)'s research interests lie in South Asian gender politics, film and performance history, and literary history. She is the author of two monographs, a recent study of women's cinemas in selected film industries of Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India titled Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia (University of Illinois Press, 2024), and an earlier book on sexual politics and postcoloniality in literature, cinema, and choreography in the Bengal region titled Empire, Media, and the Autonomous Woman: A Feminist Critique of Postcolonial Thought (Oxford University Press, 2011). Other publications include two co-edited books, from University of Washington Press and Duke University Press, and many articles. She is working on two new book projects. The first, a study of the renowned Pakistani actress-singer and film director Noor Jehan in relation to Muslim nationalist arts in the mid-twentieth century, is titled Recasting Noor Jehan:Melody Queen, Film Pioneer, and the Making of National Cultures in South Asia (co-authored with Gwendolyn Sarah Kirk). The second, a comparative study of gendered choreographies of protest in twentieth century avant-garde and industrial films, made by Zahir Raihan, Satyajit Ray, Rangeela, among others, is tentatively titled Moving Bodies Out of Line: Filmic Choreographies, Protest Movements, and Queerness in South Asian Cinemas. Esha is a Senior Lecturer in the Division of Writing Programs at UCLA and a Faculty Affiliate of the UCLA Center for India and South Asia.EVENT POSTER TBA _____________ Established in 2013 with a generous gift from the Subir & Malini Chowdhury Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subir_Chowdhury), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (https://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/) at UC Berkeley champions the study of Bangladesh's cultures, peoples and history. The first of its kind in the US, the Center's mission is to create an innovative model combining research, scholarships, the promotion of art and culture, and the building of ties between institutions in Bangladesh and the University of California. events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Amy Weeks, Assistant Professor, University of Wisconsin, MadisonNew enzyme chemistry to decipher post-translational modification function Spatial organization and temporal dynamics are essential properties of cellular signaling. Post-translational modifications (PTMs) to proteins relay biological signals by exerting precise spatiotemporal control over protein function, localization, and lifetime. A systems-level experimental map of post-translationally modified proteins across subcellular space and time would transform our understanding of how PTMs orchestrate complex cellular functions in response to biological stimuli. However, such a map is inaccessible with current technologies. To meet this challenge, the Weeks lab is focused on developing new chemical and enzymatic tools for PTM proteomics with subcellular spatial and temporal resolution. We develop chemical probes and genetically targetable, PTM-selective proximity labeling enzymes to covalently tag post-translationally modified proteins in specific subcellular locations, enabling their enrichment and analysis with mass spectrometry-based proteomics experiments. We focus on two pervasive PTMs, proteolysis and phosphorylation, both of which play critical roles in myriad biological signaling pathways relevant to human health and disease. Our technologies are broadly applicable to a wide variety of protease and kinase signaling pathways and provide an integrated view of cellular signaling with implications for both fundamental biological discovery and therapeutic innovation.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.description: CRG Forum SeriesBook TalkEvery Man’s Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern ConservatismwithJulia Bowes, Lecturer in gender history at the University of Melbourne, and author of Every Man's Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism (Princeton University Press, 2026) Dr. JuliaBowes is a lecturer in gender history at the University of Melbourne, where her research focuses on the relationship between gender, the family, and conservatism in the United States. Her first book, Every Man's Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism (Princeton University Press, 2026), examines how a sovereign conception of the white patriarchal family was at the crux of an emerging conservative ideology opposed to the modern liberal state. The book is an extended version of her dissertation, which was awarded the 2019 Lerner-Scott Prize for the best dissertation in US women's history by the Organization of American Historians. She has held fellowships from the Jefferson Scholars Foundation, the Institute of Citizens and Scholars (formerly the Woodrow Wilson Institute), and, prior to joining the University of Melbourne, was an assistant professor at the University of Hong Kong. She is now researching a project on the gendered politics of alternative health movements, including anti-vaccination, anti-fluoridation, and home birth movements, in the twentieth-century United States. *If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) to fully participate in this event, please contact Ariana Ceja at centerrg@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Importing Aggregate Demand"
events.description: Abstract: How exposed are open economies to global demand shocks? In equilibrium, foreign booms can be absorbed either by domestic consumption ("quantities") or by real exchange rate appreciation ("prices"). We show that failures of Ricardian equivalence and global financial market imperfections, two frictions popular in much recent work, have opposite effects on the split: while elevated marginal propensities to consume push towards quantities, financial frictions instead increase price adjustment. As the flexible-price equilibrium generally features a mix of quantity and price responses, policy needs to be contractionary to achieve flexible-price outcomes if the spending effect dominates, and vice-versa if financial frictions are severe. In our quantitative explorations the spending effect tends to win the race, necessitating aggressive domestic policy action.

events.title: Book Talk: An Anticolonial Development: Race, Schooling, and Emancipation in Twentieth-Century West Africa
events.description: Book Talk:An Anticolonial Development: Race, Schooling, and Emancipation in Twentieth-Century West Africa (Cambridge University Press, 2026) In what measure could education be an agent of African freedom? Combining histories of race, economics, and education, Elisa Prosperetti examines this question in two West African contexts, Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, from the 1890s to the 1980s. She argues that a Black Atlantic perspective changes how we see decolonization and development in West Africa, by revealing schooling's essential role in aspirations of African emancipation. Rejecting colonial exploitation of the African body, proponents of anticolonial development instead claimed the mind as the site of economic productivity for African people. An Anticolonial Development shows how, in the middle of the twentieth century, Africans proposed an original understanding of development that fused antiracism to economic theory, and human dignity to material productivity. Elisa Prosperetti is an Assistant Professor of History at the National Institute of Education/Nanyang Technological University, Singapore. She is a historian of modern African and global history, specializing in histories of race, development, education, and decolonization, with a geographic focus on West Africa and the Black Atlantic world. She received her PhD in History from Princeton University in 2020, and currently serves on the Editorial Review Board of the African Studies Review and as a podcast host for the African Studies channel of the New Books Network.

events.title: PMB Seminar with Vivian Irish | Thorny questions: citrus development and disease
events.description: Thorns are plant defensive structures that arise from axillary shoot apical meristems that proliferate for a time and then terminally differentiate into a sharp hard tip. Like other meristems, thorn meristems contain stem cells but, in the case of thorns, these stem cells undergo a programmed cessation of proliferative activity. Using citrus as a model system to examine this unusual form of stem cell regulation, we have characterized a transcriptional gene network necessary for thorn development. Not only has this work illuminated some of the molecular mechanisms controlling plant stem cell activity, but the methods we have developed have allowed us to tackle some of the challenges facing citrus agriculture today.

events.title: 2026 Berkeley Bioengineering Distinguished Lecture with Clifford Brangwynne, PhD
events.description: Fluid Machinery: The Nucleolus, Ribosomes, and Aging Abstract: Research combining insights from materials physics and cell biology has ushered in a new paradigm for understanding how the chaotic intracellular environment is brought to order, through the collective condensation of biomolecules into droplets of living information. In this talk, I will present an overview of these principles and ongoing work in this field, with a particular emphasis on the interplay between liquid-like condensates and traditional biomolecular machines, such as the ribosome, which forms through a complex assembly process in the multiphase nucleolus. Our lab has recently developed a set of tools to probe and engineer the nucleolus and the production of ribosomes, as well as their cytoplasmic function in protein translation. These studies are yielding new insights into how assembled ribosomes function in space and time, and how ribosomes can become dysregulated by molecular and organismal aging.

events.title: Reactionary Politics in South Korea: Historical Legacies, Far-Right Intellectuals, and Political Mobilization
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Myungji Yang (University of Hawai'i, Mānoa) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: The rise of the illiberal, far-right politics threatens democratic system throughout the world. The South Korean president Yoon Seok-yeol's martial law declaration in December 2024 stunned the world. More puzzling is that Yoon's insurrection unexpectedly gained substantial support from the ruling right-wing party and ordinary citizens. Why do ordinary citizens support authoritarian leaders and martial law in a democratic country? What draws these citizens to extreme actions and ideas? Through eighteen months of field research and drawing from rich qualitative data, this talk will provide an in-depth account of the ideas and practices of the far-right groups and organizations, and help to understand the roots of current democratic regression. Speaker Bio: Myungji Yang is Professor of Sociology at the University of Hawai'i-Mānoa. A political sociologist and social movement scholar, she is interested in the issues of power, inequality, civil society and democracy. Her research has appeared in Nations and Nationalism, Politics and Society, Mobilization: An International Inquiry, Urban Studies, and Sociological Inquiry, among other venues. She is the author of two books, From Miracle to Mirage (2018, Cornell University Press) and Reactionary Politics in South Korea: Historical Legacies, Far-Right Intellectuals, and Political Mobilization (2026, Cambridge University Press). She is currently developing a research project on young men's radicalization and anti-feminist politics.

events.title: Rhiju Das: "De novo design of RNA with deep learning"
events.description: RNA design has long been limited by the accuracy of RNA structure prediction. I will describe how the video game Eterna has elicited modeling and design tools for previously intractable pseudoknotted folds, multi-state sensors for disease states, and polymerase ribozymes that copy RNA. AI teams now work alongside Eterna players, and both are scored by prospective high-throughput experiments. Under that pressure, RNA design is improving quickly.

events.title: Lunch Poems: Bianca Stone
events.description: Lunch Poems (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/lunch-poems), Berkeley's storied noontime poetry series, welcomes Bianca Stone. Bianca Stone is the author of four collections of poetry. Her three most recent, all from Tin House Books, are The Near and Distant World (2026); What Is Otherwise Infinite (2022), winner of the 2022 Vermont Book Award; and The Möbius Strip Club of Grief (2018). Her work has appeared widely in such magazines as The New Yorker, The Atlantic, and Poetry. She is a visiting lecturer in poetry at Dartmouth College and teaches classes on poetry and poetic study at the Ruth Stone House in Goshen, Vermont, where she hosts the Ode & Psyche Podcast. Stone is currently serving as the poet laureate of Vermont (2024-28). The Lunch Poems series, founded by Professor Robert Hass, is supported by Dr. and Mrs. Tom Colby, the UC Berkeley Library, the Morrison Library Fund, the UC Berkeley English Department, and the Deans' Office of the College of Letters & Science. For more information or to be added to the Lunch Poems mailing list, please email poems-library@berkeley.edu (mailto:poems-library@berkeley.edu) or follow @PoemsLunch on Instagram (http://instagram.com/poemslunch) and X (https://twitter.com/PoemsLunch).
